results.estimate: EDE: VA -.633 (ns), vulnerable -1.755, agricultural -1.139, self-employment -1.848; advanced: 7.422, .032, .148, -.755 (all ns)
results.evidence: Tables 6-7, pp.16-17; text p.15: 'impact is insignificant for all measures for the advanced group'. Coefficient is conditional on interaction terms.

heterogeneity.finding: Positive moderating effect of ICT capital deepening levels on informality's drag appears in emerging and developing economies (.12-.21) and is absent in advanced economies, where the level interaction is insignificant and the growth interaction is negative in two models. Informality's own effect is negative and significant only in emerging and developing economies.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 6-7, pp.16-17; text p.17: 'positive interaction effect of ICT appears to be unique to the emerging & developing economy sample'

heterogeneity.finding: Results depend on the informality proxy: employment-based proxies (vulnerable, self-employed, agricultural share) give significant main effects and level interactions; informal value-added share gives null or wrong-signed results throughout.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 4-6; text p.15: 'the value added measure also gains a negative, albeit insignificant, coefficient'

heterogeneity.finding: Direct effect of ICT capital deepening growth is larger in advanced (.055-.065) than in global or emerging and developing samples (about .02-.04); author cites this as consistent with higher ICT returns in richer countries.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 7 vs Table 6, p.15-17; text p.15: 'coefficient of ICT capital deepening growth is slightly higher in the advanced economies sample'

income_group_results.high: Advanced economies (38; grouping is Conference Board, not World Bank income): informality has no significant effect; ICT capital growth positive direct effect (.055-.065, p<.05); interaction with ICT capital growth negative in two models; ICT level interaction insignificant; internet interaction positive only in agricultural model (p<.10).
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (pooled within emerging and developing group of 80 economies, which also includes high-income Gulf states)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately (pooled within emerging and developing group)
income_group_results.low: not reported separately (pooled within emerging and developing group; author notes low-income countries likely dominate the group results)

n_specifications_reported: 24 regression models in main tables and appendix (6 tables x 4 informality proxies), plus an unreported lagged-ICT-level variant (footnote 18) and growth-accounting decomposition

confounding_reverse_causation.why: No instrument or event timing. Author argues first differences mitigate reverse causality (footnote 9) but concedes no suitable instrument for informality; ICT capital deepening and internet use are plausibly endogenous to productivity and informality. Conclusions use causal language ('ICT investment ... can help reduce the negative impact of informality').
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Footnote 9, p.6; Section 6, p.18

exposure_measurement.why: ICT capital services rely on US hedonic deflators adjusted by domestic inflation and a steady-state initial stock, so cross-country measurement error is likely; internet penetration captures mostly consumer use (author's own point). Informality proxies are weak (modelled value-added share; self-employment, vulnerable employment and agricultural share are indirect). Author notes the macro measures do not show ICT adoption within the informal sector.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.3-3.5 pp.7-8, footnote 13 p.7; Section 6 p.18: 'we implicitly assume that the informal sector is gradually incorporating ICT'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 118 of 131 TED countries retained; 13 dropped for missing data and 11 begin late (unbalanced panel). Data-poor and fragile economies likely under-represented. Author notes the advanced / emerging split is not income-based, and EDE group mixes Gulf high-income and low-income countries.

outcome_measurement.why: Labour productivity is GDP (PPP) per person engaged, not per hour; labour quality is partly econometrically imputed; TED data for developing countries rely on national accounts of uneven quality. Well-established source overall.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1-3.2, pp.7; footnote 6 p.5; footnote 17 p.13

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four informality proxies x three ICT moderators (growth, level, internet) x three samples; ICT level and its interaction added after referee suggestion; dummy-informality variant and unreported lagged-level variant. Interaction significance at p<.10 only, with many tests and no multiple-testing adjustment. Models in growth rates with country FE as well as year FE (author acknowledges FE are redundant in first differences). Signs and significance change with proxy.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 2.2, pp.5-6 and footnote 8; Tables 5-7; footnotes 18 and 20, pp.15,17

selective_reporting.why: All main tables show full coefficient sets, including null results, and the abstract says evidence is 'some' and 'modest'. However the lagged-level results (footnote 18) are not reported, the conclusion foregrounds the significant level interactions in employment-based models, and the VA-based null results and negative advanced-economy interactions are given little weight in the conclusions.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract p.1; footnote 18 p.15; Section 6, p.18

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Included for family 1 (labour productivity growth); the study's primary question is a moderation effect of ICT on informality's drag, not the average effect of ICT, so direct ICT coefficients are conditional on interaction terms. Significance stars are at 10 percent for most key interaction results (author's table note: *p<.1). Internal inconsistencies noted: observations are 2411 in Table 4 but 2374 in Tables 5-7 and in the Table 2 note (791 + 1583 = 2374); text refers to 'equation (10)' for the perpetual inventory formula which is equation (5); footnote 9 says informality measures are 'four' while the text says 'three different indicators' in Section 3.5; Table 7 coefficient layout is garbled in the text extraction (row labels misaligned with coefficients) so Table 7 values for non-ICT capital, employment, labour quality, internet, institutions and trade were not used. Text states Table 6 effect range 0.12-0.2, which matches the table. The Table 5 text says level effect negative and significant in 'all' employment models but the self-employment model is only p<.10. No instruction-like content in the paper text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: 118 economies (38 advanced, 80 emerging/developing), 1997-2017, own FE estimation with informality x ICT interactions; ICT capital deepening and internet penetration are exposures (ICT also acts as moderator); outcome is aggregate labour productivity growth; explicit advanced vs emerging/developing comparison. All criteria met.

sample_corrections.economies_or_groups: Record is correct (38 advanced + 80 EDE, 13 TED countries dropped, 11 start later). Note: the later-start list also includes Bangladesh, Cameroon, Cambodia, Chad (1998), Kyrgyz Rep. (1999), Tajikistan (2000), Angola (2001), UAE (2002).
sample_corrections.n_economies: 118 (confirmed); observations 2411 in Table 4, 2374 in Tables 5 and A1, 1583 EDE, 791 advanced.

corrections.correction: Advanced sample: ΔINT is positive and significant in all three employment-share models (.031* SE .016; .038** SE .017; .03* SE .016), not two; only the VA model is null (-.001, SE .025). Global/EDE SEs range .021-.038, not up to .042 (.042 does not appear). Table 7 text is misaligned in the PDF extraction, so the advanced row assignment rests on the order of values (ΔINT SE row (.025)(.016)(.017)(.016)).

second_pass.problems: Numbers match tables except result 7. Possible mislabel in the paper that the record does not flag: the dummy ΔINF D is described as 1 for declines in informality yet its coefficients are negative (-4.8, -3.3, -5.3), the same sign as continuous ΔINF, suggesting the coding is reversed or the note is wrong; interpretation of the 'stronger moderation' robustness (Tables A1-A2, fn 20) is therefore uncertain. Record states exposure as 'ICT capital services per worker'; the level variable ln kIT is described as ICT capital stock per worker (Fig. 3, Eq. 2), so exposure definition is slightly mixed. Record says the author 'argues first differences mitigate reverse causality (fn 9)': correct.

title: Economic growth and the proliferation of ICT infrastructures: which causes the other?
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (Dumitrescu-Hurlin Granger causality, cointegration tests) of an ICT index (mobile, broadband, internet) against GDP per capita in about 41-42 Sub-Saharan African economies. Meets exposure, sample (at least 10 economies) and output outcome criteria.
technology: ICT in general (composite index of mobile subscriptions, fixed broadband, internet users)
exposure_measure: ICT index = first principal component (82% of variance) of log fixed broadband subscriptions, log internet users and log mobile cellular subscriptions (all per 100 people), from World Development Indicators.

sample.n_economies: 41 or 42 (text states both: 'Cover 41 Sub-Saharan African economies' in Section 3.1 vs '42 African countries' in abstract and conclusion; Table 1 has 820 obs = 41 x 20)
sample.economies_or_groups: Sub-Saharan African countries (list in Appendix Table A3; the page 21 list shown is truncated in the extracted text)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (SSA; income-group breakdown not analysed or reported)

design.estimator: Pesaran CD and Friedman cross-section dependence tests; CIPS unit root; Pesaran-Yamagata slope homogeneity; Pedroni and Westerlund cointegration; Dumitrescu-Hurlin heterogeneous panel Granger non-causality test with bootstrap. Coefficients of the production function are not estimated.
design.identification: other (Granger-type predictive causality only; no instrument or exogenous variation)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Solow-type production function with log capital (gross capital formation) and log employment; country fixed effects in the DH test equation; lag length not stated in the text.

results.indicator: GDP per capita (constant 2010 US$), ICT index Granger-causing GDP per capita
results.estimate: not reported (DH W-bar = 1.90, Z-bar = -0.30; no coefficient estimated)
results.evidence: Table 7, p.13: 'LICT -> LGDP 1.90 -0.30 0.77'; text p.13: findings 'unidirectional causality relationship from growth in per capita GDP to ICT services'

results.indicator: Reverse direction: GDP per capita Granger-causing ICT index (ICT adoption as outcome of growth; relevant to reverse causality, not a payoff)
results.estimate: not reported (W-bar = 3.65, Z-bar = 4.99)

results.indicator: Capital and employment Granger-causing GDP per capita (control inputs)
results.estimate: not reported (capital W-bar 2.65; employment W-bar 2.93)
results.evidence: Table 7, p.13. Capital Z-bar is printed as 20.08, which looks like a typo (p = 0.04 is inconsistent with that value).

heterogeneity.finding: Slope homogeneity is rejected (Delta 9.68, adjusted Delta 11.71), so country-specific slopes differ. No analysis of income group, institutions or human capital as moderators is reported; absorptive capacity is mentioned only as a speculative explanation.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5, p.12; Conclusion p.15: 'absence of feedback from ICT development to growth may have been due to the lack of absorptive capacity'

income_group_results.high: not reported (no high-income economy in an SSA sample apart possibly from Seychelles or Mauritius if included; no income-group split)

n_specifications_reported: about 2 (baseline ICT-index causality test with different lag lengths said to be robust; alternative AfDB ICT index robustness test described but not shown)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Granger causality in first differences is predictive, not causal, yet the title and abstract use 'causal'. No instrument or exogenous variation, and only a minimal bivariate/small multivariate system. The bidirectional test does address reverse causation descriptively. The Z-bar of -0.30 for ICT to GDP (a test of the null) is consistent with weak power with T=20 and short lags.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Abstract; Section 3.2 pp.11-12; Table 7 p.13

exposure_measurement.why: PCA index of three infrastructure access/subscription measures covers ICT adoption well but mixes mobile subscriptions (which can exceed 100 per 100, with duplicate SIMs) with very low broadband values; takes logs of values as small as 3e-14 (Table 1), which is fragile. Captures infrastructure, not use or quality.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1 p.9; Table 1 p.9 (broadband min 3.07E-14); Tables A1-A2

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only Sub-Saharan Africa, 2000-2019, balanced panel of 41 countries; the stated country count is inconsistent (41 vs 42). Limits generalisation beyond SSA but there is no obvious selective choice of years.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Abstract ('42 African economies'); Section 3.1 p.9 ('41 Sub-Saharan African economies'); Table 1 (820 obs)

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per capita (constant 2010 US$) from WDI is a standard output measure, although data quality for some SSA countries is weaker.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1 p.9: 'Y denotes GDP per capita (constant 2010 US$)'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Lag length for the DH test is not reported; capital measured as gross capital formation (flow, negative minimum in Table 1) rather than a stock; variables in levels are I(1) with possible cointegration, yet causality is run on first differences, discarding the long-run relation. No coefficients are estimated. Text states results robust to lags but shows no numbers.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 1 (capital min -6.30E+09); p.13 'findings were robust for different lag lengths'; Section 5 p.16: 'coefficients of each variable were not estimated'

selective_reporting.why: CADF unit root results and the AfDB-index robustness check are said to be 'available upon request' and are not shown; the main result is the one reported in the abstract. Table 7 has an internal inconsistency (Z-bar 20.08 for capital with p = 0.04). Text refers to 'correlation results in Table 3' when it is Table 2, and to 'Table 5' for the unit root test (it is Table 4).
selective_reporting.evidence: p.12 'CADF test results have not been presented'; Section 4.1 p.14 'not reported here but available upon request'; Table 7

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Direction of effect is a Granger-causality verdict, not an effect size: ICT index does not Granger-cause GDP per capita; GDP per capita Granger-causes ICT (demand-following). Conclusions that ICT 'contributed nothing to the living standards' go beyond the evidence (p.14). Several internal inconsistencies: 41 vs 42 countries; Table 3 vs 2 and Table 5 vs 4 cross-references; capital Z-bar typo; text says results are consistent with Shiu and Lam for 'low-income countries in Europe' although that study is about China. Section 3.1 mentions a 'landline' component in the literature but the index uses broadband, internet and mobile. No instructions embedded in the text were found. Published in Economic Research-Ekonomska Istrazivanja, 2024, open access, a standard indexed journal.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel estimation (CD tests, CIPS, Pesaran-Yamagata, Pedroni/Westerlund, Dumitrescu-Hurlin Granger tests) of an ICT index (broadband, internet, mobile) against GDP per capita for 41 Sub-Saharan African economies, 2000-2019. Meets exposure, sample (>=10) and output criteria. No coefficients are estimated, only causality test statistics, which is a weak form of 'own estimation' but acceptable.

sample_corrections.n_economies: 41 (Table A3 lists 41 countries and Table 1 has 820 obs = 41 x 20). The '42 African economies' in the abstract, introduction and conclusion is an inconsistency in the paper; the data section says '41 Sub-Saharan African economies'.
sample_corrections.economies_or_groups: The Appendix Table A3 list is complete in the text (21 + 20 = 41 names, e.g. Angola ... Zimbabwe, incl. Mauritius, Botswana, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, South Africa, Namibia, Sudan); it is not truncated. Seychelles is not in the list.
sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: mixed (low, lower-middle and upper-middle income SSA economies by name; no income-group analysis)

second_pass.problems: No invented numbers found. Record errors: (1) Table A3 country list is complete, not truncated, and shows 41 economies, no Seychelles; (2) income-group note should not speculate on Seychelles. Paper-internal inconsistencies correctly flagged (41 vs 42, Z-bar 20.08). Minor: the paper reports no lag length ('findings were robust for different lag lengths') - record is right.

title: Does artificial intelligence help in improving human capital based educational development? Evidence from 29 countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (FE, 2SLS, mediation) of AI development (Stanford Global AI Vibrancy score) on a schooling and education-quality index in 29 countries, with explicit developed/developing comparison. Meets AI sample rule (>=3 economies) and outcome family 5 (schooling), with a family 4 mediator (inequality).
technology: artificial intelligence (national AI development / vibrancy composite)
exposure_measure: Stanford Global AI Vibrancy Tool total score (8 pillars, 42 indicators), scaled 0-1 (original scaled down by 100%); robustness: Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, six AI pillar scores, 12 individual AI sub-indicators in logs (Sections 4.1, 5.4; Tables 4, A.2). Instruments: industrial robot stock/installations/total count.

sample.economies_or_groups: Mainly OECD and BRICS economies (e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, Malaysia, Turkey, Singapore, US, Japan, European countries); full list only shown in Fig. 1 panels
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (mostly high income; developing group includes large emerging economies); World Bank income groups not used, 'developed' vs 'developing' split only
sample.unit: country-year (analysed as country-month after quadratic interpolation; N=1740 in Table 2, 1734 in regressions)

design.estimator: Two-way fixed effects OLS (country and 'year' FE); subsample regressions (developed/developing; COVID/non-COVID); 2SLS with industrial-robot IVs; Sobel-Goodman mediation; PSM mentioned
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country FE, time FE; controls: ln GDP per capita, CPI growth, FX rate, personal expenditure growth, unemployment, population growth, and five Legatum education-quality sub-indices (adult, pre-primary, primary, secondary, tertiary)

results.indicator: HCBED index (World Bank HCI education component adjusted for learning-adjusted years of schooling and returns to education) on AI Vibrancy Index, full sample FE
results.estimate: 0.084 (HCBED units per unit of AI index, 0-1 scale; text misdescribes as 'a 1% increase in AI ... 0.084 increase')

results.indicator: HCBED on AI, developed-country subsample
results.uncertainty: SE 0.023, ** (p<0.05) in Table 3; text says significant at 10%
results.evidence: Table 3 Model (3), p.8; N=358; text p.8: 'coefficient for developed countries is 0.058, significant at the 10% level'

results.indicator: HCBED on AI, developing-country subsample
results.evidence: Table 3 Model (2), p.8; N=1376

results.evidence: Table 3 Model (4), p.8; N=690

results.evidence: Table 3 Model (5), p.8; N=1044; text p.9: 'coefficient is negative (-0.024)'

results.evidence: Table 4 Model (6), p.11

results.indicator: HCBED on Government AI Readiness Index
results.estimate: 0.004 per index unit (units not defined)
results.evidence: Table 4 Model (7), p.11

results.estimate: Diversity 0.010, Education 0.009, Policy 0.002, Economy 0.000 (rounded, significant), R&D -0.000, Infrastructure 0.001 (ns)

results.estimate: Significant positive: Legislative mentions 0.000, Study programs 0.002, Study program penetration 0.002, Strategy presence 0.001, Newly funded companies 0.004, Private investment 0.002, Journal publications 0.022, Patent grants 0.002; not significant: AI talent concentration, notable ML models, internet speed; gender equality 0.000*

results.estimate: 0.260 (robot stock), 0.179 (robot installations), 0.244 (total robots)

results.estimate: 2.400 (Gini units not specified)
results.evidence: Table 6, p.16, Mechanism test (1): 'Economic_inequity 2.400*** (0.2966)'

results.estimate: indirect 0.027 (about one third of total effect)

results.estimate: AI -> education inequality 0.567; education inequality -> HCBED -0.006; indirect -0.003; direct 0.088; total 0.084
results.uncertainty: AI->edu inequality SE 0.3105 (p<0.1); -0.006 SE 0.0016 (p<0.01); indirect SE 0.002 (p<0.1)

heterogeneity.finding: Positive significant effect in 'developed' subsample (0.058, N=358), no significant effect in 'developing' subsample (-0.031, N=1376). Authors attribute this to lower AI penetration per capita and infrastructure/education access limits. Subsample is not a formal interaction test and the classification criterion is not stated.

heterogeneity.finding: Time period: coefficient is +0.172 during COVID-19 (2020-21) and -0.024 in 2017-19; authors interpret as AI-enabled remote education and shift from substitution to assistance. Pandemic-period education quality measures may be affected by other contemporaneous shocks.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 Models (4)-(5), p.8; text p.9

heterogeneity.finding: AI dimension: Education, Diversity, Policy & Governance and Economy pillars positively related to HCBED; R&D and Infrastructure pillars not significant.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 4 Models (8)-(13), p.11; text p.11

income_group_results.high: Not reported by World Bank group; 'developed' subsample (N=358, about 6 countries by obs/60): AI coef 0.058 (SE 0.023)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately; pooled in 'developing' subsample: AI coef -0.031 (SE 0.034), not significant
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately; pooled in 'developing' subsample (e.g., India): not significant
income_group_results.low: not covered (authors state low-income countries lack data)

n_specifications_reported: about 35 (5 subsample models, 8 robustness models, 12 sub-indicator models, 3 IV models, 2 mediation sets)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('AI influences HCBED', 'solves the two-way causality issue'). The IV is industrial robot stock/installations, whose exclusion from education outcomes is argued only briefly and is doubtful (robots proxy for general economic/industrial development and can affect education demand through wages and automation exposure). Only about 1 year of within-country variation in a 5-year window; PSM is mentioned but no PSM results are reported. Controls include Legatum education-quality sub-indices that are components of the outcome.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 5.4 p.13, Table 5 p.14: 'use of industrial robot prevalence as an instrumental variable (IV) is appropriate and justified'; Table 3 controls Pre_edu, Prim_edu etc.

exposure_measurement.why: AI Vibrancy score is a composite of R&D, investment, talent, policy and infrastructure indicators for the national ecosystem, not adoption or use in education. Authors concede possible 'generalization bias'. Index is dominated by country size (total, not per capita) and shows little within-country variation. Weighted pillars include internet speed and supercomputers.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 4.1 p.4; Limitations p.18: 'using the AI Vibrancy Index as a proxy for AI's influence on educational development may introduce a degree of generalization bias'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 29 countries chosen by availability of returns-to-education estimates and AI indicators, mostly OECD/BRICS; only five years (2017-2021); no low-income and few lower-middle-income countries; developed subsample covers only about 6 countries (358 obs / 60 months), developing about 23, which contradicts the stated mix and the selection criterion for 'developed' is not given.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 5.1 p.5; Table 3 observations 1376 vs 358; Limitations p.18

outcome_measurement.why: HCBED is the authors' own constructed index combining years of schooling, quality scores from Legatum, and country-specific returns to education from single-country literature estimates (which vary little over time). Annual data (index, AI score) are converted to monthly by quadratic interpolation, creating 1740 country-months from about 145 country-years, which artificially inflates N and deflates standard errors. Education quality drawn from a rankings index.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 5.1 p.6: 'transformed certain annual and quarterly variables into monthly frequency using quadratic interpolation'; Table 2 N=1740; Section 4.2 p.4-5

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Standard errors do not appear clustered by country; observations are interpolated monthly and 'Year FE' on monthly data is unclear; highly collinear controls (VIF 8.4 for lnGDP, about 6.8 for adult/primary/secondary education quality); many subsample and indicator regressions; sub-indicators estimated one by one in logs; Table 6 R2 around 0.99 vs 0.598 in Table 3 for the same specification, unexplained. Interpretation misstates units ('1% increase').
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 2 VIF column p.7; Table 3 p.8 'Standard errors in parentheses'; Table 6 p.16 R-squared 0.9916 vs Table 3 0.598

selective_reporting.why: Positive full-sample result is emphasised, but null developing result, negative pre-COVID result, and non-significant pillars/IV-related caveats are reported. PSM is announced but not reported; text reports the developed coefficient 0.058 as significant at 10% while the table marks 5%, and some tables show coefficients rounded to 0.000. Full country list and classification not tabulated.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 5.4 p.13 'implementing the propensity score matching strategy' with no PSM table; Table 3 vs text p.8

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Elsevier Technology in Society 2025. Outcome is education/human capital (family 5); inequality mediator (family 4) is a secondary result. Several internal inconsistencies for a human reviewer: 1740 vs 1734 observations; Table 2 N inflated by interpolation; text speaks of 'within the specified 20 months' and 'HCBED ... from over 0.6 to less than 0.8' while data span 60 months; text says 'a 1% increase' but variables are in levels on a 0-1 scale; developed coefficient significance mismatch (** in table, 10% in text); R2 0.9916 in Table 6 vs 0.598 in Table 3 for the same model; Hypothesis 1 states AI contributes to HCBED 'by aggravating income inequality' based on a Sobel test with Gini on unclear scale and no mediator-to-outcome identification. Coverage of income groups: no low-income and few lower-middle-income countries, so evidence on the 'payoff' for poorer countries is thin. No instructions directed at the reader were found in the text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel FE/2SLS/mediation estimation of Stanford AI Vibrancy score on an education development index (HCBED) for 29 countries (>=3 for AI), with a developed/developing split. Outcome is education/human capital (living standards beyond income) with an inequality mediator. Meets criteria.

sample_corrections.years: 2017-2021 (60 monthly observations per country created by quadratic interpolation of annual data; 29 x 60 = 1740 country-months, 1734 in regressions). Underlying data are about 5 annual observations per country.
sample_corrections.economies_or_groups: 29 countries 'primarily drawn from OECD and BRICS economies'; Fig. 1 note: most white-background countries are OECD, Brazil, China, India, Russia are BRIC. The paper claims 'a balanced mix of developed and developing countries' but gives no developed/developing list in text.
sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: mixed, no World Bank income classification used; low-income countries absent (authors: many less-developed countries lack data)
sample_corrections.unit: country-month after interpolation (Table 2 N=1740); Table 5 uses N=1182

second_pass.problems: No invented numbers. Record notes that need nuance: (1) 'about 6 countries' for the developed subsample is inference, not a paper statement; (2) text claims average VIF below 4 whereas Table 2 shows VIF 8.43 for LnGDP and 6.8 for education sub-indices (record reports VIF 8.4 correctly); (3) Table 4 Infrastructure 0.001 and Table A.2 gender equality 0.000* are marginal; (4) text says 'within the specified 20 months' and 'from 2017 to 2023' for pillar figures, minor internal inconsistencies, not in record.

title: Towards ICT diffusion and trade liberalisation on inclusive growth in Sub-Saharan Africa
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 48 SSA countries (2005-2020) estimating the effect of a composite ICT diffusion index on a composite inclusive growth index (poverty, inequality, services access). Meets exposure, sample (>=10 economies) and outcome (family 4/5) criteria.
technology: ICT in general (composite index: internet use, mobile subscriptions, broadband, fixed telephone, secure servers, education items)
exposure_measure: PCA-constructed ICT diffusion index from reportedly twelve indicators (Table 3 lists eight; Appendix 2 lists twelve), three components retained (61.6% of variance); lagged one period in dynamic models. Index includes secondary/tertiary schooling items, so it mixes ICT with human capital.

sample.economies_or_groups: Sub-Saharan African countries
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (SSA region only; no income split)

design.estimator: Pooled OLS, fixed effects, random effects (Table 9, columns 1-3); one-step difference GMM (columns 4-5; text elsewhere says system GMM and xtdpdgmm)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged dependent variable, trade openness, FDI, inflation, vulnerable employment, social protection; country effects; year dummies in static models. Identification relies on internal GMM instruments only.

results.indicator: Inclusive growth index (PCA of poverty headcount, GDP per capita, Gini, sanitation, electricity access, institutions, health and education spending, etc.), baseline GMM, ICT coefficient
results.estimate: 0.034*** (text: a 1% increase in ICT results in a 0.03% increase in inclusive growth)
results.evidence: Table 9 col 4, p.11236; text p.11237: 'a 1% increase in ICT results in a 0.03% increase in inclusive growth'

results.indicator: Inclusive growth index, GMM with TRAD*ICT interaction, ICT coefficient
results.evidence: Table 9 col 5, p.11236

results.indicator: Inclusive growth index, TRAD*ICT interaction (ICT moderates trade effect)
results.uncertainty: SE (1.10) as printed; printed star level (*) looks inconsistent with coefficient/SE ratio
results.evidence: Table 9 col 5, p.11236; text p.11238: 'interaction effect of ICT on trade openness can cause a 3.741% improvement in inclusive growth'

results.indicator: Inclusive growth index, fixed effects, ICT coefficient
results.evidence: Table 9 col 2, p.11236 (authors reject FE as inconsistent, Wooldridge test)

results.indicator: Inclusive growth index, pooled OLS and RE, ICT coefficient
results.evidence: Table 9 cols 1 and 3, p.11236

heterogeneity.finding: Trade openness is negative for inclusive growth but its interaction with ICT is positive, interpreted as ICT offsetting trade's adverse effect. No heterogeneity by income group, human capital or institutions is examined.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 9 col 5, p.11236; text p.11238

income_group_results.high: not applicable (SSA only, no income split)

n_specifications_reported: 5 (three static, two GMM)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Authors acknowledge endogeneity and reverse causality; fixed effects rejected. Only internal GMM instruments are used, with no external instrument, and instrument sets and classification of regressors as endogenous or predetermined are not reported. Causal language ('ICT diffusion has positive and significant impact').
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.2 p.11231-11232; p.11237 Wooldridge test and GMM discussion

exposure_measurement.why: ICT index is a PCA composite that mixes ICT access with schooling indicators (secondary and tertiary enrolment) and appears to double count variables (mobile, broadband, fixed telephone, secure servers each listed twice in Appendix 2). Text says twelve indicators, Table 3 lists eight.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 3 p.11230; Appendix 2 p.11240; Section 4.1.1 p.11233

selection_of_countries_years.why: 48 SSA countries, 2005-2020, chosen for data availability; panel unbalanced (767 observations in summary versus 346-367 in regressions, so large loss from missing data, notably social protection with 421 obs).
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1 p.11227; Table 8 p.11235; Table 9 p.11236

outcome_measurement.why: Inclusive growth index is a PCA composite of heterogeneous indicators (poverty, GDP per capita, Gini, sanitation, institutions, government spending, labour participation) with an arbitrary scale; mean and sign interpretation unclear; coefficients not interpretable in natural units. Some control variables (vulnerable employment, social protection) overlap with index content.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 4 p.11230; Section 4.1.2 p.11233; Table 8 p.11235

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Table titled dynamic but includes static estimators; both GMM columns labelled difference GMM while the text says system GMM; 'exhaustive model search' used to choose specification; trade variable scaling unclear (mean -7.98 outside the printed min-max range); interpretation of coefficients as percent effects is inconsistent with index/level variables.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.2.2 p.11232; p.11237 'after an exhaustive model search'; Table 8 p.11235

title: Does ICT Participate in Economic Convergence among Asian Countries: Evidence from Dynamic Panel Data Model

technology: ICT in general (composite index of fixed telephone lines, mobile cellular subscriptions, fixed broadband, fixed internet subscribers, internet users)
exposure_measure: ICT Maturation Index (ICTMI) = fixed telephone lines per 100 + 0.2 x (mobile subscriptions per 100 + fixed broadband subscribers + fixed internet subscribers per 100 + internet users per 100), from ITU 2011 (Table 1, p.9). Also an interaction ICTSERT = ICTMI x tertiary enrolment.

sample.economies_or_groups: 24 Asian countries incl. Bangladesh, Brunei, China, Indonesia, India, Iran, Israel, Jordan, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Cambodia, Korea, Kuwait, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Oman, Pakistan, Philippines, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Thailand, Tajikistan, Yemen (p.11)

sample.years: 2000-2010 per text (abstract says 2001-2010); estimation uses 216 observations

design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged income, initial income YPC(0), tertiary enrolment interaction, population aged 15-64, urban population, trade openness, electricity consumption per capita, year dummies; country effects removed by GMM transformation. ICT goods imports (% of goods imports) used as an additional external instrument.

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita (PPP, constant 2005 intl $) on ICT Maturation Index

Conditional convergence: initial income coefficient YPC(0) in ICT-augmented model
results.estimate: -0.0584 (lagged income coefficient 0.9617, SE 0.0487)

heterogeneity.finding: Positive and significant ICT x tertiary-enrolment interaction: ICT is more productive where tertiary enrolment is higher. Not tested against secondary enrolment (ICTSERS dropped without estimation).

ICT goods imports as external instrument is not credibly excluded from income. The initial-condition regressor YPC(0) is time-invariant and would be absorbed by country effects in a standard setup. Causal wording ('ICT participates in convergence') with a lagged-income coefficient of 0.96.

selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.10 'dimensions of dataset are 24 countries ... 11 years ... mostly dictated by the availability of data'; p.10 'i = 1, ..., 11'

n_specifications_reported: 12 regression columns (3 models x 4 estimators)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('effect', 'impact', 'engender') with levels regressions; headline FGLS has no country or year effects; reverse causation (banking development drives ATMs, internet and mobile use) not addressed; Hausman test favours FE but FGLS (pooled) is used for inference.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section C pp.5-6; Table III-V

exposure_measurement.why: Internet users and mobile subscriptions are standard World Bank measures; mobile subscriptions are SIM counts (values up to 198 per 100), not users; ATMs used as a technology proxy though outside the listed exposures.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 20 countries, said to be chosen 'at random' but selected with China and Nigeria as focal cases, no sampling frame given; the 18 comparison countries are heterogeneous; period limited to 2005-2020 by ATM availability.

outcome_measurement.why: Single supply-side indicator: depositors with commercial banks per 1,000 adults; does not capture mobile-money or digital accounts; range 0.999 to 3000.9 in descriptives, with negative minimum for ATM (-3.1) implying data errors.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four estimators and three models; results diverge across estimators (FE vs FGLS) and the one favoured is not the one chosen by the diagnostic test; coefficients in levels but interpreted as percentages; inconsistent diagnostics (Wooldridge F(1,19) vs F(1,9); sign flip on POPL in Table V RE).
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table III-V pp.6-8; text p.5-6

selective_reporting.why: Country-difference conclusions rest on FGLS only, while significant FE interactions are not discussed; conclusion that technology raises inclusion 'regardless of income level' is not tested.

venue_quality_concern: possible (European Journal of Business and Management Research; short article with interpretation errors and table inconsistencies; not clearly indexed in leading economics databases)
notes: Interaction terms are misread as country-specific effects, so the headline statement that technology has 'insignificant positive effects' in China and Nigeria is not supported by the design. Table I has garbled entries (POPL mean 9.4, min 82858, max 1.4; ATM min -3.1). Table III FE shows '1..54' typo. Abstract says GDP growth negative. Hausman and Breusch-Pagan results conflict (text says LM favours pooled OLS in one place and random effects in another). Financial inclusion is the only outcome (family 5); no income-group classification beyond the China/Nigeria dummies. No text in the paper attempted to direct the extractor.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel regressions on 20 countries (>=10); internet users and mobile subscriptions are listed exposures. Outcome is financial inclusion (bank depositors per 1,000 adults), which is not one of the listed outcomes by name; eligible only if the protocol's 'living standards beyond income' family covers financial inclusion (the paper links it to poverty reduction but does not estimate poverty). Borderline but accepted. ATMs are not a listed technology (supplementary).

corrections.correction: The paper has no income-group analysis. It contrasts China and Nigeria with 18 other countries by country dummies and frames them as 'developed and emerging' economies; the 'upper-middle' and 'lower-middle' labels are the extractor's, not in the text. The remaining content (insignificant FGLS differences, several significant FE differences, authors misread insignificant interactions as 'insignificant positive effects') is supported.
corrections.quote: A significant β*c means a difference between China and the rest of the sample

second_pass.problems: Numerical entries in the record match Tables III-V. Items to flag: (a) outcome eligibility is borderline (see note); (b) text p.8 gives Wald chi2(8)=26.98 for Table V while the table shows 526.54; (c) text states the Wooldridge F p-value of 0.000 'is greater than 0.05'; (d) abstract says Pooled OLS and FGLS, Section III.C says FE and RE; (e) the baseline internet and mobile coefficients differ across Tables III-V (2.33/2.32/2.25 and 0.70/0.66/0.71) although they are the same variable in the same sample; (f) result 6 is a mix of three FE coefficients from different models, not one estimate.

title: Information and communication technology and labour productivity growth: a production-frontier approach
decision_rationale: Quantitative DEA/Malmquist decomposition of labour productivity growth with ICT capital change as an explicit component, 24 OECD economies (>=10), outcome in family 1 (output and productivity).
technology: ICT in general (ICT capital: computer hardware, telecommunication equipment, software and databases)
exposure_measure: ICT capital stock per hour worked from OECD database (hardware + telecom equipment + software/databases); exposure enters as ICT capital change (DACC) component of a four-way decomposition of labour productivity growth (EFF x TECH x KACC x DACC), a counterfactual movement along the frontier.

sample.economies_or_groups: OECD members: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Czech Rep., Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Lithuania, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovak Rep., Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, UK, US; grouped as Western Europe, Central-Eastern Europe, Northern America, Asia-Australia
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed OECD (predominantly high income; the text does not classify by World Bank income group)

design.estimator: Non-parametric Data Envelopment Analysis with Malmquist/Fisher-ideal decomposition (Kumar and Russell type, extended to ICT capital); bootstrap-based Li et al. distribution test (5,000 replications); dip test of unimodality; simple regressions of TECH and EFF on DACC and lagged DACC across 5-year intervals
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: No controls or fixed effects; accounting decomposition with constant returns to scale, frontier built without technology regress; output GDP, inputs labour hours, non-ICT capital, ICT capital; PPP and 2015 prices

results.indicator: Labour productivity growth 1995-2019, contribution of ICT capital change (DACC), geometric average across 24 countries
results.estimate: DACC index 1.1389 geometric average (1.2241 arithmetic), vs KACC 1.1499, TECH 1.1306, EFF 1.0486; total LABPROD CHG 1.5526 (geometric); index of 1 = no contribution
results.uncertainty: not reported (accounting decomposition, no standard errors)
results.evidence: Table 3, p.136; text: 'most significant improvement ... similarly attributable to technological change, ICT and non-ICT capital change'

results.indicator: Country heterogeneity of DACC contribution 1995-2019
results.estimate: DACC ranges from 0.8212 (Slovak Republic) to 4.0281 (Latvia); below 1 in 12 of 24 countries (Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Germany, Japan, Portugal, Slovak Rep., Slovenia, Sweden, UK, US; US 0.9862)
results.evidence: Table 3, p.136; Czech, Finland, Hungary, Latvia, Poland growth 'driven primarily by ICT capital change'

results.indicator: Contribution of ICT capital change over time (5-year windows)
results.estimate: Central-Eastern Europe DACC 1.2094 (1995-2000), 1.1152, 1.1044, 0.9721 (2010-2015), 0.9968 (2015-2019); Western Europe 1.0271 to 0.9811; Northern America about 1.00 to 0.986; Asia-Australia 0.9973 to 0.9627
results.evidence: Table 4, p.137; 'ICT capital change is mainly responsible for the growth of labour productivity ... 1995-2010, but this turns into a lower coefficient after 2010'

results.indicator: Technological change (TECH, frontier shift) regressed on ICT capital change, same period
results.evidence: Sect. 4.2, p.138, Fig. 1a: 'does not affect technological change in the short term'

results.indicator: Technological change (TECH) regressed on ICT capital change lagged 5 years
results.estimate: beta = 0.095
results.evidence: Sect. 4.2, p.138, Fig. 1b: 'positive effect on technological progress in the next 5 years'

results.indicator: Efficiency change (EFF) regressed on ICT capital change, same 5-year period
results.evidence: Sect. 4.2, pp.138-139, Fig. 2: 'negative relationship between efficiency and ICT capital during the transition period'

results.indicator: Cross-country distribution of labour productivity (convergence): ICT capital change as a driver of change in the 1995-2019 distribution
results.estimate: Li et al. test statistic Tn = 0.772 for f(y2019) = g(y1995) x DACC; not rejected
results.evidence: Table 5, p.140: 'efficiency change and ICT capital change are only responsible for moving the 1995 distribution to 2019'; abstract says 'ICT capital contributes to convergence'

heterogeneity.finding: Contribution of ICT capital change is large in Central-Eastern Europe in 1995-2010 (catch-up, e.g. Latvia 4.03, Hungary 1.56, Poland 1.44) and weak or below 1 in Western Europe, Northern America and Asia-Australia after 2000; European decline after 2010 stronger than Northern America.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 3 p.136, Table 4 p.137; 'in the last decade, the total contribution of ICT ... in European countries ... is more downwards than that of Northern American countries'

heterogeneity.finding: Time lag: ICT capital change has no contemporaneous effect on frontier shifts but a positive effect five years later, and a negative contemporaneous association with efficiency (interpreted as an organisational adjustment period, general-purpose technology).

income_group_results.high: Sample is mostly high-income OECD; reported by region (Western Europe, Northern America, Asia-Australia), not income group; DACC about 0.96-1.03 in later windows
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported (Central-Eastern European transition economies are grouped by region, with largest DACC contributions 1995-2010)

n_specifications_reported: unclear (one main decomposition with 15 distribution tests and a few bivariate regressions; 4-year interval robustness in Appendix B)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Descriptive decomposition and simple bivariate regressions of TECH/EFF on DACC with no controls, fixed effects or instruments; abstract and conclusions use causal language ('impact of ICT'). ICT capital accumulation is itself endogenous to productivity and the paper does not address reverse causation.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Abstract, p.123; Sect. 4.2, p.138 (regressions without controls)

exposure_measurement.why: ICT capital stock from OECD includes hardware, telecoms and software/databases, which directly measures ICT investment capability; however DACC is a counterfactual component and the text itself notes ICT capital falls in constant-price terms because prices of ICT assets fall.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Sect. 3 p.134; Table 2 p.135 (D median growth 123.7%, min -66.9%)

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample of 24 OECD countries, 'the most prominent sample possible' limited by data availability; mostly high income so results do not extend to developing countries; no income-group comparison.

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per hour worked from OECD, PPP and price corrected to 2015, a standard measure of labour productivity.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: DEA is deterministic and sensitive to outliers; constant returns to scale and no-technological-regress assumed; ordering of components in decomposition is arbitrary (handled by Fisher-ideal averaging); no standard errors on decomposition; regressions on 5-year windows use few observations.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Sect. 2, pp.131-134 (Eqs. 6-8: 'choice between (6) and (7) is arbitrary')

selective_reporting.why: All 24 countries and all 15 counterfactual distribution tests are reported; appendix tables give full detail; 4-year interval robustness shown. Table 5 reports no multiple-testing adjustment.
selective_reporting.evidence: Table 3 p.136, Table 5 p.140, Appendices A-C

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Decomposition values are multiplicative indices (1 = no contribution) and are not regression coefficients. Abstract states 'positive impact of ICT', but DACC is below 1 for 12 of 24 countries including the US, Germany, Japan and Canada, and the contribution fades after 2010; a contemporaneous negative efficiency association is also reported. I did not read Appendix tables 14-25 and Appendices B-C in full. Nothing in the text attempted to direct the extraction. Text extraction garbled equation symbols (e.g. '='); the text states 'ICT capital contributes to convergence' but Table 5 p-value for DACC counterfactual is 0.108, a non-rejection.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own DEA/Malmquist decomposition and regressions on 24 OECD economies (>=10), ICT capital stock as exposure, labour productivity as output outcome. Eligible, though the main result is an accounting decomposition without standard errors.

corrections.correction: Numbers are right (Tn=0.772, bootstrap p=0.108), but the direction should be null/inconclusive rather than positive: it is a non-rejection of equality between the 2019 distribution and the 1995 distribution scaled by DACC, not a positive estimate. Non-rejection also occurs for EFF alone (p=0.093) and for several other combinations, so the test does not isolate ICT. The authors' 'ICT capital contributes to convergence' is an interpretation of the counterfactual and Fig. 3.

second_pass.problems: No invented numbers found. Points to correct: (a) result 7 direction; (b) the record's claim that regressions 'use few observations' cannot be verified, since the paper reports no N or SE for the Fig. 1-2 regressions; (c) the abstract's 'positive impact' and 'contributes to convergence' go beyond what a non-causal decomposition and a non-rejection test support; (d) record exposure description 'ICT capital stock per hour worked' matches the paper's d = D/L normalisation.

title: Total Factor Productivity, Demographic Traits and ICT: Empirical Analysis for Asia
decision_rationale: System GMM panel of 24 Asian countries (2000-2010) with a composite ICT index as exposure and TFP as outcome. Meets ICT exposure, at least 10 economies and an output/productivity outcome; income groups are mixed within Asia.
technology: ICT in general (composite maturation index including fixed broadband, internet, fixed telephone, mobile)
exposure_measure: ICTMI = ICT Maturation Index, author-constructed composite inspired by the ITU ICT Development Index; the listed components are fixed broadband subscribers, fixed internet subscribers, internet users, fixed telephone lines and mobile subscriptions per 100. Construction method (weights, scaling) not reported. ICTSERT = ICT x tertiary enrolment interaction.

sample.economies_or_groups: Asian countries, 'few DCs and mostly UDCs'; country list not reported
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (not reported by group)

design.estimator: Two-step System GMM (xtabond2) with small-sample and robust options, lagged TFP as regressor
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged TFP, ICT x tertiary enrolment, population aged 15-64, urban population share, HDI, time dummies. ICT goods imports (% of goods imports, ICTM) named as external instrument. 29 instruments for 24 countries.

results.indicator: TFP on ICT Maturation Index (ICTMI)
results.estimate: 0.0156 (units and any log transformation not reported; TFP construction uses unreported factor share)
results.evidence: Table 5 (p.11) ICTMI 0.0156; coefficient on lagged TFP 0.9394

results.indicator: TFP on ICT x tertiary enrolment (ICTSERT)
results.evidence: Table 5 (p.11); text p.12 says significance 'only at 10%', which conflicts with the table

heterogeneity.finding: Positive ICT x tertiary enrolment interaction: ICT is more productive where tertiary enrolment is higher. Main effect of tertiary enrolment alone is not in the reported model.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5; p.12 'ICT has complementarity with tertiary level of education'

heterogeneity.finding: Urban population share positively related to TFP (0.0713, p=0.009); working-age share (0.0135, p=0.186) and HDI (0.0117, p=0.821) not significant. These are controls, not interactions with ICT.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5 (p.11)

n_specifications_reported: 1 System GMM specification (IV tests shown in Tables 2-3 only for diagnostics)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: System GMM with lagged TFP and an ICT-goods-import instrument addresses endogeneity in principle, but the instrument's validity is argued only through Hansen tests; 29 instruments versus 24 countries (instrument proliferation) and a Hansen p of 0.935 suggest weak diagnostics. AR(1) p=0.077 is not rejected at 5%.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Table 5 p.11 'Instruments = 29', 'Hansen J-Test = 0.935', 'M1: p = 0.077'; Section 7.1-7.2

exposure_measurement.why: Composite ICT index covers several ICT forms but its construction is not documented; the interaction term ICTSERT is included without the tertiary enrolment main effect.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 2 p.8-9 on ICTMI; Section 7 p.11 definition of ICTSERT

selection_of_countries_years.why: 24 Asian countries chosen 'depending on availability of data'; list not given; short 11-year window.

outcome_measurement.why: TFP is a residual 'YCD - alpha L - (1-alpha) K' with the factor share and the capital measure unreported, and units are not stated.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Only one final model is shown; no robustness checks, alternative lags or exclusion of the interaction. GMM tables (Table 4) and Table 1 are missing from the text and the table numbering jumps.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table numbering Tables 2, 3, 5 only; Table 5 p.11

selective_reporting.why: Text misstates results: says HDI is 'positive and statistically significant' while Table 5 gives p=0.821; says ICTSERT significant at 10% while table gives p=0.000; third C-test p given as 0.222 in text vs 0.822 in Table 5; text cites 240 observations while table shows 216.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Implied long-run effect of ICTMI from the dynamic coefficients would be about 0.0156 / (1 - 0.9394) = 0.26, but the paper does not report this; it is my arithmetic and not an extracted result. The paper cites Roodman (2009) as a source for the ICT-import instrument, which is a paper on too many instruments and does not appear to propose that instrument. Population aged 15-64 is described as 'youth' in the text. No embedded instructions to the reader were found in the text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own system-GMM estimation, 24 Asian economies (>=10), composite ICT index exposure, TFP outcome (productivity). Eligible.
second_pass.problems: Record matches the text and Table 5; its inconsistency list (HDI, 10% vs p=0.000, C-test 0.222 vs 0.822, 240 vs 216) is correct, as are the missing-table observation (tables numbered 2, 3, 5). Additional points: (a) same authors, same 24-country 2000-2010 sample and same ICTMI/ICTSERT setup as paper 302, so not independent evidence; (b) the text calls the AR(1) p=0.077 acceptable but AR(1) is expected to reject; (c) the Fig. 1 'ICT Augmented Convergence Hypothesis' diagram is carried over from 302 and does not match this paper's TFP model.

title: The impact of information and communication technologies on export diversification: Evidence from developing countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study (system GMM) of ICT index effects on export concentration/diversification in about 100-110 emerging and developing economies; outcome is export structure (structural change family). Meets exposure, sample and outcome criteria.
technology: ICT in general (composite index of fixed telephone, internet users, fixed broadband, mobile cellular)
exposure_measure: ICT index built by PCA from four WDI indicators (fixed-telephone subscriptions per 100, % individuals using the internet, fixed-broadband subscriptions per 100, mobile-cellular subscriptions per 100), rescaled to 0-1; robustness uses UNCTAD Productive Capacities ICT index (range 1 to 81.23).

sample.n_economies: 110 stated in text/abstract; 100-106 in regression tables (102 in Tables 6-7)
sample.economies_or_groups: IMF-classified emerging market and developing countries; country list in Appendix 2 (not in the extracted text)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (split into 'high-income' = high + upper-middle, and 'low-income' = low + lower-middle, per WB classification)

design.estimator: One-step and two-step system GMM (Blundell-Bond, orthogonal deviations, robust SE); robustness with two-way fixed effects with lagged DV
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged dependent variable, GDP per capita, population, natural resource rents, private credit, primary school enrollment; year dummies; trade, FDI and electricity access used as additional instruments; max two lags as instruments

results.indicator: Export product concentration (normalised HHI, UNCTAD); higher = more concentrated
results.estimate: -0.0339 (two-step system GMM, ICT index 0-1); -0.0473 (one-step)

results.indicator: Export diversification index (absolute deviation from world export structure; higher = less aligned with world structure)
results.estimate: -0.0968 (two-step); -0.0908 (one-step); negative sign means export structure moves closer to world structure

results.indicator: Export concentration, long-run effect computed by authors
results.estimate: -0.1638 (concentration); -0.3424 (diversification index)
results.evidence: Table 14, p.154: 'ICT Index -0.1638 0.006'; 'ICT Index -0.3424 0.000'; method of computing long-run coefficients not described

results.indicator: Export concentration, alternative ICT measure (UNCTAD ICT index)
results.estimate: -0.0011 (two-step); -0.0012 (one-step)

results.indicator: Export diversification index, two-way FE with lagged DV
Export concentration, split by income group (two-step system GMM)
results.estimate: High+upper-middle: -0.0204 (concentration), -0.0591 (diversification); Low+lower-middle: -0.1550 (concentration), -0.1090 (diversification)
results.evidence: Table 11, p.152, ICT Index row; N=644/554 (high), 584/522 (low)

heterogeneity.finding: ICT coefficient larger in magnitude in low and lower-middle income group (-0.1550 concentration) than in high and upper-middle group (-0.0204). No formal test of difference reported.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 11, p.152; text p.150-151: 'coefficients of the ICT index are higher for low-income countries'

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of ICT index with primary school enrollment is positive (0.0015*** two-step; 0.0008 one-step, insignificant) on concentration, i.e. the diversifying effect of ICT weakens as enrollment rises, which the authors read as complementarity; the sign pattern actually implies the negative ICT effect shrinks at high enrollment, which is at odds with the authors' conclusion that ICT and human capital reinforce each other. UNCTAD ICT interaction: 0.00002***.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 7, p.147: 'Interaction of ICT and school enrollment 0.0008 / 0.0015***'; Table 13, p.153: '0.00002***'; text p.147 'the adverse effect of the ICT index ... becomes less pronounced or even reversed'

income_group_results.high: Pooled with upper-middle: ICT index -0.0204** (SE 0.0098) on concentration; -0.0591** on diversification index (Table 11)
income_group_results.lower_middle: Pooled with low: ICT index -0.1550** (SE 0.0770) on concentration; -0.1090** on diversification index (Table 11)

n_specifications_reported: about 10 (Tables 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 (4 columns), 12, 13)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: System GMM with internal instruments addresses endogeneity in principle, but instrument set is loosely described (trade, FDI, electricity access used as 'instrumental variables' although plausibly not excluded from the outcome equation), no instrument count reported, Hansen p-values of 0.14-0.55 are reported. Causal language ('impact', 'accelerates') used.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 4.1 pp.139-140; Section 5.2 p.145; Tables 6-7 Hansen and AR(2) rows

exposure_measurement.why: Composite PCA index of four indicators (fixed telephone, internet, broadband, mobile) with no quality, skill or usage-intensity component despite being described as following the ITU IDI. Fixed telephone included in an index of ICT development. Robustness with UNCTAD's index is helpful.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 4.2 p.141; Table 3 ICT Index N=1662

selection_of_countries_years.why: Developing/emerging countries only; countries dropped for missing data ('various cutoffs'); unbalanced panel (N obs 1052-1551 of 2200). Sample size varies between 100 and 106 countries; text says 110.

outcome_measurement.why: Standard UNCTAD normalised HHI and export diversification (deviation from world structure) indices at 3-digit SITC level; merchandise exports only (excludes services).

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Controls differ between Tables 6, 9, 10, 12 (e.g. school enrollment omitted in Table 12; trade included as control only there, as instrument elsewhere); one- and two-step results reported; the TWFE table includes a lagged DV with unit FE (Nickell bias). Interaction specification omits ICT-human capital sample splits; heterogeneity by income group uses a custom grouping.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 6, 9, 12; Section 6 pp.150-153

selective_reporting.why: All reported ICT coefficients are significant and in the hypothesised direction (one-step interaction in Table 7 insignificant); the long-run coefficients lack SEs and a described derivation. Authors' interpretation of the interaction sign is internally inconsistent with the headline claim of complementarity. No preregistration or failed specifications shown.
selective_reporting.evidence: Tables 7, 14; Section 5.3 p.147 and Conclusion p.155

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Outcome is export concentration/diversification only; no GDP, growth or productivity outcome is estimated (GDP per capita appears only as a control), so no MRA records. Inconsistencies: abstract and Section 4.2 say 2000-2019, conclusion says 1995-2019; text states 110 countries, tables show 100-106 (102 for the benchmark); Section 5.3 says trade/FDI/electricity are instruments while Table 12 includes trade as control; Section 6 states 'high-income' group = high plus upper-middle. Appendix 1-2 (PCA results, country list) not present in extracted text. Authors state the one-unit change of the 0-1 ICT index. Table 6 'GDP per capita (thousand US dollars)' but Table 3 describes it in dollars. No instructions directed at the reader were found in the text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own system GMM estimation; exposure is a PCA ICT index (fixed telephone, internet, fixed broadband, mobile) plus UNCTAD ICT index; 100-110 emerging/developing economies with explicit high/upper-middle versus low/lower-middle comparison; outcome is export concentration/diversification (structural change). All criteria hold.

sample_corrections.n_economies: 110 in abstract, Section 4.2 and Appendix 2 Table B1 (110 countries listed); regressions use 100 to 106 (Table 6/7: 102; Table 9: 100; Table 10: 106; Table 12: 102; Table 13: 106; Table 11 subgroups 45/50 high, 51/50 low)
sample_corrections.years: 2000-2019 (abstract and Section 4.2; 2200 obs = 110 x 20 in Table 3). The conclusion's '1995 to 2019' is an inconsistency in the paper, not the sample.
sample_corrections.economies_or_groups: Record says the country list is not in the text; it is: Appendix 2, Table B1 (p.162) lists 110 countries
sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Mixed: list includes high-income economies (e.g. Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Chile, Poland, Hungary, Uruguay, Barbados, Trinidad and Tobago) as well as low-income ones (e.g. Burundi, Chad, Niger); paper splits into high+upper-middle vs low+lower-middle by World Bank class.

second_pass.problems: (1) Record says Appendix 2 country list is 'not in the extracted text'; it is present as Table B1 (110 countries), so the extractor should fill economies_or_groups. (2) Years: sample is 2000-2019; the conclusion's 1995-2019 is the paper's own inconsistency (2200 obs = 110 x 20). (3) Abstract and conclusion misdescribe the interaction result (positive sign on concentration index read as ICT being enhanced by human capital); record handles this correctly. No numbers invented; all quoted coefficients match tables.

title: Digital Divide, Credit Financing and Financial Inclusion: Changing Patterns of Poverty, Employment and Income Inequalities
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel regressions on up to 148 countries with internet use, mobile payments and fintech credit as exposures and poverty, Gini, labour force participation, unemployment and growth as outcomes. Meets exposure, sample and outcome criteria.
technology: mobile telephony (mobile phone used to pay bills)
electronic payments / fintech and big-tech credit flows (context)
exposure_measure: INTRNT = individuals using the internet (% of population, WDI); MBLPMT = mobile phone used to pay bills (% age 15+, Global Findex); ELCPMT = electronic payments (% age 15+); FINTCBIG = credit flows by fintech and big tech companies (% of GDP); CRCRD = credit card users (% age 15+). Table 5.

sample.n_economies: 148 stated overall; regressions use 62 to 155 depending on table (70, 62, 64, 147, 148, 95, 155)
sample.economies_or_groups: Global unbalanced sample; countries not listed. Descriptive tables by World Bank region and by high/middle income.
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (not reported by group in the regressions)
sample.years: 2008-2021 stated; individual tables use 2013-2019, 2008-2019, 2008-2020, or 2021 cross-section

design.estimator: Panel Least Squares (unbalanced) for Tables 7-12; OLS cross-section for Tables 13-14. Five alternative 'options' per equation, adding controls.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Controls vary by option: ease of doing business, domestic credit to private sector, GDP per capita or GDP growth, interest spread, NPL, new business density, corruption, tax rate. The estimating equation shows country and time effects, but tables do not report FE and the text says 'pooled data'; unclear whether FE were used.

results.indicator: Poverty headcount ratio at national lines (PVRTY) on internet users
results.estimate: -0.17 (option I) to -0.22 (options IV, V) percentage points of poverty per 1 pp internet users; -0.13 in option II
results.evidence: Table 7 (p.34), 70 countries, 235 obs, 2013-2019; text p.32 'significant and robust in all alternative options'

results.indicator: Poverty headcount ratio on fintech and big-tech credit flows (% GDP)
results.evidence: Table 7 (pp.33-34), FINTCBIG row

results.indicator: Gini index on internet users
results.estimate: -0.08 (I) to -0.13 (II, V) Gini points per 1 pp internet users
results.evidence: Table 8 (p.34), 62 countries, 336 obs, 2008-2019

results.indicator: Income share of lowest 20% on internet users and on mobile payments
results.estimate: INTRNT 0.01 (t=1.76 in I, 1.78 in III, insignificant in IV-V); MBLPMT 0.08 (II)
results.uncertainty: t = 1.76, 1.78, 1.29, 1.38 for INTRNT; t = 2.11 for MBLPMT
results.evidence: Table 9 (p.35), 64 countries, 361 obs; weak and not robust across options

results.indicator: Labour force participation rate on internet users and on mobile payments
