confounding_reverse_causation.why: Single cross-section with GDP level and internet hosts jointly determined. SURE only exploits error correlation between equations and gives no exogenous variation; the paper itself says the two are endogenous and then reads coefficients as growth effects. CMI is built from the same variables that drive both sides. No controls for institutions, geography or population in the GDP equation.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.2 (Eqs 3-6); Section 3.3 Simulation 1

exposure_measurement.why: Internet hosts per 10,000 are a poor measure of e-commerce or of use in a country (hosts are tied to domain registration, which the authors acknowledge is biased). E-commerce itself is never measured.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 2 p.9: 'a biased measurement of the state of e-commerce diffusion'

selection_of_countries_years.why: Regression sample falls from 205 to 126 states because of missing data; one year (2000) only; non-random loss, and small-state sample is 33.

outcome_measurement.why: Outcome is level of real GDP (constant 1995 US$), not growth, although the title and text refer to growth. Reported magnitudes look inconsistent with a log outcome (small-state dummy of -209 on LGGDP, constants of 23 to 82).
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 1 (LgGDP = log of real GDP); Table 3

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Unusual SURE set-up with the dependent variable of one equation as the regressor in the other; two versions with and without the dummy. The authors admit the size-dummy result 'may be affected by data specification and other statistical problems'. Table headings repeat ('Model specification 1' twice). Identical t-ratios (6.425, 6.196) appear in both equations, which suggests duplication or a mechanical artefact.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.3 p.17; Table 3

selective_reporting.why: All four simulations are shown, but no robustness checks, no diagnostics, and text describes Simulation 2 loosely (e.g. says 'regresses CMI on hosts'). Draft paper not peer reviewed.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 3.3, Simulation 2; cover note 'should not be cited or quoted'

venue_quality_concern: possible (unreviewed working paper prepared for a conference; author note says draft should not be cited)
notes: Abstract and introduction describe the paper as a synthesis plus research agenda; the empirical part is small and labelled 'initial'. Title speaks of growth but the model estimates GDP levels in a single year. Only the LHosts-to-LGGDP coefficient is treated as the payoff estimate; the CMI coefficient mixes telephone lines, schooling and capital formation and is not an ICT exposure estimate. Table 3 oddities: reported SMALL coefficients of -209.499 and -179.145 are implausible for a log outcome, and t-ratios are duplicated across the two equations. Possible duplicate or later version in a journal not checked. No instruction-like content found in the text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own cross-sectional SURE estimation (126 economies, year 2000) of internet hosts on log real GDP; exposure is internet; output outcome; income-group comparison is only descriptive (box plot), but the 126-economy sample meets the 10-economy rule. sample_corrections.n_economies: 205 states in the descriptive data (129 large, 76 small); the box plots in Figures 2 and 3 use 161 states (113 large, 48 small; income groups 54+44+28+35); 126 in the SURE regressions (93 large, 33 small)

title: Digitalisation and structural change: Evidence from cross-country analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative cross-country panel (FE, FE-IV, system GMM) of 51 economies, exposure is internet penetration (with mobile penetration as robustness), outcomes are structural change (between-sector productivity component) and manufacturing employment share, with explicit income-group comparisons. All criteria met.
exposure_measure: Internet penetration (% of population with internet access), entered in logs in the structural change equation and in levels in the manufacturing employment equation; mobile subscriptions per 100 people as alternative measure (Table 3 Model 7, Table 5 Model 5). Source stated as ITU in Section 3.2 but as WDI in Table A1.

sample.n_economies: 51 (47-49 in most regressions; 36-42 in the manufacturing employment models)
sample.economies_or_groups: Economies in the GGDC/UNU-WIDER Economic Transformation Database, mostly developing (Africa, Asia, Latin America) plus some high-income; Table A2 note lists 6 high-income, 9 low-income, 19 lower-middle-income, 16 upper-middle-income
sample.income_groups_covered: high, upper-middle, lower-middle, low (only 6 high-income economies)

design.estimator: Two-way fixed effects (country and year) with country-clustered SE; FE-IV (regional average internet penetration and lagged internet penetration as instruments); two-step system GMM with collapsed instruments
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged log labour productivity, lagged FDI/GDP, lagged backward and forward GVC linkages (or aggregate GVC index), lagged human capital index; robustness adds gross capital formation, agricultural employment share, REER. Manufacturing equation adds log population and GDP per capita and their squares. Country and year FE (Table 2 and Table 4 report time FE only in the table rows; Table 3 lists both).

results.indicator: Economy-wide structural change (between-sector component of labour productivity growth, McMillan-Rodrik decomposition) on log internet penetration, FE
results.estimate: 0.126 to 0.137 (Table 2 Models 1-4; Model 4 = 0.137) per unit of log internet penetration; 0.171-0.180 in robustness (Table 3 Models 5, 6, 8)
results.uncertainty: Model 4 SE 0.0759, significant only at 10%; Table 3 Models 5, 6, 8 SE 0.072-0.079, p<0.05
results.evidence: Table 2 Model 4; text p.319: 'positive and significant effect on economy-wide SC (albeit at the 10%)'

results.indicator: Structural change on log internet penetration, FE-IV (regional average and lagged internet penetration as instruments)
results.estimate: 0.204 to 0.341 (Table 4 Models 1-6)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.116-0.157; significance 10% to 1%; Kleibergen-Paap p=0.00, Hansen p 0.11-0.33
results.evidence: Table 4, row 'Log (internet pen) _IV'

results.indicator: Structural change on log internet penetration, two-step system GMM
results.estimate: 0.118 to 0.186 (Table A3 Models 1-5)
results.evidence: Table A3 row 'Log (internet penetration)'; text p.323: 'estimates comparable to the FE regressions'

results.indicator: Structural change on log mobile penetration, FE (alternative exposure)
results.estimate: 0.177 (Table 3 Model 7)
results.evidence: Table 3 Model 7, row 'Log (mob penetration)'

results.indicator: Manufacturing share of total employment (percentage points) on internet penetration (% points), FE
results.estimate: -0.0782 to -0.0596 (Table 6 Models 1-4; Model 4 = -0.0596) pp of employment share per pp of internet penetration
results.evidence: Table 6, row 'Internet penetration'

results.indicator: Manufacturing employment share on internet penetration, FE-IV
results.uncertainty: SE 0.0103, 0.0236, 0.0247; Model 7 significant only at 10%. Table 6 reports no instrument test statistics.
results.evidence: Table 6 Models 5-7

results.indicator: Manufacturing employment share on internet penetration, low- and middle-income subsample
results.estimate: -0.0707 (internet, Table A4 Model 1); -0.116 (server penetration, Model 2)
results.evidence: Table A4 Models 1-2; text p.325: 'negative and significant impact ... in low- and middle-income countries'

heterogeneity.finding: Positive effect of internet penetration on structural change is larger in low and lower-middle income economies than in upper-middle and high-income ones. The interaction of internet penetration with an upper-middle/high-income dummy is negative; the main internet term is itself not significant in this specification.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5 Model 1: UMIC-HIC# internet pen -0.0147** (SE 0.00556); internet pen 0.00660 (SE 0.00966)

heterogeneity.finding: Effect on structural change is largest in structurally underdeveloped (agrarian) economies and smaller in structurally developing and developed economies (Sen 2019 classification based on 2018 employment shares). Same pattern with mobile penetration, though only the 'developing' interaction is significant at 10%.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5 Models 3-5: internet pen 0.0463**, ST developing# -0.0448***, ST developed# -0.0499***; mobile Model 5 ST developing# -0.00932*

heterogeneity.finding: Effect on structural change is stronger where forward GVC linkages are higher (positive interaction of log forward linkages with internet penetration).
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 5 Model 2: L.logFL# internet pen 0.0105** (SE 0.00515)

heterogeneity.finding: Manufacturing employment effect is negative in South Asia subsample (5 countries) and not significant in sub-Saharan Africa subsample (13 countries).

income_group_results.high: Not estimated separately (only 6 high-income economies). Upper-middle and high are pooled in the interaction; the effect on structural change is smaller than for low/lower-middle income (Table 5 Model 1, -0.0147**).
income_group_results.upper_middle: Pooled with high income; smaller effect on structural change than for low/lower-middle (Table 5 Model 1).
income_group_results.lower_middle: Pooled with low income in the interaction; larger positive effect on structural change. Manufacturing employment effect negative in low- and middle-income subsample (Table A4 Model 1, -0.0707***), not split further.
income_group_results.low: Pooled with lower-middle income; larger positive effect on structural change (Table 5 Model 1). Not estimated separately.

n_specifications_reported: about 36 (Table 2: 4; Table 3: 5; Table 4: 6; Table 5: 5; Table 6: 7; Table A3: 5; Table A4: 4)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('isolate the causal effect'), but the sole external instrument is the regional average of internet penetration, whose exclusion restriction is not defended (regional diffusion can be correlated with regional structural change and common shocks); the other instrument is lagged internet penetration. Footnote 3 argues reverse causality is absent for the manufacturing equation because the outcome is sectoral and the regressor national, which is not a valid argument. FE-IV estimates are larger than FE, unexplained. Table 6 Models 5-7 report no instrument tests.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.2 p.318-319; Section 4.3 p.319-322; footnote 3 p.319; Table 4 notes; Table 6

exposure_measurement.why: Internet penetration is a single access proxy for 'digitalisation'; the authors acknowledge this. Data source is given inconsistently (ITU in text, WDI in Table A1). Internet penetration is 0 at the minimum and 1230 observations versus 1398 for other variables, so early years have many zeros/missing; log of zero values not discussed.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.2 p.318; Table A1; Table 1; conclusion p.325

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample is restricted to the ETD's 51 economies, mostly developing, with only 6 high-income; unbalanced panel with 36-49 countries depending on specification; the 1990-2018 window is set by data availability. Income groups are not separately estimated, only through an interaction. Sample size is inconsistent: 51 stated, Table A2 note adds to 50.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1 p.318; Table A2 note; Tables 2-6 observation counts

outcome_measurement.why: Structural change is computed from the standard McMillan-Rodrik decomposition on ETD sectoral value added and employment, and manufacturing employment share is measured directly. The paper concedes manufacturing share is an imperfect industrialisation indicator.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many specifications with varying control sets across models and estimators (about 36). Control sets differ between models (for example GCF is -0.019 insignificant in FE but -2.4 significant in FE-IV, with unexplained scale differences), the stated 'doubling' interpretation of a log coefficient is incorrect, and the preferred model is not declared. Significance of the headline FE effect is only 10% in Model 4. Some tables list no country FE row. Table 6 Model 5 omits year FE.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 2-6, A3-A4; p.319: 'A doubling of internet penetration is associated with a 0.14-unit increase'

selective_reporting.why: The abstract reports a 0.14 to 0.18 range drawn from FE models, omitting the larger FE-IV estimates (0.20-0.34), and states that the effects are stronger for low and lower-middle-income economies, although the main effect is insignificant in the income interaction. Manufacturing employment effect in SSA is insignificant, and appendix tables report only a few of the many specifications. Robustness text claims all results hold, but Table 3 Model 5 has insignificant forward linkage and backward linkage coefficients.

ICT use at work and task content come from the same respondents' questionnaire and are plausibly co-determined (jobs with abstract tasks use spreadsheets and the internet, so the link may be partly mechanical). The paper itself says it cannot observe dynamics. The abstract speaks of whether computer adoption 'leads to' the differences.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Introduction p.4-5 ('we cannot account for time dynamics'); abstract

exposure_measurement.why: Individual-level PCA index built from a self-chosen subset of items ('arbitrary decision'), not national adoption or investment. It is a worker/occupation characteristic, which differs from the country-level price-of-computers driver in the theory.

selection_of_countries_years.why: All PIAAC participants with usable data, mostly rich OECD economies; the wage analysis drops three countries; the three wage-based country groups are arbitrary.

outcome_measurement.why: Self-reported task frequencies; indices rescaled to 0-10 with values below 0.1 reset to 0.1 before logs; manual tasks cannot be separated into routine and non-routine, so RTI omits them. Conclusions weaken (about 10%) when manual tasks are included.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Several alternative RTI definitions, item subsets and country groupings; the headline uses the definition with the stronger ICT result. Robustness checks on some choices are reported.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: footnotes 14, 19, 22; Tables A.3-A.4

selective_reporting.why: Both RTI definitions are reported, but the abstract features the 41% / 25% figures from the manual-excluded index. The wage-inequality conclusion rests on graphs without formal tests.

title: The Race between Technological Progress and Female Advancement: Changes in Gender and Skill Premia in OECD Countries
decision_rationale: Structural-econometric study with its own GMM/IV estimation of ICT-capital/labour substitution on cross-country cross-industry panel data from 11 OECD economies; exposure is ICT capital (ICCT) quantity and its falling relative price; outcomes are gender and skill wage gaps and labour shares (families 3 and 4). Sample of 11 meets the at least 10 economies rule for non-AI technology, but all are high income.
technology: ICT capital (computing equipment, communications equipment, software; called ICCT capital)
exposure_measure: Quantity of ICCT capital (k_i) and ICT investment-specific technological change, measured as the fall in the relative price of ICCT investment (q_i, ratio of ICCT investment price to output price); EU KLEMS capital services by asset type, rental prices computed from Jorgenson user-cost formula (internal or external rate of return).

sample.economies_or_groups: Australia, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, United Kingdom, United States; four non-primary sectors (manufacturing, utilities, construction, services)
sample.income_groups_covered: high (all 11 are advanced OECD economies; no income-group comparison)

design.estimator: Multi-level nested CES sectoral production function; five first-difference (5-year differences) cost-minimisation equations estimated jointly by GMM with country-clustered SEs; sectoral parameters aggregated to aggregate Morishima elasticities of substitution (bootstrap SEs, 500 reps); effects of ICCT technological change are model-based counterfactuals (steady-state comparison) rather than reduced-form coefficients; preliminary OLS and first-difference IV regressions (eq. 23).
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: First-differencing removes country-specific fixed effects; instruments are lagged population size by demographic group and lagged ICCT investment price relative to consumption; robustness adds collective bargaining coverage, employment protection, minimum wages, external-rate-of-return rental prices (markups), country-specific trend polynomials. Wages adjusted for age and education composition.

results.indicator: Skilled gender wage gap (male skilled / female skilled), effect of ICCT-embodied technological change 1980-2005 (log change in relative wage)
results.estimate: -0.886 with exogenous labour supply; -0.486 with unit-elastic labour supply (about 49 percentage points as stated in text); observed change in the data is only +0.012 (Table 5)
results.evidence: Table 7, p.34, row Delta ln(w_mh/w_fh); Intro p.4: 'would have reduced the skilled (unskilled) gender wage gap by 49 (10) percentage points'

results.indicator: Unskilled gender wage gap (male unskilled / female unskilled), effect of ICCT-embodied technological change
results.estimate: -0.074 (exogenous labour supply); -0.096 (unit elastic)
results.evidence: Table 7, p.34, row Delta(w_mu/w_fu)

results.indicator: Male skill wage gap (male skilled / male unskilled), effect of ICCT-embodied technological change
results.estimate: +0.262 (exogenous); +0.264 (unit elastic); about 26 percentage points as stated
results.evidence: Table 7, p.34, row Delta(w_mh/w_mu)

results.indicator: Female skill wage gap (female skilled / female unskilled), effect of ICCT-embodied technological change
results.estimate: +1.283 (exogenous); +0.767 (unit elastic; text says 77 percentage points)
results.evidence: Table 7, p.34, row Delta(w_fh/w_fu)

results.indicator: Income share of male unskilled labour (w_mu l_mu / py), effect of ICCT-embodied technological change
results.estimate: -0.039 (exogenous labour supply); -0.070 (unit elastic; text: reduced by 7.0 percentage points, about half the observed decline)
results.evidence: Table 7, p.34, row Delta(w_mu l_mu/py); Conclusion p.36: 'about half of the decline in the income share of male unskilled labor'

results.indicator: Income shares of skilled labour (male, female), effect of ICCT-embodied technological change
results.estimate: male skilled +0.006 (exogenous), +0.014 (unit elastic); female skilled +0.017, +0.020
results.evidence: Table 7, p.34, rows Delta(w_mh l_mh/py) and Delta(w_fh l_fh/py)

results.indicator: Aggregate labour share (sum over the four labour types), effect of ICCT-embodied technological change
results.estimate: -0.001 (exogenous labour supply); -0.009 (unit elastic); -0.013 (labour supply elasticity 2). Observed log change in labour share 1980-2005 is -0.075 (Table 6)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.004 in each of these columns, so not distinguishable from zero in the exogenous case
results.evidence: Table 7, p.34, last row; text p.35: 'it is obscured when aggregated across different types of labor'. Abstract claims ICT contributes to 'declining labor shares'

results.indicator: Aggregate elasticity of substitution between ICCT capital and each labour type (production-function version, row labour type, column k_i)
results.estimate: male unskilled 1.07, female unskilled 1.05, male skilled 0.99, female skilled 0.76 (cost-function version: 1.67, 1.31, 1.12, 0.75); ICCT capital is more complementary to skilled than unskilled and to female than male labour
results.evidence: Table 4, p.29, column k_i; text p.29: 'ICCT capital is consistently more substitutable with male unskilled labor than with the other three types'

heterogeneity.finding: Capital-skill-gender complementarity found in manufacturing, utilities and services; in construction (under 10 percent female and college share) the four substitution parameters cannot be distinguished (restricted equal, p=0.39). Parameters differ across sectors (equality across sectors rejected at 2 percent level).
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 6.1.1 p.27 and footnotes 13-14; Table 2 p.27

heterogeneity.finding: Sign of ICCT effects is the same in all 11 countries (narrower gender gap, wider skill gap, higher skilled and lower unskilled income shares) but magnitudes differ widely; Denmark largest (skilled gender gap effect -3.325 vs -0.886 average), Finland smallest (-0.264). Effects on gender gaps shrink as labour supply is more elastic. Substitution between ICCT and unskilled labour smaller in 1990-2005 than 1980-1995.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table A3 p.68 (country columns); Table 7 p.34; Table 1 p.22-23

heterogeneity.finding: Not examined: all 11 economies are high-income advanced OECD members, so nothing can be said about middle- or low-income economies.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4.1 p.16 sample list

income_group_results.high: ICCT-embodied technological change narrows gender wage gaps, widens skill wage gaps, raises skilled and lowers unskilled labour income shares (Table 7, p.34); aggregate labour share effect not distinguishable from zero in the exogenous labour-supply case

n_specifications_reported: approximately 10-15 distinct model specifications (Tables 1-3, A1 alternative nesting, aggregate versus sectoral production function in Table A4), plus counterfactual variants (labour supply elasticity 0, 0.5, 1, 2; imperfect labour mobility in Table A2); Table 1 alone contains 144 coefficients (3 periods x 4 sectors x 4 labour types x 3 estimators)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Uses IV (lagged group population, lagged ICCT investment price) and first differences, and shows robustness to institutions, markups and country trends, which is more than a standard panel. But the exclusion restriction for lagged ICCT price is not tested and the headline effects are counterfactuals derived from a maintained nested-CES structure (steady-state, competitive markets), not directly identified causal effects of ICT adoption on outcomes.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 5.2 p.24-25 (instruments); Section 6.1.2 p.27-28 (robustness)

exposure_measurement.why: ICCT capital and its investment price come from EU KLEMS asset-level capital accounts, a direct measure of ICT capital stock and price decline. Rental prices are constructed and rely on assumptions (internal rate of return), partly checked with external rate of return.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 11 high-income countries with EU KLEMS 2008 coverage, 1980-2005, which stops before smartphones, broadband diffusion and AI; countries included when data available; no developing economies, so results do not speak to income-group differences.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 4.1 p.16: 'we include all countries and years in the sample for which required data are available'

outcome_measurement.why: Wages are labour compensation divided by hours, adjusted for age and education composition; education-based skill classification (college versus not) is coarse but standard. Labour shares built from the same accounts.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Results depend on the chosen four-level nesting order, the consumption elasticity set at 0.9 from Baqaee and Farhi, the choice of lagged population instrument (chosen because 'more precise'), and the labour-supply elasticity scenario; authors argue alternatives are rejected by tests (Table A1) and report robustness.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 5.1 p.23; Section 5.3 p.25; Section 6.1.1 p.27; Table A1 p.60

selective_reporting.why: Several instrument choices, robustness controls, labour-supply scenarios and country-level results are reported, including cases where effects are small or insignificant (non-ICCT capital, aggregate labour share). Introduction highlights unit-elastic labour supply numbers rather than the exogenous baseline in Table 7 first column, and abstract states 'declining labor shares' although the aggregate labour-share effect is small relative to its SE in the exogenous case.

venue_quality_concern: possible (text is arXiv:2005.12600v9, October 2025, a preprint; no journal named in the text; acknowledges anonymous referees)
notes: The text file title is 'The Race between Technology and Woman: Changes in Relative Wages and Labor Shares in OECD Countries' (arXiv v9, 25 Oct 2025), which differs from the title in the assignment ('The Race between Technological Progress and Female Advancement: Changes in Gender and Skill Premia in OECD Countries', 2020); this appears to be a later version of the same work, so check for a duplicate or earlier version in the review set (DUP). Effects are structural counterfactuals, not reduced-form estimates. Labels such as 'OECD countries' cover only 11 economies. Family coding: wage gaps coded as labour market (3), income shares as distribution (4). No instruction-like text found in the paper.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Structural CES model estimated by GMM/IV with its own data (EU KLEMS, 11 OECD economies, 1980-2005, four non-primary sectors); exposure is ICT capital (ICCT) and its falling price; outcomes are gender/skill wage gaps and labour income shares (labour market, distribution). Meets 10-economy rule. All economies high income, no income-group comparison. Headline effects are model-based counterfactuals.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Trade Convergence and Deglobalisation: A Cross-country Analysis
decision_rationale: Outcomes are trade-to-GDP ratios and cross-country dispersion of those ratios, which belong to none of the six outcome families. Reclassified from include after the second-pass check. Reversible: a human reviewer should confirm.
exposure_measure: Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index (AIRI), total score from 3 pillars (Government, Technology, Data and Infrastructure), 10 dimensions, 39 indicators; entered in logs. It measures government readiness to deliver AI public services, not AI adoption or use by firms.

sample.economies_or_groups: 12 advanced economies (USA, Singapore, UK, France, Korea, Japan, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Austria, Israel, Czech Republic) and 16 EMDEs (China, Russia, India, Chile, Hungary, Turkiye, Colombia, Viet Nam, Ukraine, Mexico, Armenia, Sri Lanka, Georgia, Kenya, Lao PDR, Ghana)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (advanced vs emerging/developing; EMDEs span upper-middle and lower-middle income; no clearly low-income country); income groups are not formally classified in the paper
sample.years: 2020-2023 for regressions (112 obs); 2005-2023 for GE inequality measures (without AIRI)

design.estimator: Fixed-effects panel regression of ln(trade ratio) on ln(AIRI) interacted with AE/EMDE group dummies (Breusch-Pagan LM and Hausman tests used for choice); beta-convergence panel regressions (absolute and conditional on ln AIRI); sigma-convergence via standard deviation; Generalised Entropy measures (MLD, Theil, half CV) with within/between decomposition.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country fixed effects; controls ln REER, ln FDI, ln GDP per capita (some columns omit GDP or FDI/REER); time dummies mentioned for convergence equation only. Standard errors not stated to be clustered.

results.estimate: Initial Y 0.007 (conditional, EMDEs); absolute 0.0116; ln AIRI coefficient 0.198
results.uncertainty: Initial Y SE 0.0056 (conditional); ln AIRI SE 0.0513, ***

results.estimate: -0.345 initial Y (absolute: -0.249); ln AIRI coefficient 0.278

results.estimate: SD rose from 7.34 (2020) to 9.42 (2023); AEs fell 17.87 to 16.94; global 13.51 to 13.81
results.evidence: Table A4. Text p.11: 'in the case of EMDEs, sigma-divergence is apparent'

results.indicator: Cross-country inequality (GE measures) of digital service trade/GDP, 2005-2023, between AEs and EMDEs
results.uncertainty: not reported (descriptive, no test); AIRI not entered into these measures
results.evidence: Tables A5 and A6, Figure 3. This is dispersion of a trade ratio across countries, not poverty or distribution within countries; recorded under family 4 only as an inequality-between-countries indicator and attributed to AIRI by the authors without any test

heterogeneity.finding: AIRI elasticity is larger for AEs than EMDEs for all three outcomes (0.916 vs 0.853; 0.445 vs 0.303; 0.558 vs 0.364). The authors state the impact is stronger for AEs but run no test of equality. Confidence intervals overlap for Trade/GDP (roughly 0.74-1.09 vs 0.72-0.99), so the gap is not shown to be significant. Beta-convergence in digital service trade holds for AEs but not for EMDEs.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table A2; text p.11: 'impact of AIRI is found to be stronger for AEs than EMDEs, as the associated coefficients are greater in magnitude'

heterogeneity.finding: Authors argue EMDEs with weak AI readiness (Ghana, Kenya, Georgia) fall into a 'low level equilibrium trap' in digital services and rely on merchandise trade; EMDEs with improving AIRI (China, India) are expected to expand digital service trade. This is narrative interpretation; no estimate by AIRI level within EMDEs is reported.
heterogeneity.evidence: pp.13-14: 'low growth in AIRI spells low growth (or even negative) in trade flows among EMDEs'

income_group_results.high: Advanced economies (12; mostly high income): ln AIRI elasticity 0.9158 (Trade/GDP), 0.4451 (digital service trade/GDP), 0.5584 (merchandise trade/GDP), all significant at 1% (Table A2). Sigma and beta convergence found for all three ratios.
income_group_results.upper_middle: Not separated. Included in the EMDE group (e.g. China, Mexico, Turkiye, Colombia, Russia); EMDE elasticities 0.8534, 0.3032, 0.3644 (Table A2).
income_group_results.lower_middle: Not separated. Included in the EMDE group (e.g. India, Viet Nam, Kenya, Ghana, Lao PDR, Sri Lanka); pooled into the EMDE estimates.
income_group_results.low: not reported (no low-income country appears to be in the sample; classification not given)

n_specifications_reported: about 20 regression columns (3 FE columns in Table A2; 18 beta-convergence regressions in Table A3), plus descriptive sigma and GE tables; the paper also refers to a 'robustness check' control set that is not reported

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('AI can accelerate trade') drawn from FE regressions of trade ratios on a readiness index with no instrument or timing strategy. Reverse causation is plausible (trade-open, digitalised economies score higher on readiness), the sample is 4 years, and the AIRI has little within-country variation, so FE identification is thin. GE and sigma analyses attribute inequality patterns to AIRI without including it.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Conclusions p.16: 'AI can accelerate trade as the coefficient of AIRI is positive and highly statistically significant'; Eq. (1) p.9; Limitations p.16

exposure_measurement.why: AIRI measures government readiness to deliver AI public services, not AI adoption, investment or capability in the private sector or trade. Only 2023 scores and ranks are shown (Table 1), and the paper does not explain how the index varies over 2020-2023. Scores may be partly constructed from digital infrastructure and data indicators correlated with digital trade.
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.5 'AIRI attempts to examine country-wise readiness of the government to deliver AI as public services'; Table 1 (2023 only)

selection_of_countries_years.why: 28 countries chosen as 'representative' with no stated rule; 12 AEs and 16 EMDEs. Only 4 years (2020-2023), all in the COVID shock and recovery. Trade/GDP values extrapolated for Japan, USA, Viet Nam (2023) and for Lao PDR for the whole period. No low-income countries.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.9 'year, 2020-2023'; Table 2 note on extrapolated values; p.16 limitation 'data on AIRI is only available from 2020 onwards'

outcome_measurement.why: Trade/GDP, merchandise trade/GDP (World Bank) and digital service trade/GDP (WTO) are standard measures, but none is a productivity or welfare outcome, and extrapolated values enter the data. Trade/GDP is mechanically affected by GDP, which is also a control and in the denominator.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Controls differ across columns in Table A2 (GDP absent in digital column; the 'controls included after the robustness check' row implies a search over controls), AIRI is interacted with group only, and no test of the AE-EMDE difference is given. Several coefficients carry significance stars that do not fit their reported SEs (ln REER -0.0832 with SE 0.0712 marked *; ln REER and ln FDI SEs inconsistent in scale). Conditional beta-convergence regressions have very small SEs (0.0043) and within R2 near 0.99 on 36-84 observations, which suggests specification problems (e.g. mechanical correlation of lagged level, AIRI and the constant).
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table A2 rows LNREER, LNFDI and 'Controls included after the Robustness check'; Table A3 conditional columns

selective_reporting.why: Control-variable results are 'not discussed' beyond the table, robustness checks are mentioned but not shown, and the narrative stresses significant results. Non-significant EMDE digital-service convergence is reported. Between-group R2 values in Table A2 are near zero, which is not discussed. The correlation text and the Table A2 column order are inconsistent.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.11 'regression result of the control variables ... corroborates the theoretical literature, hence not discussed here'; Table A2 R2 rows

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Foreign Trade Review (Sage, Indian Institute of Foreign Trade), 2025. Table A2 column header order (Trade, Digital service, Merchandise) differs from the text order (Trade, Merchandise, Digital), so the assignment of coefficients to digital vs merchandise outcomes follows the table header and may be wrong. Table A2 shows within R2 of 0.8584 for Trade/GDP but 0.0561 and 0.1868 for the others, and between and overall R2 near zero. The abstract and text call the AE/EMDE split '28 nations in two sets' (12 + 16). Claims of 'deglobalisation' and 'polarisation' rest on descriptive GE time series (2005-2023) that do not include AIRI, and the link to AI is asserted, not tested; GE measures also rise sharply for 2020 (COVID). The text cites 'Baldwin et al., 2004' where the reference list has 2024. Outcome fit is borderline (trade ratios, not output, labour, poverty or welfare); family 2 was used for the digital-versus-merchandise composition framing. The 'pollution haven' and 'low level equilibrium trap' interpretations are speculative. No text in the paper attempted to direct the extraction.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Quantitative with own FE and convergence estimation, AI exposure (government AI readiness), 28 economies with explicit AE vs EMDE comparison, so the economy-count and design criteria hold. The outcome criterion fails: the dependent variables are Trade/GDP, merchandise trade/GDP and digital-service trade/GDP, which are not output/productivity, labour-market, poverty/distribution, living-standard or resource-cost outcomes. Digital versus merchandise trade composition is not structural change of the economy (no sectoral output or employment shares), and the GE measures are cross-country dispersion of trade ratios, not income distribution. Recommend exclusion (at most borderline).

sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Groups are AE vs EMDE as defined by the authors; the paper gives no income classification. Outside the paper, some EMDEs listed (e.g. Chile, Hungary) are high-income by World Bank classification; the paper does not say so
sample_corrections.years: 2020-2023 (112 observations = 28 x 4; beta-convergence 84 observations = 28 x 3 intervals); GE inequality 2005-2023 without AIRI - confirmed

second_pass.problems: Record is faithful to the tables. Main problem is eligibility (outcome not in the listed families). Also note inconsistency between Table A2 column order and text order, and the unsupported claim in the abstract that inequality in digital trade is rising in EMDEs (true only after 2020).

title: AI capability and labor productivity in low- and middle-income countries: An absorptive capacity approach
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 63 low- and lower-middle-income economies (2005-2019) estimating the association of a PCA-based AI capability index (AI-related hardware imports plus digital/financial/electricity readiness) with labour productivity. Meets AI sample threshold (>=3 economies) and outcome family 1; the AI exposure is a loose proxy, which is handled in risk of bias rather than eligibility.
technology: artificial intelligence (AI-related hardware imports, capability index)
ICT in general (internet use, fixed broadband, mobile cellular subscriptions as index components)
exposure_measure: National 'AI Capability Index' = first principal component (PCA, standardised) of six variables: annual (flow) or 3-year cumulative (stock) per-capita AI-related hardware imports (23 HS 6-digit categories from CEPII BACI, selected using UNCTAD ICT goods list, expert judgement and ChatGPT), plus internet users (% pop), fixed broadband per 100, mobile cellular per 100, electricity access (%), and account ownership (%). Five of six components are general ICT/infrastructure/finance indicators. Alternative interaction specification uses log AI imports per capita x a PCA Domestic Readiness Index; a narrow index uses only GPU/TPU/FPGA/ASIC/memory HS codes.

sample.economies_or_groups: Low- and middle-income countries; initial panel of 80 LMICs, effective sample 63 with complete data; country list not given in the main text. Heterogeneity analysis only splits low-income vs lower-middle-income.
sample.income_groups_covered: low and lower-middle (the income dummy is LMI=1, low-income=0); upper-middle inclusion unclear

design.estimator: Pooled OLS, random effects, two-way fixed effects (preferred; country-clustered robust SEs); interaction FE models; two-step system GMM (xtabond2, Windmeijer-corrected, collapsed instruments, 30-35 instruments); FE with regressors lagged 1-6 years.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country and year FE; controls: gross fixed capital formation, human capital index, population growth, strength of legal rights index, R&D % GDP, FDI % GDP, trade % GDP. GMM treats lagged productivity and the AI index as endogenous using own lags. Authors explicitly say estimates are associations, not causal.

results.estimate: 0.0920 log points (about 9.2%) per 1 SD; pooled OLS 0.450, RE 0.115
results.evidence: Table 4, p.10: 'AI Capability Index (Flow-based) 0.450*** 0.115*** 0.0920***'; abstract: '9.20-9.37% increase in labor productivity'

results.estimate: 0.0937 log points (about 9.4%) per 1 SD; pooled OLS 0.449, RE 0.118
results.evidence: Table 5, p.10: 'AI Capability Index (Stock-based) 0.449*** 0.118*** 0.0937***'

results.indicator: Log labour productivity; AI-related hardware imports x domestic readiness interaction (TWFE, broad flow measure)
results.estimate: Log AI imports per capita 0.0497; interaction with Readiness Index 0.0108
results.uncertainty: t = 3.100 (imports), t = 2.106 (interaction), p<0.05 for interaction; narrow measure interaction 0.00952, t=1.812 (p<0.1)
results.evidence: Table 6, p.11, columns (2) and (4); text p.11: 'interaction coefficient is positive and significant at the 5% level for broad AI imports and at the 10% level for narrow'

results.indicator: Log labour productivity; AI imports x readiness, stock-based
results.estimate: Interaction 0.00986 (broad stock, t=1.736, p<0.1); narrow stock interaction 0.00901 (t not significant, 1.386)
results.uncertainty: see estimate; narrow stock interaction not significant
results.evidence: Table 7, p.12, columns (2) and (4); text: 'it is not statistically significant for the narrow stock-based measure'

results.indicator: Log labour productivity; system GMM with lagged AI Capability Index (flow-based)
results.estimate: 0.0681 to 0.0716 (spec 6 = 0.0681); lagged dependent variable about 0.91-0.93
results.uncertainty: z = 1.971 in fullest spec (p<0.05); AR(2) p=0.250, Hansen p=0.179; N=810, 35 instruments
results.evidence: Table 11, p.15: 'L.AI Capability Index (Flow-based) ... 0.0681**' (column 6)

results.estimate: 0.0655 in fullest spec (range 0.0655-0.0733)
results.uncertainty: z = 1.810 (p<0.1) in fullest spec; AR(2) p=0.214, Hansen p=0.140
results.evidence: Table 12, p.16: 'L.AI Capability Index (Stock-based) ... 0.0655*' (column 6)

results.indicator: Log labour productivity; FE with AI Capability Index (flow-based) lagged 1 to 6 years
results.uncertainty: t = 5.423 (lag 1) to 3.821 (lag 6); all p<0.01; N falls from 810 to 503
results.evidence: Table 13, p.16; text: 'remains positive and highly statistically significant across all lags from one to six years'

results.indicator: Log labour productivity; narrow AI-hardware-only index (flow and stock), TWFE
results.estimate: 0.0859 (flow, spec 6) and 0.0859 (stock, spec 6)
results.evidence: Tables D.5 and D.6, Appendix D, pp.23-24: 'AI Capability Index ... 0.0859***'

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of AI index with lower-middle-income dummy (vs low-income) is small and insignificant in all specifications (FE: 0.00413, t=0.223); no evidence that returns differ between low and lower-middle income. Authors conclude effect is similar across groups.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 10, p.14, column (5): 'Low Middle Income * AI Capability Index (Flow-based) ... 0.00413 (0.223)'

heterogeneity.finding: Association of AI-related imports with productivity is larger where domestic readiness (connectivity, electricity, financial inclusion index) is higher (positive interaction, about 0.01).
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 6, p.11: 'Domestic Readiness Index * Log of AI Import Per Capita (Flow) 0.0108** (2.106)'

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of AI index with FDI (% GDP) is negative (-0.00126, p<0.05), with gross fixed capital formation positive and marginal (0.00114, p<0.1). Authors compute a sign-reversal FDI threshold of 73.6% of GDP (inside sample range but in extreme tail); GFCF threshold -52.2% (infeasible). Net marginal effect at means 0.0868.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: FDI 73.6% of GDP (sign change); GFCF none (-52.2, outside range)
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 8 col (4), p.12 and Table 9, p.14: 'Net marginal effect of AI capability at means 0.0868'

income_group_results.high: not applicable (high-income economies not in sample)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (unclear whether any upper-middle economies are included; the heterogeneity dummy contrasts only LMI vs low-income)
income_group_results.lower_middle: FE: marginal effect not different from low-income (interaction 0.00413, t=0.223); implied marginal effect about 0.0954 (0.0913+0.0041) from Table 10, derived not reported
income_group_results.low: FE reference-group coefficient on flow-based AI index 0.0913 (t=5.898), Table 10 column (5)

n_specifications_reported: approximately 80 regression columns (Tables 4-8, 10-13 and D.1-D.6, including pooled/RE/FE, GMM, lags, narrow indices)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Two-way FE plus controls, a system GMM with internal instruments, and 1-6 year lags are used, and the authors repeatedly disclaim causality. But the index is a generic digital/infrastructure development composite, so time-varying omitted factors (reforms, structural change, overall development) and reverse causation (richer countries import more hardware and have better connectivity) are not excluded; GMM instruments are internal lags only, and the AI index is a lagged regressor in GMM. No external instrument or event timing.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Sec. 5.6, p.14-15: 'does not fully address potential simultaneity'; Sec. 5.7, p.16-17: 'does not eliminate endogeneity arising from time-varying omitted factors'; Sec. 6.4: 'results remain associative'

exposure_measurement.why: Only 1 of 6 index components is AI-related (per-capita imports of 23 dual-use ICT hardware HS codes, partly selected with ChatGPT; includes laptops, phones, monitors, keyboards). The other five are general ICT, electricity and financial inclusion. PCA first component therefore mostly measures general digital/infrastructure development; the authors state it does not capture realised AI use. Narrow index (GPU/TPU/ASIC etc.) gives similar results but still reflects imports of chips that are largely general electronics and is also mixed into the index with the same readiness variables. Readiness variables come from an imputed dataset.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Sec. 4.1.1, p.7 and fn 2-4: 'many of these goods are not uniquely AI-specific'; Sec. 4.1, p.7: 'does not capture realized AI use or economic outcomes'; Table 1, p.6

selection_of_countries_years.why: 63 of an initial 80 LMICs retained based on data availability for all variables; effective N=871 of up to 945 country-years (unbalanced), yet descriptive statistics show 1200 obs for many variables, indicating the 80-country panel was completed by multiple imputation (MICE). Country list not shown in main text. No bias analysis of excluded countries; sample restricted to 2005-2019, pre-generative AI, so results describe general ICT/hardware accumulation.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Sec. 4, p.6: 'effective sample ... comprises a robust panel of 63 LMICs'; Table 2, p.7 (obs 1200 vs 1093 for labour productivity)

outcome_measurement.why: Log real GDP per worker from WDI is a standard measure, but the paper defines it inconsistently (GDP / total labour force in Table 1; GDP per capita divided by total employment in Sec. 4.3; real GDP per worker in Sec. 5.1). WDI data quality for low-income economies and the imputation of some covariates add noise.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 1 p.6: 'Log (GDP constant 2015 USD/Total Labor Force)'; Sec. 4.3, p.9: 'GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) divided by total employment'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Index weights are data-driven (PCA), flow versus stock versions, broad versus narrow HS lists, many control sets and estimators were tried (about 80 specs). However, headline TWFE results are stable across controls, with and without year effects, and estimators; no p-hacking signals beyond the flexibility of index construction. Several control coefficients (human capital) flip sign in GMM; some FE results (GFCF) only marginally significant. Construct overlap between AI index components and development level may mechanically load on productivity.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables D.1-D.3 pp.21-22, Sec. 5.8; Sec. 6.4: 'composite index may also overlap with broader digital and infrastructural development'

selective_reporting.why: Single outcome (labour productivity) with all reported AI-index estimates positive; null or weak results are reported where they occur (insignificant narrow-stock interaction, insignificant income interaction, insignificant R&D/FDI/trade). No pre-registration or mention of unreported specifications; the authors choose a PCA construction and not alternative indices (e.g., equal weights, other components) in the main text. Index diagnostics in appendix only.
selective_reporting.evidence: Sec. 5.3, p.11-12 (narrow stock interaction not significant); Sec. 5.5, p.14; Appendices A-D

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: No text attempting to direct the reviewer was found. Technovation (Elsevier), open access, accepted July 2026. Key caveat for synthesis: despite the AI label, the exposure is a composite dominated by general ICT/infrastructure indicators (internet, broadband, mobile, electricity, account ownership) plus imported ICT hardware, so results speak as much to ICT/digital infrastructure as to AI; the stream is coded 'both'. Dependent variable is in logs, so '9.2%' is the approximate effect per 1 SD of the index (exp(0.092)-1 is about 9.6%). Abstract range 9.20-9.37% comes from flow vs stock FE coefficients (0.0920, 0.0937). Text states pooled OLS magnitudes of about 45% are inflated by omitted-variable bias. The HS code list and its AI relevance were partly generated with ChatGPT (disclosed in fn 2). Table D.3 repeats column labels (1)-(3) twice. Income-group analysis only compares low vs lower-middle income, so it cannot speak to upper-middle or high-income economies; despite the 'low- and middle-income' framing the sample's coverage of upper-middle income countries is unclear. Table 6 and 7 observation counts 871/870; Table 4 labels 'Number of cnumber' in Tables 6-7.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Quantitative panel (TWFE, system GMM, lags) on 63 low/middle-income economies 2005-2019; exposure is an AI Capability Index (AI-related hardware imports plus ICT/electricity/finance indicators), outcome is labour productivity; income-group comparison (low vs lower-middle) included. Eligible under AI (3+ economies) and under ICT in general, since five of six index components are general ICT or infrastructure indicators.

title: Can Artificial Intelligence Drive Sustainable Growth? Empirical Evidence on the AI-Energy-Growth Nexus in Advanced Economies
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (fixed effects, Driscoll-Kraay SEs) of AI investment (an ICT-trade proxy and Stanford private AI investment) on GDP per capita and energy use per capita in 9 economies (G7, China, South Korea). Meets the AI threshold of at least 3 economies and has outcomes in families 1 and 6.
technology: ICT (goods and services export shares used as an AI proxy)
exposure_measure: Models A1/A2: 'AIProxy' = mean of ICT goods exports (% of goods exports) and ICT service exports (% of service exports), an ICT-trade composite used as a proxy for AI investment (first-differenced). Models B1/B2: log of real total AI private investment (Stanford Global AI Vibrancy Tool, nominal USD deflated by US CPI). Interacted with renewable electricity capacity share (RE).

sample.economies_or_groups: G7 countries (USA, Japan, Germany, UK, France, Italy, Canada), China, South Korea
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported explicitly (described as 'advanced and emerging economies'; G7 and Korea high-income, China emerging)
sample.years: Models A: 2010-2025 (T=16, 144 obs); Models B: 2017-2025 stated in estimation sections (2017-2024 stated in data/model sections), T=9; some recent-year values extrapolated

design.estimator: Country fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay robust standard errors (Stata xtscc, lag 2); no cointegration found so short-run models only; some variables first-differenced, others in levels
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country FE; controls: ln energy use per capita, ln CO2 per capita, R&D % GDP, IMF financial development index, trade % GDP, ln energy price level (PPP), GFCF % GDP; AI x renewable-share interaction

results.estimate: coefficient not printed in text (Table S16 is in the supplement); text says p = 0.807; Discussion describes sign as 'positive but not statistically significant'
results.evidence: Sec 5.1, p.23-24: 'changes in AI activity (ΔAIProxy) do not have a statistically significant direct effect on economic growth in the short run (p = 0.807)'

results.evidence: Sec 5.1, p.24: 'negative and weakly significant coefficient (β = −0.0002, p < 0.10)'

results.indicator: Model B1: ln AI private investment on ln GDP per capita (level)
results.evidence: Sec 5.2, p.27: 'negative but statistically insignificant coefficient (β = −0.0134, p > 0.10)'

results.evidence: Sec 5.2, p.27: 'highly significant and positive (β = 0.0004, p < 0.01)'

results.estimate: not reported in text (both terms insignificant; turning point arithmetic uses -0.0026 and 0.0003)
results.evidence: Sec 5.1, p.24: 'coefficients of both AI activity (ΔAIProxy) and its squared term (ΔAIProxy2) are statistically insignificant'

results.indicator: Model B2: ln AI investment and its square on ln energy use per capita
results.estimate: linear beta = 0.0898; squared beta = -0.0021 (inverted U, turning point about 21.4)
results.evidence: Sec 5.2, p.28: 'positive and statistically significant effect on energy demand (β = 0.0898, p < 0.05)'; squared 'β = −0.0021, p < 0.05'

heterogeneity.finding: Renewable electricity capacity share as moderator of AI on GDP per capita: interaction weakly negative with the ICT-trade proxy (Model A1) but positive and significant with Stanford AI investment (Model B1); sign flips across the two AI measures and samples.
Nonlinear AI-energy use relation (inverted U): insignificant in A2 (implied turning point 43.3 as printed), significant in B2 (turning point about 21.4).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: 21.4 (Model B2); 43.3 as printed for Model A2

n_specifications_reported: 4 main models (A1, A2, B1, B2), one specification each; no further robustness tables in the main text

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Contemporaneous FE regressions with N=9 and no instrument, lag or timing strategy; GDP per capita and AI investment/ICT exports likely co-determined. Energy use per capita (itself an outcome in other models) is a control in the growth model. Interpretation uses causal language ('effects').

exposure_measurement.why: Models A use ICT goods and services export shares (trade composition) as an 'AI proxy', which does not measure AI adoption or investment; the authors concede it 'may capture broader digitalisation effects'. Models B use Stanford private AI investment (nominal USD deflated by US CPI), a narrow flow measure that is closer to AI investment but covers only 2017-2024/25.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Sec 4.1, p.12-13: 'AIProxy may capture broader digitalisation effects beyond pure investment'

selection_of_countries_years.why: Nine hand-picked economies (G7, China, Korea), so little scope for generalisation; data-availability driven windows; missing recent values (including the whole of 2025 for several series) filled by growth-rate extrapolation and a moving-average smoother, so part of the sample is imputed.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Sec 4.1 p.15 and Sec 4.2 p.15-16: 'missing observations ... completed using standard and conservative extrapolation methods'

outcome_measurement.why: WDI real GDP per capita and energy use per capita are standard, but the 2025 values and some inputs are extrapolated; A1 uses first differences of log GDPpc while B1 uses the log level, so the outcomes are not comparable across models.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Sec 4.6 p.20: variables 'in first differences' (A) vs 'levels' (B)

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Mix of differenced and level variables chosen per model by unit-root tests with admitted unreliable CIPS at T=9; lag(2) Driscoll-Kraay SEs with T=9 and N=9; very high within R2 and F-stat (14,482.80) in B1 suggest overfitting or level-variable issues; two different AI proxies and samples; no robustness exercises beyond switching proxy.

selective_reporting.why: Abstract highlights the positive significant AI x renewable interaction (B1) while the A1 interaction is negative and weak; the headline is not clearly pre-specified. Full regression tables are in the Supplement; the main text reports only selected coefficients.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract vs Sec 5.1 p.24 and Sec 6 p.29

venue_quality_concern: possible (MDPI Sustainability; sloppy details such as a mis-expanded abbreviation list, an arithmetic error in a turning-point calculation, Figure 1 produced by an AI tool, and heavy data extrapolation)
notes: Regression tables (S16, S17, S23, S24) are in supplementary material and not in the text file, so only coefficients quoted in the prose are extracted. Internal inconsistencies: Model B window is given as 2017-2025 (Sec 4.6, 5.2) and 2017-2024 (Sec 4.1, 4.4); B2 text mixes 'AIProxy' and 'lnAIInvest'; Sec 4.1 says the main analysis used a long-run proxy but Sec 4.6 says first-differenced short-run models; the A2 turning point as printed (0.0026/0.00006 = 43.3) appears to mis-compute 2 x 0.0003 (which is 0.0006, giving about 4.3), and the sign of the A2 squared term is not stated; in Sec 5.2 the first sentence of Table S24 discussion refers to 'AIProxy' though Model B2 uses lnAIInvest; Sec 6 says A1 AIProxy coefficient is positive while it is not printed. Abbreviation list has misassigned definitions (e.g. G7, OECD, FMOLS). The author used an AI tool to draw Figure 1 (stated in its caption). Energy use per capita is the family 6 outcome (resource cost); AI exposure in Models A is an ICT-trade measure, so stream is AI but the A-model evidence is effectively about ICT export intensity. No text in the paper attempted to direct the extraction.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own FE estimation with Driscoll-Kraay SEs; exposure is AI (Stanford private AI investment in B models; ICT export-share composite, an ICT measure, in A models); 9 economies >= 3 for AI; outcomes are GDP per capita (output) and energy use per capita (resource cost). Eligible, although the A-model exposure is an ICT-trade composite and not a measure of AI.

sample_corrections.years: B models: abstract, Sec 5.2 and Table S18 text give 2017-2025 (T = 9, consistent with 9 years), whereas Sec 4.1, 4.4 and 4.5 say 2017-2024; the T = 9 count supports 2017-2025. A models 2010-2025 (T = 16, 144 obs) is correct.
sample_corrections.controls: Energy models (A2, B2) also include ln GDP per capita and RE as regressors, and growth models (A1, B1) include ln energy demand; the record's control list omits that GDPpc is a regressor in the energy equations.

corrections.correction: B2 turning point 21.4 is correct. The A2 turning point is an arithmetic error in the paper: with the printed -0.0026 and 0.0003, 2 x 0.0003 = 0.0006 (printed as 0.00006), giving 0.0026/0.0006 = 4.33, not 43.3. Both A2 terms are insignificant, so no turning point is estimated; the authors' claim that 43.3 lies 'well beyond the observed range' rests on the erroneous number. Record should say 'as printed, erroneous'.

second_pass.problems: No invented numbers found. Points to flag: (1) A2 turning point 43.3 is an arithmetic error (should be about 4.33 from the printed coefficients); the record kept 'as printed' but heterogeneity item should carry the correction. (2) B-model sample years inconsistent within the paper (2017-2024 vs 2017-2025); T = 9 supports 2017-2025. (3) Record controls list omits that GDPpc/energy cross-enter the two equation types. (4) Main text does not print the A1 and A2 coefficients (supplement), so only p-values and signs are verifiable for results 1 and 5. (5) The paper's text calls the B2 exposure 'AIProxy' although B2 uses Stanford AI investment; record handles this correctly.

Sec. 6 (p. 10): 'our results represent theoretical model implications under specified parameters rather than empirical estimates'. Headline numbers (1% more robots: GDP per worker +0.29%, skill premium +0.23%; 1% more AI: GDP +0.03%, skill premium -0.018%) are model outputs under fixed parameters (theta 0.75, gamma 0.33, phi 0.5, beta1 0.9, beta2 0.95, beta3 0.66), with TFP calibrated so that model GDP matches data. The text refers to Table 8 in Section 5.4 and to a 'reviewer' within the article. Section 3.3.7 refers to Section 3.3.5 for within-country SDs of LGDP, but these appear in Table 7 (Section 4.6).
