title: IMPACT OF ICT ON ECONOMIC GROWTH: CASE OF OECD AND MENA COUNTRIES
decision_rationale: Quantitative system-GMM growth regressions of internet, mobile, fixed-telephone and ICT-import indicators for 18 OECD and 14 MENA economies (32 economies, explicit region comparison); outcome is GDP growth (family 1).
exposure_measure: Internet use rate (INTERNET), mobile subscriptions (MOBILE), fixed telephone subscriptions (TELEPH), ICT goods imports as share of total imports (ICT_IMPORT); WDI 2024. Entered one at a time (one ICT variable per specification), plus interactions with secondary enrolment (CAPH) and with private credit/GDP (DF).

sample.n_economies: 32 (18 OECD + 14 MENA)
sample.economies_or_groups: OECD: Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Poland, Portugal, Sweden, Spain, Switzerland, UK, USA (footnote 2; figures also label Australia). MENA: Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Syria, Tunisia, UAE.
sample.income_groups_covered: OECD mostly high income (Hungary, Poland, Greece etc. high/upper-middle); MENA mixed (high-income Gulf states, upper-middle, lower-middle e.g. Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia); no low-income; comparison is by region not income group

design.estimator: Two-step system GMM (Blundell-Bond), Stata xtbond2
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged dependent variable, investment rate, private credit/GDP, government spending/GDP, trade openness, inflation, secondary enrolment; country-specific and year-specific effects stated in the equation.

results.indicator: Growth, internet use, MENA (Table 6 spec 1)
Growth, mobile subscriptions, MENA (Table 6 spec 2)
results.evidence: Table 6 p.24.

results.indicator: Growth, ICT goods imports, MENA (Table 6 spec 3)
results.evidence: Table 6 p.24; text p.20: 'positive and statistically significant effect of approximately 10% (Specification 3, p-value = 0.064)'.

results.indicator: Growth, fixed telephone, MENA (Table 6 spec 4)
results.evidence: Table 6 p.24.

results.indicator: Growth, fixed telephone, OECD (Table 5 spec 1)
Growth, ICT goods imports, OECD (Table 5 spec 2)
results.evidence: Table 5 p.22.

results.indicator: Growth, mobile subscriptions, OECD (Table 5 spec 3)
results.evidence: Table 5 p.22; text p.21: 'negative and insignificant effect (Table 5, scenario 3, p-value = 0.393)'.

results.indicator: Growth, internet use, OECD (direct effect)
results.estimate: not reported in Table 5 (INTERNET row is blank, only 3 of 4 specifications shown); Table 7 spec 4 with interaction: INTERNET 0.01659737, INTERNET x CAPH 0.0014415
results.uncertainty: p=0.000 for both in Table 7 spec 4
results.evidence: Table 5 p.22 has an empty 'INTERNET' row; text p.21 says all OECD ICT effects are positive and significant except mobile; Table 7 p.26.

heterogeneity.finding: Direct ICT effects are positive and significant for OECD for fixed telephone and ICT imports, null for MENA except ICT imports at p=0.064; author concludes OECD uses ICT more effectively. Region comparison, not income-group estimation.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 5 and 6 pp.22-24; abstract: 'OECD countries have been more proactive and effective than MENA countries'.

heterogeneity.finding: ICT x secondary enrolment interactions positive and significant in OECD for ICT imports (0.00073, p=0.017) and internet (0.00144, p<0.01); not significant in MENA. Author states that the threshold condition (opposite sign of ICT and interaction) is not met in either region so ICT impact 'cannot be demonstrated'.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 7-8 pp.26-27; text p.25: 'This is not the case for the two regions under consideration'.

heterogeneity.finding: ICT x private credit interactions positive and significant for OECD (fixed telephone, internet, mobile) and for MENA (internet, mobile, fixed telephone); the fixed-telephone effect in MENA turns positive above a financial-development threshold of 88% of GDP (author's figure; -0.01515413/0.00017465 is about 86.8).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: 88% private credit to GDP (fixed telephone, MENA); computed ratio is about 86.8
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 9-10 pp.29-30; text p.28 and footnote 3 'Limit= -0.01515413 /0.00017465'.

income_group_results.high: OECD (mostly high income): fixed telephone and ICT imports positively associated with growth; mobile null; internet significant only in interaction model
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported (some MENA and OECD members fall here but no split)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported (Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia within MENA pooled sample)

n_specifications_reported: about 23 (Table 5: 3, Table 6: 4, Tables 7-10: 4 each)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: System GMM with internal instruments is the only strategy; instrument validity relies on Sargan tests (p up to 1.000), N=14 MENA countries with only 73 observations and 10 instruments, AR2 p-values below 0.10 in several models contrary to the text, and no external instrument. Causal language ('impact', 'catalyst') is used.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Tables 5-10 (Observations, instruments, AR2, Sarganp); text p.11: 'p-value greater than 10%' vs Table 6 AR2 0.0629-0.0962 and Table 10 spec 1 AR2 0.0172.

exposure_measurement.why: Penetration rates and ICT import share are standard but coarse; ICT imports as share of total imports is not a measure of ICT adoption; telephone and mobile subscriptions saturated in OECD.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Selection of 18 OECD and 14 MENA countries is not justified (OECD has 38 members; Australia appears in figures but not in country list; Iraq, Libya, Syria with conflicts included); effective observations (156 and 73) are far below the potential country-year count, so panel is heavily unbalanced; very short 2010-2023 window includes COVID and conflict shocks.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Footnotes 1-2 p.9; Tables 5-6 observation counts; Figure 1 labels Australia.

outcome_measurement.why: The text defines the dependent variable as growth of real GDP, but the tables report L.log_PIB (log of GDP) as lagged dependent variable and descriptive statistics for TX_PIB show a MENA growth range of -32.2 to +121.8 and mean -0.515, which is implausible for real GDP growth; the outcome is therefore unclear.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Equation p.10; Table 3 p.15 (TX_PIB max 121.78, kurtosis 63.6); Tables 5-10 'L.log_PIB'.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four ICT variables entered separately across six tables with interactions; discussion of results frequently misreports signs or significance (e.g. says financial development 'remains positive' in OECD while text on inflation says OECD effects significant only for specs 1 and 3, 'four scenarios' for OECD but only three columns in Table 5); threshold discussion applies a rule that the author's own results fail but is then used elsewhere.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: pp.18-21 narrative versus Tables 5-6; p.28 threshold statement.

selective_reporting.why: OECD Table 5 omits the INTERNET specification entirely (blank row, three columns) although the text discusses four scenarios; the abstract and conclusion state ICT promotes growth and that OECD benefit more, while most MENA ICT coefficients are null and the author's own threshold test says ICT impact 'cannot be demonstrated'.
selective_reporting.evidence: Table 5 p.22; abstract; text p.25 and conclusion p.31-32.

venue_quality_concern: possible (venue not clearly identified in the text, only '2024 406(11)' header; multiple internal inconsistencies between text and tables, duplicated paragraph in Section 2.4, references listed that are not relevant, e.g. Keller 1998 on brand management, and wrong dates, suggest weak editorial review)
notes: Internal contradictions: text claims four OECD scenarios but Table 5 shows three; text claims AR2 p>10% for all models but several tables report AR2 below 0.10; the correlation-matrix paragraph in section 2.4 is repeated verbatim and contradicts itself (inflation described as both positively and negatively correlated); text describes inflation in MENA as 'positive and statistically insignificant' and then interprets this as harmful; MENA growth descriptive statistics are implausible (max 121.78). References include items unrelated to the study (Keller 1998) and some cited sources (Global Risks Report) used to support empirical claims. Author's text says 'Table 2' reports MENA correlations in places. Only direct-effect results (Tables 5-6) were taken as headline. No instruction-like text found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own system-GMM estimation, 32 economies (18 OECD, 14 MENA), exposures internet, mobile, fixed telephone and ICT imports, outcome GDP growth (output). Eligible, although the dependent variable is inconsistently defined (see problems).

sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: The paper gives no World Bank income classification and no income-group results; comparison is by region only. The record's 'no low-income' is not supported by the text (Syria is on the MENA list and is World Bank low-income by external classification), and its remark on OECD members being 'high/upper-middle' is not from the paper.

corrections.correction: The OECD direct internet coefficient is not in Table 5 (blank INTERNET row, three columns) while the text says all OECD ICT effects but mobile are positive and significant. Direction should be recorded as not reported / unverifiable, not 'mixed'. Table 7 spec 4 INTERNET 0.01659737*** is the coefficient at CAPH=0 in an interaction model and is not a direct effect; Table 9 spec 3 INTERNET 0.00759160* (p=0.068) is likewise conditional.
corrections.quote: the effect of all the variables mapping information and communication technologies (ICTs) is positive and significant, with the exception of the variable of mobile telephony

second_pass.problems: No invented numbers. Issues to carry: (1) 'two-step' in the record's estimator cannot be confirmed because the Table 5 note is truncated ('stage Generalized Method of Moments'). (2) The record's country lists, years and observation counts (156, 73) are right; the text says the model includes both country and year effects, with no coefficients shown. (3) The record places OECD under 'high income' and states no low-income economies; the paper does not classify income. (4) Direction 'mixed' for result 8 should be 'not reported'. (5) Text claim 'OECD fixed telephone, internet, mobile all positive in interaction with credit' is true only at 10 percent for fixed telephone (p=0.091).

title: IMPACT OF DIGITALISATION ON PRODUCTIVITY GROWTH IN EU MEMBER STATES
decision_rationale: Panel fixed-effects regression of TFP on the DESI digitalisation index for 27 EU countries plus the EU aggregate, 2017-2022; ICT exposure, at least 10 economies and a productivity outcome are all met.
technology: ICT in general (digitalisation, DESI composite covering connectivity, human capital, integration of digital technology, digital public services)
exposure_measure: European Commission Digital Economy and Society Index (DESI), natural log, 32 indicators in 4 sub-indices

sample.n_economies: 27 EU member states plus the EU aggregate (28 units)
sample.economies_or_groups: EU-27 and EU as a whole
sample.income_groups_covered: high (EU members; paper gives no income classification)

design.estimator: Country fixed-effects OLS (within) on log TFP; robustness with FE plus Durbin-Watson/AR(1) residual correction and GLS random effects with Breusch-Pagan LM test
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country FE; log exports/GDP, log imports/GDP, log IPR receipts, log tertiary-educated labour share; extended: FDI (% GDP), log R&D, log Economic Freedom index. No year effects.

results.indicator: log TFP (Cobb-Douglas residual) on log DESI, basic specification
results.estimate: 0.099 (elasticity: 1% rise in DESI associated with about 0.1% higher TFP)
results.evidence: Table 2, column (1): 'lnDigital 0,099*** (4,00)'; abstract: 'a 1% increase in the digitalisation index leads to an increase in TFP by about 0.1%'

results.indicator: log TFP on log DESI, fullest extended specification with institutions
results.estimate: 0.040 (not significant)
results.evidence: Table 2, column (4): 'lnDigital 0,040 (1,43)'; text p.11 says significance 'decreases to 1.43'

results.indicator: log TFP on log DESI, robustness estimators
results.estimate: 0.111 (FE with DW, 140 obs), 0.106 (FE with AR residuals), 0.102 (GLS random effects, 168 obs)
results.evidence: Table 3, row lnDigital

heterogeneity.finding: Adding the Economic Freedom index (log) cuts the DESI coefficient from about 0.09 to 0.040 and removes significance; the institutions coefficient is 0.033 (t = 1.95).
heterogeneity.evidence: Table 2, column (4) and text p.11

income_group_results.high: EU sample pooled; coefficient 0.099 in the basic specification (income groups not separated)

n_specifications_reported: about 9 (2 in Table 1, 4 in Table 2, 3 in Table 3)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('It is proved', 'causal effect') with country FE only; no instruments, lags, or year effects; reverse causation (richer, more productive countries digitise) and common shocks such as COVID-19 are not addressed. The headline coefficient loses significance when institutions are added.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3 p.11: 'the model proves the causal effect'; Table 2 column (4)

exposure_measurement.why: DESI is a broad composite that mixes human capital and public services with infrastructure; it is a plausible ICT capability index for the EU but is not an adoption or investment measure and the DESI methodology may change across editions (not discussed). Log of an index has no natural unit.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only six years (2017-2022) and 28 units; the EU aggregate is included as a 'country' alongside its members, double counting; spans COVID-19 shock. Within-country variation in a slow-moving index over six years is limited.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 5 p.11: '168 observations (28 countries and 6 years)'

outcome_measurement.why: TFP is a Cobb-Douglas residual computed by the author; the capital share alpha and capital series construction are not reported. The text alternately calls the outcome TFP, labour productivity and productivity growth although the regressand is the TFP level in logs.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 2 p.9-10, Eq. (1); Section 5 p.11 'labour productivity growth'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four nested specifications and three estimators reported; headline taken from the basic specification, while the institutions-augmented model gives a null. Robustness checks vary only the estimator, not controls or identification. Autocorrelation is reported (rho_ar 0.28 to 0.51) and FE-AR models drop to 140 observations.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 2 and 3; Section 6 p.12

selective_reporting.why: Abstract and conclusion report 0.1% without noting the loss of significance in column (4); non-significant R&D, FDI and human capital results are reported. Some table inconsistencies (Table 1 vs Table 2 constants).

venue_quality_concern: possible (Green, Blue & Digital Economy Journal, a small Ukrainian-published journal; short article with no identification strategy)
notes: Standard errors not reported, only absolute t statistics. Reported elasticity treats a level regression as 'productivity growth'. The paper's Section 5 refers to 'labour productivity growth' when the outcome is TFP, which looks like text carried over from another study. No instruction-like text found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel estimation, 27 EU members plus the EU aggregate (28 units), ICT exposure via the DESI composite, outcome TFP (productivity). Meets the at-least-10-economies rule; no income-group comparison is needed.

sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: The paper gives no income classification; the record's 'high' is the extractor's inference (EU members, mostly high-income by external classification).

corrections.correction: Numbers are right (0.093 in col 3 to 0.040 in col 4, institutions 0.033, t 1.95, 10 percent), but this is a control-sensitivity result, not heterogeneity: there is no interaction, subgroup or threshold. Reclassify as sensitivity to adding the Economic Freedom index.
corrections.quote: the coefficient of institutional index has a small economic value (0.033) and the minimum acceptable value of statistical significance

second_pass.problems: The record's statement 'Some table inconsistencies (Table 1 vs Table 2 constants)' is not supported: Table 1 lnTFP column and Table 2 col (1) give identical coefficients and constant (4.941). The only different constant is for the TFP_ind column in Table 1 (-1.373), which has a different dependent variable. Other facts check out: 168 observations, 28 units, 140 observations in FE-AR models, rho_ar values. The Table 3 col (1) header says Durbin-Watson test but it reports rho_ar, so it is an AR(1) FE estimator.

title: The Effect of Artificial Intelligence Investments on Economic Development: Panel Data Analysis
decision_rationale: Own panel estimation (CS-ARDL) of AI investment (VC investment in AI) on the Human Development Index across 8 economies (at least 3 for AI); outcome is HDI (family 5, living standards beyond income).
technology: artificial intelligence (venture capital investment in AI, USD million)
exposure_measure: Venture capital investments in AI, USD million, from OECD (Table I), entered in logs. Methodology section also says robot installation numbers are used as an indicator of AI and used to select countries (inconsistent).

sample.economies_or_groups: Germany, United States, China, France, South Korea, India, Italy, Japan (selected as leading robot-installation markets)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (paper does not classify; includes high-income countries plus China and India by external classification)

design.estimator: CS-ARDL (Chudik and Pesaran 2015) after Pesaran-Yamagata slope homogeneity, Pesaran CD and CIPS unit root tests
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Three separate models each with two of PCI (GDP per capita), inflation and FDI as controls; country effects; no model includes all three controls

results.indicator: Log HDI vs log AI investment, long run, Model 1 (controls PCI, INF)
results.estimate: 0.206952 (log-log elasticity)
results.evidence: Table V, Equation 1, p.424

results.indicator: Log HDI vs log AI investment, long run, Model 2 (controls PCI, FDI)
results.evidence: Table V, Equation 2, p.424; 'AI coefficient is not statistically significant' in Model 2

results.indicator: Log HDI vs log AI investment, long run, Model 3 (controls FDI, INF)
results.evidence: Table V, Equation 3, p.424

heterogeneity.finding: Pesaran-Yamagata test rejects slope homogeneity in all three models (Delta 3.408, 3.153, 2.091), so effects differ by country; country-specific coefficients are not reported and no moderator is tested.
heterogeneity.evidence: Table II, p.423; Conclusion p.425: 'impact of AI investments on development varies depending on country characteristics'

income_group_results.low: not applicable (no such economies in sample)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: CS-ARDL on N=8, T=12 with no instrument or timing design; AI venture capital is plausibly driven by country development level; causal 'effect' language in title and conclusion.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Methodology p.422; Conclusion p.424

exposure_measurement.why: VC investment in AI in USD millions (not scaled by GDP) is a funding flow concentrated in a few economies; the text also says robot installations are the AI indicator, which conflicts with Table I.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Eight countries hand-picked as leading robot markets; very short panel (T=12); the conclusion mislabels the sample as G7 though it includes China, India and South Korea.

outcome_measurement.why: HDI is a slow-moving composite that includes an income component, while GDP per capita is also a regressor; the source of HDI is listed as World Bank.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Three alternative models each omit one control; lag structure, number of CSA terms and diagnostics not reported; Model 3 standard errors (0.0015, t-stats of 50-62) are implausibly small for N=8; AI is significant in 2 of 3 models.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Equations Models 1-3 p.422; Table V p.424

selective_reporting.why: Abstract promises long- and short-term relationships but only long-run estimates are reported; conclusion states a significant positive AI effect despite the null result in Model 2; table captions and footnote errors (Table IV caption repeats 'Cross-sectional Dependency Test'; significance stars legend reversed: '* 1%, ** 5%, *** 10%').
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract p.420; Table IV note p.424; Table V p.424

venue_quality_concern: possible (economics paper in Balkan Journal of Electrical & Computer Engineering; manuscript received 13 Oct 2025 and accepted 15 Dec 2025)
notes: Short-run CS-ARDL estimates are not shown. Unit-root results in Table IV mark HDI, PCI and FDI as I(1); AI and INF as I(0) with no stars shown in the table, yet text treats them as stationary at level. Conclusion calls the sample G7. No instructions embedded in the text were found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own CS-ARDL estimation; exposure is AI (VC investment in AI); 8 economies meets the 3-economy AI threshold; outcome is HDI (living standards beyond income). Eligible, though the AI measure is internally inconsistent (see problems).
second_pass.problems: Internal inconsistencies in the paper rather than in the record: (a) methodology says robot installations are the AI indicator but Table I says VC investment in AI (OECD); (b) conclusion says 'G7 countries' but lists China, India, South Korea; (c) Table IV caption repeats 'Cross-sectional Dependency Test' and its star legend is reversed ('*, ** and *** represent 1%, %5 and 10%'); (d) abstract says short-run relationships analysed but only long-run is in Table V; (e) in Equation 2 and 3 the PCI/INF terms are inconsistently included (Model 3 has no PCI). Record is otherwise accurate; no invented content found.

title: Testing the impact of ICT in developed countries during 1980-1995: distributional analysis in Solow's growth accounting framework
decision_rationale: Quantitative study with its own distributional tests (Li test, Silverman test) on growth-accounting contributions of ICT capital for 15 developed economies; non-AI technology with at least 10 economies and a productivity outcome.
exposure_measure: Contribution of ICT capital per hour to growth of GDP per hour (percentage points), taken from Timmer, Ypma and van Ark (2003) growth accounting; not re-estimated here.

sample.n_economies: 15 (stated in text; Table 1 lists US plus 14 EU countries)
sample.economies_or_groups: US, Ireland, Spain, Germany, Finland, France, UK, Belgium, Portugal, Italy, Denmark, Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Greece
sample.income_groups_covered: high (developed countries)

design.estimator: Solow growth accounting decomposition (taken from secondary source) combined with kernel density estimates, Li (1996) bootstrap test of equality of distributions (5000 replications) and Silverman test of multimodality
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: None; counterfactual distributions set other sources of growth to zero one at a time

results.indicator: Distribution of labour productivity in 1995 when only ICT-capital deepening is accounted for, vs 1980 distribution
results.estimate: Average ICT contribution 0.32 percentage points to growth in GDP per hour (unweighted mean; non-ICT 0.79, TFP 1.06, GDP per hour 2.17)
results.uncertainty: Li-test p=0.9040 (Table 2); author warns of low power with 15 countries
results.evidence: Table 1 p.22 and Table 2 p.23; text p.12: 'this contribution was statistically insignificant'

results.indicator: Distribution with ICT and non-ICT capital deepening together (TFP set to zero)
results.estimate: not applicable
results.evidence: Table 2, p.23

results.indicator: Distribution with TFP change only
results.estimate: not applicable
results.uncertainty: Li-test p=0.2938 (not significant) but Silverman multimodality p=0.0422; TFP plus ICT p=0.5776; TFP plus non-ICT capital p=0.0330
results.evidence: Table 2 and text pp.13-14

results.indicator: Overall change in distribution of labour productivity 1980 to 1995 (all sources)
results.estimate: Unimodal in 1980 to three-club distribution in 1995; not an ICT effect
results.uncertainty: Li-test p=0.0062; Silverman unimodality rejected p=0.0414
results.evidence: pp.11, Table 2

heterogeneity.finding: Three productivity 'clubs' in 1995 (richest: Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, US; middle: Austria, Finland, Spain, Sweden, UK; poorest: Greece, Portugal). The paper attributes the multi-modality mainly to TFP, not to ICT.

income_group_results.high: All sample economies are developed; no ICT estimate by income group

n_specifications_reported: 7 Li-tests and 2 Silverman tests

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Growth accounting contributions are accounting identities, not causal effects; TFP residual absorbs ICT spillovers (acknowledged by the author as an indirect channel not measured). No strategy for reverse causation.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 5, p.16

exposure_measurement.why: ICT-capital contributions are borrowed from Timmer et al. (2003); deflator and capital-stock construction are not described in this paper, so quality cannot be checked from the text.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 15 developed countries, and the window 1980-1995 stops before the main ICT boom; author admits small sample and short time span.

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per hour from a secondary source; reported as contributions, not levels, so the 'fitted' labour-productivity levels depend on the author's reconstruction with base-year values.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Null results from tests with n=15 have little power (the author says so); bandwidth rule-of-thumb 'for the sake of time'; informal reading of plots; the conclusion that TFP is the driver rests on Silverman test while the Li test on the same counterfactual is insignificant.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: footnote 5, p.29; pp.12-13

selective_reporting.why: All seven Li-tests are reported in Table 2, but interpretive emphasis is placed on the one significant Silverman result.

venue_quality_concern: possible (MPRA preprint dated April 2005; no peer-review information in the text)
notes: Uses secondary growth-accounting data and provides distributional tests only; no regression coefficient or elasticity. Text says 15 countries but the club description (14 countries) omits Ireland, which is in Table 1. Table 1 column headers are garbled in conversion (ICT / Non-ICT) and the unit is given only as '%-point contribution' (likely average annual). Text states ICT 'significant' contribution can be identified in one place (p.12) but no ICT test is significant at conventional levels. No instruction-like text found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Borderline but acceptable: ICT-capital contributions are taken from Timmer et al. (2003), but the author performs own kernel-density, Li bootstrap and Silverman tests on 15 developed economies; outcome is labour productivity. No regression estimate of an ICT effect.

sample_corrections.n_economies: 15 (US plus 14 EU countries; Table 1 also prints an 'European Union' aggregate row that is not a country). Printed unweighted averages recompute to the 14 non-US rows (non-ICT about 0.79, TFP about 1.07, GDP per hour about 2.18), not the 15-country mean, so the record's description of the average as a 15-country mean is not supported by the table.

second_pass.problems: No invented content. Minor points: the Table 1 'unweighted average' row does not recompute as a 15-country mean (see sample_corrections); the 'European Union' row in Table 1 is an aggregate; the text sentence about Li-test power at p=0.2480 is garbled and contradicts the surrounding 'not significant' reading; footnote 5 on the rule-of-thumb bandwidth is on p.29 as the record says.

title: The nonlinear link between AI and energy poverty: Empirical evidence from global data
decision_rationale: Quantitative cross-country panel (64 economies, 2000-2019, high/upper-middle/lower-middle income) estimating the association of an AI proxy with an energy poverty index (electricity access, clean cooking, per capita energy and electricity), which is a living-standards/resource outcome. Borderline on exposure: the AI measure is industrial robot stock, and the paper itself says results are evidence on industrial automation rather than AI broadly; kept because the paper frames and tests it as AI (with an AI-patent robustness check).
technology: artificial intelligence (proxied by industrial robot stock per million employees; AI patent stock in robustness)
exposure_measure: Natural log of IFR total industrial robot stock per million employees (lnRobot_Stock); robustness uses AI patent stock (WIPO/OECD). Authors state it captures embodied automation, not software AI.

sample.economies_or_groups: Balanced panel of 64 countries listed in Appendix A (28 high-income, 24 upper-middle, 12 lower-middle); selected by IFR and energy-poverty data availability; Sub-Saharan Africa underrepresented
sample.income_groups_covered: high, upper-middle, lower-middle (no low-income countries)

design.estimator: Two-way fixed effects with country-clustered SEs; system GMM (Blundell-Bond, collapsed instruments, lags t-2 to t-3); quadratic specification with Lind-Mehlum U test; interaction models; stepwise mediation with bootstrap; 2SLS and Bartik shift-share IV and spatial lag as robustness
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: ln GDP per capita, urbanization, industry share, trade openness, FDI; country and year fixed effects; lagged dependent variable in GMM

results.indicator: Composite energy poverty index (0-1; geometric mean of electricity access, clean cooking access, per capita electricity use, per capita energy supply; higher = more poverty), quadratic in lnRobot_Stock, preferred system GMM with controls
results.estimate: Inverted U. lnRobot_Stock 0.0517, lnRobot_Stock^2 -0.0044; turning point lnRobot_Stock 5.88 (about 358 robots per million employees). Two-way FE with controls: 0.0370 and -0.0030, turning point 6.17.
results.uncertainty: GMM p=0.017 and p=0.016 (** level); Lind-Mehlum p=0.039; AR(2) p=0.198; Hansen p=0.387. FE with controls p=0.051 and 0.057; Lind-Mehlum p=0.047.
results.evidence: p.13 Table 6 col 4: "lnRobot_Stock 0.0517** (0.017) ... lnRobot_Stock2 -0.0044** (0.016)"; Turning point 5.88

results.indicator: Marginal effect of lnRobot_Stock on EP_Index at lnRobot_Stock=7.0 (about 1,100 robots per million employees), GMM col 4
results.estimate: About -0.010 per unit of lnRobot_Stock; a further 1 SD (1.89) rise implies about -0.019 EP_Index units (about 10% of EP SD 0.19). At the sample mean (5.21, on the rising arm) the marginal effect is small and positive.
results.uncertainty: not reported (no SE or CI given for the marginal effect in text; Fig. 7 shows 95% CI)
results.evidence: p.12 Section 4.2: "At lnRobot_Stock = 7.0 ... marginal effect on EP_Index is approximately -0.010"

results.indicator: Alternative specifications of the inverted-U (robustness): AI patent stock, electricity access rate as DV, excluding oil exporters, excluding 2008-10, 2SLS, Bartik IV, spatial lag
results.estimate: Inverted U retained in all eight reported checks; linear coefficient 0.0420 to 0.0552, quadratic -0.0034 to -0.0048, turning points 5.75 to 6.18 (2SLS 0.0535/-0.0045, TP 5.94; Bartik 0.0494/-0.0042, TP 5.88)
results.uncertainty: Significance stars only: * to *** (10% to 1%); no SEs shown in text; full tables said to be in an Online Appendix
results.evidence: p.17 Table 10: "Inverted U Confirmed? Yes" for all rows; "full coefficient tables are available in the Online Appendix" (p.16)

results.indicator: Energy intensity (MJ per $ PPP GDP) as mediator: Step 1 AI to energy intensity, quadratic
results.estimate: Linear -0.152 (FE), -0.168 (GMM); quadratic +0.013 (FE), +0.014 (GMM); bootstrap indirect effect -0.004 (FE), -0.005 (GMM)
results.uncertainty: *** on linear terms, ** on quadratic; bootstrap 95% CI [-0.008,-0.001] (FE) and [-0.009,-0.001] (GMM)
results.evidence: p.15 Table 8 Panel A and Table 9: "Energy Efficiency FE -0.004 [-0.008, -0.001]"

results.estimate: Linear +0.118 (FE), +0.130 (GMM); quadratic -0.008 (FE), -0.009 (GMM); bootstrap indirect effect -0.002 (FE), -0.003 (GMM) on EP_Index
results.uncertainty: *** on linear, * on quadratic; bootstrap 95% CI [-0.005,-0.001] (FE), [-0.006,-0.001] (GMM)
results.evidence: p.15 Table 8 Panel B and Table 9: "Renewable Energy Sys-GMM -0.003 [-0.006, -0.001]"

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of lnRobot_Stock^2 with human capital is positive (0.002, p about 0.065-0.078), read by the author as higher human capital flattening the curve and lowering the EP level (main effect of HC -0.120 to -0.135***). Median-split grouped regressions: low-HC group has larger coefficients (GMM 0.0890/-0.0090***, TP 4.94) while high-HC group is insignificant (GMM 0.0310/-0.0020, TP 7.75). Text turning points by HC: about 5.0 (low) and 5.83 (high).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: none (turning points 4.94-5.17 low HC; 7.75-9.00 high HC in grouped regressions)
heterogeneity.evidence: p.14 Table 7 cols 1-2: "lnRobot_Stock2 x Z 0.002* (0.078) / 0.002* (0.065)"; p.20 Table B1

heterogeneity.finding: Interaction of lnRobot_Stock^2 with institutional quality (rule of law, government effectiveness) positive (0.001, p about 0.082-0.091); main effect of Z -0.095 to -0.110***. Grouped: low-institution group significant (GMM 0.0950/-0.0100***, TP 4.75), high-institution group insignificant (0.0280/-0.0020, TP 7.00).
heterogeneity.threshold_value: none (turning points 4.75-5.07 low institutions; 7.00-11.00 high institutions)
heterogeneity.evidence: p.14 Table 7 cols 3-4; p.21 Table B2

heterogeneity.finding: No formal income-group split in the regressions; income groups appear only descriptively in Fig. 4(b). Authors state results mainly characterise middle- and high-income economies and have limited applicability to Sub-Saharan Africa. No low-income country is in the sample.
heterogeneity.evidence: Abstract and p.19 Section 5.4; Appendix A note: "high-income (n = 28), upper-middle-income (n = 24), and lower-middle-income (n = 12)"

income_group_results.high: not reported separately (sample includes 28 high-income countries; only pooled results)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (24 countries in pooled sample)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately (12 countries in pooled sample)
income_group_results.low: not applicable: no low-income countries in the sample

n_specifications_reported: about 35 (Table 6: 4; Table 7: 4; Tables B1-B2: 10; Table 8: 8 plus Table 9: 4; Table 10: 8 rows)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Authors explicitly frame results as conditional associations, not causal. Sys-GMM, a 2SLS with frontier-country patent stocks and a Bartik shift-share instrument are offered, but exclusion restrictions are argued only verbally, no first-stage statistics or overidentification results are reported in the text, and it is unclear how the quadratic term is instrumented. Robot adoption is strongly tied to income and industrialisation (r=0.71 with GDP per capita).
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.10 Section 3.3.3 ("robust conditional associations rather than identified causal parameters"); p.16-17 Section 4.5 IV description; p.17 Table 10

exposure_measurement.why: Industrial robot stock per million employees is a measure of manufacturing automation, not AI in the sense of machine learning or generative AI; the author concedes it does not capture software AI. Patent stock is the only alternative and is also imperfect. Robot stock is near zero in many low-income economies.
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.9 Section 3.1: "central findings should be read as evidence on industrial automation rather than AI broadly construed"; p.19 Section 5.4

selection_of_countries_years.why: Balanced panel of 64 countries chosen by data availability and IFR coverage; no low-income countries and almost no Sub-Saharan Africa (only South Africa appears in the list despite the note saying 'fewer than 10'). Turning point is derived mainly from industrialised economies. 20-year window.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: p.9 Section 3.1; p.20 Appendix A country list and note; p.19 Section 5.4

outcome_measurement.why: Composite index of four standardised sub-indicators combined by geometric mean; two components (per capita electricity use and energy supply) measure consumption levels that rise with income and industrialisation, so the index partly reflects development. Direction coding of these components within a poverty index is not explained. Electricity-access-only robustness is provided.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.10 Table 4: "geometric mean of four standardised sub-indicators"; p.17 Table 10 Alt. DV: Electricity access

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Quadratic functional form chosen a priori but the U-shape is tested only within one parametric form; many specifications (FE and GMM, with and without controls, interactions, groups, robustness). GMM instrument count not reported. The Table 7 interaction coefficients differ greatly in magnitude from baseline (linear 0.12 vs 0.05), and the 'three-way interaction' label actually refers to two-way interactions of AI and AI^2 with a moderator.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.10 Eq. 1-3; p.14 Table 7 (linear 0.095-0.121, quadratic -0.006 to -0.011); p.13 Table 6

selective_reporting.why: All eight robustness checks and both mechanism channels confirm the hypotheses; the full robustness tables are not in the paper (Online Appendix). Heterogeneity interaction terms are significant only at the 10% level yet read as support. Marginal effects quoted in text for human capital levels do not reproduce from Table 7 (see notes). Table notes contain leftover revision language.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.16 Section 4.5 ("full coefficient tables are available in the Online Appendix"); p.14 Table 7 and Section 4.3 text

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Exposure is industrial robots labelled as AI: borderline for the AI exposure criterion; included because the paper tests AI patents as well and frames the study as AI, but a human reviewer may prefer to reclassify as automation. Internal inconsistencies found: (1) Table 7 text gives marginal effects at the sample mean of lnRobot_Stock of about -0.010 (mean HC), +0.008 (HC -1 SD) and -0.028 (HC +1 SD); recomputing from Table 7 col 2 (0.121, -0.011, interactions -0.018 and 0.002, SD of HC 0.58) gives roughly +0.006 at mean HC, +0.005 at -1 SD and +0.008 at +1 SD, so the stated values and their ordering do not reproduce (my own calculation, check). (2) Descriptive ranges differ between text and Table 5 (text: human capital 1.6-4.4, institutions -1.8 to 1.9; Table 5: 1.81-4.39 and -1.43 to 2.11). (3) Appendix A note says fewer than 10 Sub-Saharan African countries but only South Africa is a Sub-Saharan country in the list (Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia are North African). (4) Table notes (Tables 5, 6, 10) and text refer to earlier versions ('previously 5.21', 'formerly Table 3', 'Coefficients are now reported to four decimal places so the implied turning point is internally consistent') indicating post-hoc rounding to match the headline turning point; two-decimal coefficients would not give 5.88. (5) Reference list problems: Dong et al. (2021) is cited as digital finance IV study but listed as a low-carbon energy transition causality paper; Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson 'colonial origins' given as 2007 vol 91(5). (6) Policy section says the high-capacity marginal effect is about three times larger than for low-capacity countries, while Section 4.3 shows the low-capacity effect positive. Result contrasts with Zhu et al. (2025) cited in the paper (AI effect stronger in low-income countries). Data available only on request. No prompt-injection or directive text found in the paper.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Borderline on exposure: the AI measure is industrial robot stock per million employees, and the author states findings are about industrial automation rather than AI broadly (AI-patent stock only in a robustness row). Kept because it is framed and tested as AI; 64 economies, own FE/GMM estimation, outcome energy poverty (living standards/resource cost). Reviewer may wish to flag as robot-proxy.

sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Paper states high (28), upper-middle (24), lower-middle (12), no low-income. However, by usual World Bank classification the Appendix A list appears to contain well over 28 high-income economies (e.g. about 38 by my count of Belgium, Canada, Chile, ..., US); the 28/24/12 split cannot be reconciled from the printed list, so treat the income counts as unverified.

corrections.correction: Table 10 lists seven alternative specifications (patent stock, electricity access, excluding oil exporters, excluding 2008-10, 2SLS, Bartik, spatial lag) plus the baseline row, not eight separate checks; the text nevertheless says eight. Ranges 0.0420 to 0.0552, -0.0034 to -0.0048 and TP 5.75 to 6.18 are correct for the seven. Significance for patent stock (*) and spatial lag (*) is only 10%, while the table note says the Lind-Mehlum test rejects at 5% for all rows and no test statistics are shown.
corrections.quote: We subject our findings to eight robustness tests, each addressing a specific econometric concern.

second_pass.problems: Record is accurate on all checked numbers. Additional issues in the paper: Table 7 text marginal effects do not reproduce from the table (record already notes this); Table 10 note says the inverted-U is confirmed at 5% for all rows although several coefficients are only significant at 10% and no Lind-Mehlum statistics are shown; the introduction describes the index as three components while Table 4 lists four; Appendix A says fewer than 10 SSA countries but the list has only South Africa; and the income-group counts (28/24/12) look inconsistent with the printed list. The record's statement 'all eight reported checks' should read seven alternative specifications plus baseline.

title: Exploring the Moderating impact of ICT Infrastructure on Trade Openness-Sectoral Growth Nexus in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA)
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study (PMG/ARDL) of 26 SSA economies with ICT infrastructure (internet, mobile, fixed-line, composite index) as exposure and sectoral value added (output / structural change) as outcome; meets the 10-economy threshold.
exposure_measure: Individual internet users (% pop), mobile cellular subscriptions per 100, fixed telephone subscriptions per 100, and a PCA-based ICT infrastructure index (ICTINF); each interacted with trade openness (trade/GDP).

sample.economies_or_groups: 26 Sub-Saharan African countries (names not listed in the text read)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported

design.estimator: Pooled Mean Group ARDL (PMG/ARDL), long-run and short-run; Pesaran CD, CIPS/CADF unit root, Pedroni and Kao cointegration tests
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Gross fixed capital formation/GDP (labelled human capital investment), labour participation, FDI/GDP, GDP per capita (log); country-specific short-run heterogeneity; no instrument.

results.indicator: Agriculture value added: long-run trade openness (ln TO) in models with ICT interactions
results.estimate: -0.0921 to -0.1807 (log-level coefficients, columns 1-4)
results.evidence: Table 9, Long Run LNTO; text p.113: 'a 1% increase in LNTO associated with a 0.13-0.18% decline in agricultural sector growth'

results.indicator: Agriculture value added: ICT infrastructure index (ICT_INF)
results.evidence: Table 9, column 4, ICT_INF

results.indicator: Agriculture value added: fixed telephone subscriptions (FTS)
results.evidence: Table 9, column 3, FTS

results.indicator: Agriculture value added: trade openness x fixed telephone interaction (TO_FTS)
results.evidence: Table 9, column 3, TO_FTS; interactions with IUI, MCS, ICTINF not significant

results.indicator: Industry value added: ICT infrastructure index (ICT_INF), internet (IUI), mobile (MCS)
results.evidence: Table 10, Long Run, columns 1, 2, 4; text p.115: 'ICT_INF emerges as a positive and significant driver in model 4'

results.indicator: Industry value added: trade openness x ICT interaction (TO_ICTINF, TO_IUI, TO_MCS)
results.estimate: TO_ICTINF -0.0648; TO_IUI -0.0154; TO_MCS -0.0013
results.evidence: Table 10, Long Run interaction rows; text: 'growth-enhancing effects of ICT are dampened in more open trade environments'

results.indicator: Industry value added: trade openness (ln TO)
results.evidence: Table 10, Long Run LNTO

results.indicator: Services value added: ICT infrastructure index (ICT_INF) and internet use (IUI)
results.evidence: Table 11, Long Run, columns 1 and 4 (ICT_INF figures identical to Table 10)

results.indicator: Services value added: trade openness x ICT interactions
results.estimate: TO_IUI -0.0328; TO_MCS -0.0013; TO_ICTINF -0.0648
results.evidence: Table 11, Long Run interaction rows

results.indicator: Sector value added: short-run effects of trade openness, ICT and interactions (all three sectors)
results.estimate: mostly insignificant; e.g. agriculture short-run LNTO 0.0940 to 0.1232
results.evidence: Tables 9-11 Short Run; text p.114: 'trade openness, ICT variables, and their interactions are largely insignificant'

heterogeneity.finding: ICT effect positive and significant for industry and services in the long run, but not for agriculture, where only fixed-line (negative alone, positive when interacted with trade) is significant.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 9-11; Conclusion p.118: 'ICT infrastructure generally supports industrial and service sector growth in the long run'

heterogeneity.finding: Trade openness moderates ICT: interaction terms are negative in industry and services, so the ICT coefficient falls as openness rises (authors interpret ICT and openness as substitutes). Sign of net effect depends on the level of ICT.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 3.2 eq. 7 and Tables 10-11; text p.117: 'each 1% increase in openness lowers ICT's contribution to service growth by 0.03%-0.06%'

n_specifications_reported: 12 main long-run/short-run model columns (4 ICT measures x 3 sectors)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: PMG/ARDL with contemporaneous ICT and trade; no instrument or event timing. The text claims the model accounts for endogeneity, but the Conclusion concedes results are correlational. Interaction terms are not separately identified.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 4.3 p.113; Conclusion p.118: 'results remain correlational and cannot establish definitive causality'

exposure_measurement.why: The PCA ICT index is internally inconsistent: Table 3 shows ICTINF with skewness and kurtosis identical to MCS and a correlation of 1.000 with MCS, and Tables 6-7 show ICTINF test statistics identical to IUI. It is unclear what the index captures. Fixed-line telephony is included, which the authors admit may overstate relevance.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 2, Table 3, Table 4 (ICTINF row), Table 6, Table 7; Limitations p.118

selection_of_countries_years.why: 26 SSA countries chosen by data availability; balanced panel 1992-2023 (26 x 32 = 832 observations). Methods text gives two different periods (1992-2023 and 1991-2022). Country list not shown in the text read.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1 p.107 'Data availability dictated the choice of economies and periods'; Section 3.3 p.109; Table 9 N=832

outcome_measurement.why: The dependent variables labelled 'sectoral growth' are sector value added as a share of GDP (mean 21.3, 26.1, 45.9), not growth rates; interpretation as growth effects is inconsistent. Shares are legitimate structural-change measures but the paper does not treat them as such.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 3 (Agric. sector value added mean 21.3032; Serv. 45.8963); text p.110: 'Agriculture growth (AGRV) shows a mean of 21.3%'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Four alternative ICT measures each entered one at a time with interactions in three sectors; variables of mixed order I(0)/I(1) fed to PMG; ICT/trade enter partly in logs and partly in levels; control sets and column contents differ; table numbering in text (4.10, 4.12, 4.13) does not match the tables. Uncorrected multiple testing.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 7 (mixed integration orders); Tables 9-11; Section 4.3.1 'Table 4.10'

selective_reporting.why: Table 10 (industry) and Table 11 (services) report identical coefficients and standard errors in columns 2-4 for long-run and short-run rows (e.g. LNTO -0.0396, -0.1151, -0.0978; ICTINF 0.2594), which is implausible for different dependent variables and suggests a copy-paste error. Text then reports the same 0.26 ICT effect for both sectors. Unclear whether reported results are the actual estimates.
selective_reporting.evidence: Table 10 columns 2-4 versus Table 11 columns 2-4; p.116 and p.117 text on ICT_INF 0.2594

venue_quality_concern: possible (NIU Journal of Humanities, a humanities-titled journal with an economics paper; apparent duplicated result tables; at least one irrelevant citation)
notes: Outcome is sector value-added share, so results are about structural composition as much as output. Duplicated columns across Tables 10 and 11 and the ICT index inconsistency should be checked by a human; effect estimates for industry and services cannot be told apart in 9 of 12 columns. Reference list contains a mismatched citation: Varriale et al. (2024) is 'Coal and Mines in the Era of Fascist Ventennio in Italy' but is cited in the text as a study of renewable energy and growth in the E-7. Several citations (e.g. Swammy and Dharni, 2020) look unrelated to the claims. Text claims on ICT index percent effects treat a standardised PCA index as a log. No instruction-like text found in the paper.

second_pass.eligibility_note: 26 SSA economies, own PMG/ARDL estimation, ICT (internet, mobile, fixed line, index) as exposure, sector value-added shares as outcomes (structural change/output). Eligible, although the ICT index is not a reliable measure of exposure.

corrections.correction: Agriculture short-run LNTO in Table 9 is 0.0940, 0.1066, 0.0768, 0.1232* so the range is 0.0768 to 0.1232 (record says 0.0940 to 0.1232); SE 0.0701 to 0.1445 is right. Not all insignificant: col 4 LNTO is significant at 10%, services short-run TO -0.0814* (Table 11 col 1), and control variables (FDI, labour) are significant in places. Overall 'largely insignificant' for ICT and interactions holds.
corrections.quote: trade openness, ICT variables, and their interactions are largely insignificant
corrections.locator: text p.115 (record cites p.114); Tables 9-11 short-run rows

corrections.correction: Negative significant interactions are TO_IUI, TO_MCS, TO_ICTINF only; TO_FTS in Tables 10-11 is +0.0026 {0.0019}, insignificant, although the text says all four are negative and significant. In agriculture interactions are insignificant or positive (TO_FTS). No ICT-level or openness-level threshold is computed.
corrections.quote: each 1% increase in openness lowers ICT's contribution to service growth by 0.03%-0.06%

second_pass.problems: Record is accurate on printed values. Issues beyond the record: (a) Table 10/11 columns 2-4 duplication and the identical control blocks in columns 2 and 4 of Tables 9-11 indicate copy-paste or generation errors, so sector attribution of printed results is unreliable; (b) text says all four interactions are negative and significant but TO_FTS is not; (c) text says 0.13-0.18 for agriculture LNTO while the table range is 0.09-0.18; (d) record locators: the 'largely insignificant' sentence is on p.115 and the ICT_INF 0.26 text is on p.115 (industry) and p.116 (services), not p.114 and p.116/117; (e) mixed I(0)/I(1) variables are not by themselves a problem for PMG/ARDL, so the record's point is weaker than stated, but I(0) dependent variables with ln of non-positive minima (Table 3) are.

title: The Digital Maturity Paradox: The Divergent Impact of Network Readiness and FDI Across Development Tiers
decision_rationale: Quantitative cross-country OLS on 121 economies with an explicit developing vs developed comparison; exposure is the Network Readiness Index (ICT capability) and the outcome is GDP per capita growth (family 1).
technology: ICT in general (composite Network Readiness Index)
exposure_measure: Network Readiness Index 2023 (Portulans Institute), 0-100 composite of ICT capability, min-max rescaled to [0,1] (NRIT). Composite index, not a direct adoption or investment measure.

sample.economies_or_groups: 76 developing and 45 developed economies (2023 World Bank classification); Malta and Singapore flagged as outlier hubs and dropped in a robustness run (N=43)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (binary split developing vs developed; sub-groups of low, lower-middle, upper-middle not separated)

design.estimator: Cross-sectional OLS with HC1 (White) robust standard errors, estimated separately for developing and developed cohorts; Chow breakpoint test for the split; VIF, RESET, BPG, Cook's D, DFBETAS diagnostics
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Only FDI inflows (% GDP, IHS-transformed) and trade openness (% GDP, IHS-transformed); no income level, human capital, institutions, investment or population controls; no fixed effects; no lags.

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth on NRIT, developed economies N=45
results.uncertainty: p = 0.0895 (10% level only); adj R2 = 0.0161; overall F p = 0.3072

results.indicator: GDP per capita growth on NRIT, developed economies excluding Malta and Singapore N=43
results.evidence: Table 6, p.13: 'Normalized Network Readiness (NRIT) -0.734 * (0.0895) | -0.693 (0.1166)'

results.estimate: developing 0.246; developed 0.036 (N=43: -0.050)
results.uncertainty: developing p = 0.0116; developed p = 0.6724; N=43 p = 0.5433
results.evidence: Table 4, p.10 and Table 6, p.13

heterogeneity.threshold_value: none (exogenous split at the World Bank high-income boundary, observation 77; no endogenous threshold estimated)
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4.3.4, p.13: 'Chow Breakpoint Test (CBPT) at the high-income transition boundary (Observation 77) ... F = 11.91, p < 0.01'

income_group_results.high: Developed cohort (N=45): NRIT -0.734 (p=0.0895), not robust once Malta and Singapore are dropped (-0.693, p=0.1166); model jointly insignificant (F p=0.3072)
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (pooled in developing cohort, NRIT +1.106, p=0.0027)
income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately (pooled in developing cohort)
income_group_results.low: not reported separately (pooled in developing cohort)

n_specifications_reported: about 3 (developing, developed, developed excluding two outliers), plus diagnostics

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Single-year cross-section of growth on a contemporaneous composite readiness index with only FDI and trade as controls; no income level, human capital, institutions or investment controls; no instrument or timing. NRI is strongly correlated with income and development, so it proxies for general development. Authors use causal language ('growth multiplier', 'catalysts', policy prescriptions).
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.5 Eq. (3), p.7; Section 5.2, p.15 policy prescriptions based on 'growth elasticity of network readiness (beta = 1.106)'

exposure_measurement.why: NRI is a composite that includes technology, people, governance and impact pillars; it is not a measure of ICT adoption or investment and may mix in outcomes. Min-max rescaling makes the coefficient hard to interpret.

selection_of_countries_years.why: One year (2023), 121 economies chosen by NRI availability; 2023 growth is a noisy single-year observation that includes post-pandemic rebound and shocks. Developed group includes small hubs (Malta, Singapore); developed mean growth of -0.37% in 2023 looks unusual and is not discussed. Sample splitting at the group boundary is then 'validated' by a Chow test at that same boundary.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.2, p.6; Table 3, p.8; Section 4.3.4, p.13

outcome_measurement.why: WDI real GDP per capita growth is standard, but it is a one-year rate and is passed through an inverse hyperbolic sine transform, which is unusual for a growth rate near zero (approx. identity for small values) and complicates the reading of 'elasticity'.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Missing trade values imputed with group medians (landlocked/coastal); split by development tier chosen by the authors; outlier exclusion after looking at diagnostics; very low explanatory power (adj R2 0.016 in developed cohort). Developed-cohort NRI result significant only at 10%. No test of the NRI coefficient difference with an interaction term beyond the Chow test.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.4, p.7; Section 4.4, p.13; Table 4, p.10

selective_reporting.why: Few specifications and results are reported in full, including null ones, but the interpretation overstates weak evidence ('conclusive empirical weight', 'mathematically proves', 'fully supported') and the abstract headlines the 10%-level negative coefficient.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract and Section 4.4, p.14: 'The Fitness Gap mathematically proves that advanced economies have entirely outgrown infrastructure-led development'

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Treat as descriptive cross-sectional association, not causal. Internal inconsistencies: Section 4.1.2 states developing NRI std. dev. 10.37 and mean 41.6 while Table 3 gives 9.81 and 41.67; Table 5 reports BPG p < 0.10 / p < 0.05 for both cohorts as 'non-constant variance' while Section 4.3.3 says p = 0.0502 'marginal homoskedasticity'; abstract says R-squared < 2% for developed cohort but Table 4 R2 is 0.0832 (only adjusted R2 is 0.0161). Section 4.4 says '1.03%' for adj R2 0.0103, which is 1.03%, and the abstract cites baseline adj R2 1.61%. The 'sensitivity' run drops the NRI significance, so the headline negative developed coefficient is not robust. AI is mentioned only in policy discussion, not estimated. Publication date in the text (August 2026) is later than the recorded year field context; no instruction-like text found in the paper.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own cross-sectional OLS on 121 economies with an explicit developing vs developed split; exposure is the Network Readiness Index (ICT in general); outcome is real GDP per capita growth. All criteria met, although the exposure is a composite index.
second_pass.problems: No invented numbers found. Minor: the record's unit 'country-year' is a single cross-section. The FDI row (result 4) is a control, not an ICT exposure, and should not be used as an ICT result.

notes: Major abstract/body mismatch. Abstract (p. 2488): 'global panel of sixty countries from 2015 to 2024' with 'AI adoption intensity', R&D and FDI and GDP growth. Body: 'Nigeria and 37 other African countries', 2010-2024, dependent variable 'Inclusive Development' (HDI, GINI, financial inclusion composite), regressors digital infrastructure, digital literacy, human capital, institutional quality and DI x IQ (Section 3.1-3.4, pp. 2500-2505). Section IV contains only descriptive Table 4.1.1 (532 obs; note 38 countries x 15 years would be 570) and a regional means table; text says 'Chapter Four will apply econometric estimation' (p. 2504) and 'regression model developed in Chapter Three', but no regression results, Hausman, robustness or diagnostics output is shown even though the methods describe them in the past tense ('VIF scores remain below 5').
