title: The relationship between inequality and poverty in developing countries: mitigating role of virtual social network and internet access in schools
decision_rationale: Quantitative cross-country Tobit study of 57 developing economies in which the use of virtual social networks and internet access in schools (internet use, survey-based) moderate the effect of inequality on the poverty headcount (family 4). Meets the at least 10 economies rule.
technology: internet (use of virtual social networks; internet use in schools)
exposure_measure: Two Global Information Technology Report executive-survey indices, each scored 1-7: extent to which virtual social networks (Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn) are used in the country, and extent to which the internet is used in schools for learning; not a measure of subscriptions or users. Appendix notes that zero is assigned when there is no official data.

sample.n_economies: 57 (stated); regression uses 43 observations
sample.economies_or_groups: 57 non-OECD developing countries with available data (footnote 1 list, e.g. Bangladesh, Benin, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Nigeria, Pakistan, Philippines, Ukraine, Vietnam, Yemen, Zimbabwe)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (non-OECD developing economies, predominantly low and lower-middle income; no income-group split)

design.estimator: Double-censored Tobit regression (censoring at 0 and 100 percent) of poverty headcount on Gini, technology indicator, Gini x technology interaction and controls; marginal effects (dy/dx) also reported; thresholds computed as ratio of Gini coefficient to interaction coefficient.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Remittances (% GDP), log population, gender parity in school enrolment, adult literacy; no country or time fixed effects; no instruments. Authors state that cross-sectional dependence, reverse causality and unobserved country and time heterogeneity are 'shortcomings in the present study'.

results.indicator: Interaction of virtual social network use with Gini on poverty headcount (% of population, national poverty lines)
results.estimate: -33.506 (Tobit coefficient), -32.607 (dy/dx); unconditional Gini effect +118.022 / +114.855; implied technology threshold 3.5224 (on a 1-7 scale, sample mean 4.83)
results.uncertainty: p-values: 0.004 (coefficient), 0.002 (dy/dx); Gini main effect p=0.024 / 0.016; no confidence interval for the threshold; Fisher test 3.87***
results.evidence: Table 1, p.12, Models 1-2, row '[Social Network] x Gini'

results.indicator: Interaction of internet use in schools with Gini on poverty headcount
results.estimate: -54.278 (coefficient), -52.841 (dy/dx); Gini main effect +132.410 / +128.906; implied threshold 2.4394 (sample mean 3.24)
results.uncertainty: p-values: 0.027 (coefficient), 0.018 (dy/dx); Gini main effect p=0.080 / 0.067; Fisher test 3.11**
results.evidence: Table 1, p.12, Models 3-4, row '[Internet in Schools] x Gini'

results.indicator: Unconditional (own) effect of technology indicators on poverty headcount, at Gini = 0
results.estimate: Social network +18.257 (dy/dx +17.767); internet in schools +28.820 (dy/dx +28.058). Reviewer calculation from the table: at the sample mean Gini of 0.501 the implied marginal effect of the technology measure is still positive (about +1.5 for social network, +1.6 for internet in schools)
results.uncertainty: p=0.006 and 0.003 (social network); p=0.022 and 0.014 (internet in schools)
results.evidence: Table 1, p.12; text p.11: 'the unconditional effects of the moderators ... are not relevant for the outcome of the study'

heterogeneity.finding: The effect of inequality on poverty is modelled as conditional on the technology level: positive below a threshold and negative above it. Thresholds 3.52 (virtual social networks, range 2.571-6.234) and 2.44 (internet in schools, range 1.339-5.050) are said to be below the sample means. No heterogeneity by income group, region or institutions is examined.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: 3.5224 (virtual social network index); 2.4394 (internet in schools index)
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4, p.10-11; Table 1 p.12

n_specifications_reported: 2 regression specifications (one per technology indicator), each shown as coefficient and marginal effect, so 4 columns

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Pooled Tobit with four controls, no country or time effects, no instruments; poverty, inequality and technology use are jointly determined with income, yet the abstract uses causal language (technology 'mitigates' the effect of inequality). Authors concede reverse causality and cross-sectional dependence are unaddressed.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Conclusion p.14: 'adopt the relevant estimation techniques that take into account apparent concerns of cross-sectional dependence and reverse causality'; Section 3.2 p.9

exposure_measurement.why: Exposure is a perception-based executive survey score of how widely social networks are used and how far the internet is used in schools; it does not measure adoption, users or access. Appendix says zero is assigned when official data is missing, which, if present in the regression sample, would be a gross measurement error (reported minimum is 2.571, so unclear). Correlation between the two indices is 0.84.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Appendix 1 notes p.15; Appendix 2 p.15; Appendix 3 p.15

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample determined by availability of GTIR data and by non-OECD status; 57 countries named but only 43 observations in regressions (poverty has 84 observations over five years), so the estimation sample is small and countries entering it are not identified.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1 p.7 and footnote 1; Appendix 2 p.15 (Poverty 84 obs); Table 1 p.12 (Observations 43)

outcome_measurement.why: Poverty headcount at national poverty lines (WDI) is not comparable across countries and years and is available for few observations. Gini from GCIP is described as measuring 'distribution of wealth' although it is an income measure.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Tobit with limits 0 and 100 although observed poverty ranges only 0.4-66.5, so no censoring occurs and the choice is not warranted by the data; about 43 observations for 7 regressors and an interaction; thresholds are point estimates from ratios with no confidence interval; interaction result relies on Gini scaled 0-1.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.2 p.9; Appendix 2 p.15 (poverty min 0.400, max 66.500); Table 1 p.12

selective_reporting.why: Only two models are shown, no robustness checks or alternative estimators. The positive unconditional effects of the technology variables on poverty are reported but set aside as 'not relevant', while the abstract emphasises the mitigating role.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 4, p.11 (paragraph on unconditional effects); Table 1 p.12

venue_quality_concern: possible (working paper of the first author's own research centre, EXCAS WP/24/011, stated as forthcoming in International Journal of Social Economics; heavy self-citation)
notes: Parentheses in Table 1 are p-values, not standard errors (inferred from layout, e.g. constant -40.802 (0.339); not stated explicitly in the table note). The 57-country list and 43 regression observations are not reconciled. Net-effect arithmetic in the text (threshold 3.5224) checks out against the coefficients. Not a payoff-for-technology study in the usual sense: technology enters as a moderator of the inequality-poverty link. No instruction-like text found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own Tobit estimation; exposure is internet (survey indices of virtual social network use and internet use in schools); 57 named developing economies; outcome is poverty headcount. Criteria met, although the exposure is a perception-based survey index and the effective number of distinct countries in the 43 regression observations is not reported.
second_pass.problems: No invented numbers found. The record is faithful to Table 1 and the appendices. Only the income composition remark is unsupported by the text. Interaction interpretation: the technology marginal effect is 18.257 - 33.506 x Gini, so it turns negative only above a Gini of about 0.545, above the sample mean of 0.501.

title: Mobile banking usage, quality of growth, inequality and poverty in developing countries
decision_rationale: Cross-country quantile/OLS regressions on 93 developing countries; exposure is mobile phone use for payments and money transfers (mobile telephony), outcomes are quality of growth index, Gini and poverty (families 1 and 4).
technology: mobile telephony / mobile banking (mobile phone used to pay bills; to send or receive money)
exposure_measure: Share of adults using mobile phone to pay bills (Mobile.Pay) and to send/receive money (Mobile.SR) in 2011, from Mohseni-Cheraghlou (2013) (World Bank/Findex-based) (Sec 3.1, Appendix 1).

sample.n_economies: 93 stated (effective n 73 for quality of growth and poverty, 67 for inequality in regressions)
sample.economies_or_groups: developing countries; no list in the text
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (developing countries; not stratified)
sample.years: cross-section: mobile banking 2011; outcomes and controls 2005-2011 average

design.estimator: OLS and interactive (quadratic) quantile regressions at Q10, Q25, Q50, Q75, Q90
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Educational spending, government stability, inflation, private credit, FDI, remittances; no fixed effects (cross-section)

results.indicator: Quality of Growth Index (IMF composite, 0-1), Mobile.Pay linear term
results.estimate: OLS -0.005; Q90 -0.006 with quadratic +0.0002 (derived threshold 15% of adults); other quantiles not significant
results.uncertainty: OLS p=0.090; Q90 p=0.000; quadratic Q90 p=0.000
results.evidence: Table 1 Panel A: 'Mobile.Pay -0.005* ... Q.90 -0.006***'; text 'increased use of the mobile to pay bills increases growth quality at the 90th decile'

results.indicator: Quality of Growth Index, Mobile.SR
results.estimate: OLS -0.002; Q10 -0.008 with quadratic +0.0001 (threshold 40); Q75 -0.003 with quadratic +0.00003 (threshold 50)

results.indicator: Gini inequality index, Mobile.Pay
results.estimate: OLS linear 0.550, quadratic -0.030 (both ns); only Q90 quadratic -0.049 significant
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel A; text notes the constitutive term (0.399) is not significant

results.indicator: Gini inequality index, Mobile.SR
results.estimate: OLS 0.327 (ns); Q75 linear 0.708, quadratic -0.011 (threshold 32.18); Q90 quadratic -0.006; Q10 quadratic +0.006
results.uncertainty: Q75 linear p=0.075, quadratic p=0.093; Q90 quadratic p=0.035; Q10 quadratic p=0.000
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel B

results.indicator: Poverty rate (one USD a day), Mobile.Pay
results.estimate: OLS 0.006 (ns); no significant mobile term at any quantile
results.evidence: Table 3 Panel A; text 'evidence of threshold ... is not apparent'

results.indicator: Poverty rate, Mobile.SR
results.estimate: OLS -0.001 (ns); Q10 -0.0005 and Q25 -0.0007 with positive quadratic (+0.00002); ns at Q50 linear, Q75, Q90
results.uncertainty: Q10 and Q25 linear p=0.000; OLS p=0.465

heterogeneity.finding: Effects differ across the conditional distribution of the outcome (initial level of inclusiveness), with significant coefficients concentrated at high or low tails; OLS mean effects mostly null or weakly negative for quality of growth
heterogeneity.threshold_value: Mobile.Pay 15 (QGI Q90); Mobile.SR 40 (QGI Q10), 50 (QGI Q75); Gini Mobile.SR 32.18 (Q75); poverty Mobile.SR 12.5 (Q10), 17.5 (Q25), 16.66 (Q50) (percent of adults)
heterogeneity.evidence: Sec 4.1 threshold discussion, Tables 1-3

n_specifications_reported: 36 (3 outcomes x 2 mobile measures x OLS plus 5 quantiles)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Single cross-section, no instrument or timing strategy; authors concede 'we can only infer correlations and not causality' yet policy conclusions are drawn; mobile banking use in 2011 postdates part of the 2005-2011 outcome average.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Sec 4.2: 'we can only infer correlations and not causality'

exposure_measurement.why: Direct survey-based share of adults using mobile for payments, but only one year and highly collinear (corr 0.865) measures; many zero values (min 0.000).

selection_of_countries_years.why: Stated 93 countries but regressions use 73 or 67 observations; sample drops not explained; country list not given; one year only.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Abstract '93 developing countries'; Tables 1-3 Observations 73/67; Appendix 2 Obs 80

outcome_measurement.why: Composite Quality of Growth Index from IMF is not a direct output measure; poverty defined as share living on one USD a day but summary statistics look inconsistent (poverty max 28.127 equals inequality min 28.127; poverty mean 0.062 with max 28).

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Quadratic interaction terms at five quantiles and two exposure measures for three outcomes with n of about 70 and 7 covariates; thresholds computed from coefficients and some thresholds rest on insignificant constitutive terms; many quantile estimates sign-flip versus OLS.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Sec 4.1 'estimates are different from the OLS estimates in terms of signs and significance'; Table 2 text on insignificant constitutive terms

selective_reporting.why: Abstract highlights the few significant quantile estimates ('broadly show that increasing mobile banking ... would increase (decrease) ... inequality') although most of 36 coefficients are null and OLS effects for quality of growth are negative; no correction for multiplicity.

venue_quality_concern: possible (this is a working-paper version issued by the authors' own institute network; paper states publication in Information Development 2019, published version not seen)
notes: Working paper WP/17/046, January 2017; header says published in Information Development 35(2) 2019. The text uses 'mobile' interchangeably with mobile telephony. Text says in Table 2 discussion 'negatively correlated with growth quality' for an inequality table (apparent typo). Conclusion calls findings 'exploratory'. No text tried to direct the reviewer.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own OLS and quantile regressions on 93 developing countries (73/67 used); exposure is mobile phone use for bill payment and money transfer (mobile); outcomes are quality of growth, Gini and poverty. Criteria met.

sample_corrections.unit: country (single cross-section: mobile banking 2011; outcomes and controls 2005-2011 average; not country-year)

second_pass.problems: No invented numbers found. Unsupported detail: the record says the exposure data are 'World Bank/Findex-based'; the text only says Mohseni-Cheraghlou (2013), published by the World Bank, and never mentions Findex. The record's note on the odd poverty summary statistics (max 28.127 equals the inequality minimum) is correct and bears on the poverty results, which should be treated as unreliable. The authors disclaim causality ('we can only infer correlations') yet say mobile banking 'would increase (decrease)' outcomes, hence mixed causal language.

title: IMPACT OF MOBILE PHONES AND INTERNET USE ON FINANCIAL INCLUSION: EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE FROM THE EU POST-COMMUNIST COUNTRIES
decision_rationale: Own panel cointegration and causality estimation of mobile subscriptions and Internet use on financial inclusion indices for 11 economies (meets the 10-economy threshold for non-AI technology). Outcome is financial inclusion (family 5).
exposure_measure: Mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people and individuals using the Internet (% of population), World Bank (Table 1)

sample.economies_or_groups: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Czech Republic, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia (EU post-communist)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (single regional group, EU post-communist members)

design.estimator: Westerlund-Edgerton (2008) panel cointegration test with structural breaks; AMG (Augmented Mean Group) long-run coefficients; Dumitrescu-Hurlin (2012) panel Granger causality; CIPS unit root, CD and slope-homogeneity pretests
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: No control variables; two bivariate-style models (FIA or FMA on MOBILE and INTERNET); country-specific coefficients and break dates; AMG common dynamic process handles cross-section dependence

results.indicator: Financial institutions access index (FIA: bank branches and ATMs per 100,000 adults), effect of mobile subscriptions, panel AMG
results.estimate: 0.0015297 index units per 1 additional subscription per 100 people (authors call it 'very low')
results.uncertainty: significant at 5% (** in Table 7a); se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7a, Panel row; text p.733: '1 unit change in mobile cellular subscriptions led a 0.0015297 increase'

results.indicator: FIA, effect of Internet users (% pop), panel AMG
results.uncertainty: no significance stars (not significant); se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7a, Panel row, INTERNET column

results.indicator: Financial markets access index (FMA: market cap outside top 10 firms, number of debt issuers), effect of mobile subscriptions, panel AMG
results.uncertainty: no significance stars; se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7b, Panel row, MOBILE column

results.indicator: FMA, effect of Internet users (% pop), panel AMG
results.estimate: 0.0025709 index units per 1 percentage point of Internet users
results.uncertainty: significant at 10% (* in Table 7b); se not reported
results.evidence: Table 7b, Panel row, INTERNET column; text p.733: 'Internet usage positively influenced financial markets access'

results.indicator: Country-level long-run effects (11 countries x 2 outcomes x 2 exposures)
results.estimate: Mobile to FIA significantly positive in Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovenia (largest Latvia 0.0070) and negative in Czech Republic (-0.0014). Internet to FIA positive in Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Rep., Hungary, Poland; negative in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovenia (e.g. Latvia -0.0157)
results.evidence: Table 7a and 7b; text p.734: 'The effect of Internet usage rate on financial institutions' access is negative in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Slovenia'

results.indicator: Short-run Granger causality (first differences)
results.estimate: DMOBILE to DFIA: W=4.77, Zbar=2.93; DINTERNET to DFIA: Zbar=2.07; reverse DFIA to DINTERNET: Zbar=1.97; no significant causality involving FMA, no reverse causality from FIA to mobile
results.uncertainty: p=0.0034 (mobile to FIA); p=0.0381 (Internet to FIA); p=0.0485 (FIA to Internet); FMA links p=0.26 to 0.94
results.evidence: Table 8, p.734

heterogeneity.finding: Effects differ in sign and significance across countries (e.g. mobile to FIA positive in 5 countries, negative in Czech Republic; Internet to FIA negative in 4 countries). Authors note a Central Europe vs South-East Europe/Baltic grouping by financial development but do not test it.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 7a-7b; Introduction p.724-725; Section 3 p.734

n_specifications_reported: about 4 main long-run models (2 outcomes, each with panel + 11 country estimates), plus 8 causality tests and 3 versions of cointegration test (no break, level break, regime shift)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: No control variables (income, banking regulation, financial development) and causal 'impact' wording; the causality test itself shows feedback from financial institutions access to Internet use, and no instrument or timing design.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 2.2; Table 8 (DFIA does not Granger-cause DINTERNET rejected at p=0.0485)

exposure_measurement.why: Standard World Bank indicators (subscriptions per 100 people; % Internet users), but subscriptions count SIMs, not users, and the two exposures are entered jointly without interaction.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 11 post-communist EU members chosen by transition history; N=11 and T=22 limit the power of the panel tests; authors acknowledge the small sample as the main limitation.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 2.1 p.728; Conclusions p.735: 'main limitation of our research is the sample size'

outcome_measurement.why: FIA is branches and ATMs per 100,000 adults (supply of outlets) and FMA is market capitalisation outside the top 10 firms plus number of debt issuers (market depth). Neither measures household account ownership or use; authors admit no single indicator captures inclusion.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 2.1 p.727-728: 'not a single indicator that can capture accurately the multidimensional concept of financial inclusion'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Several test variants and break structures; cointegration is rejected for 'no break' only weakly in Model 1 (Zf p=0.091) and not rejected for level-break; Model 2 shows no cross-section dependence yet the same dependence-robust AMG estimator is applied. Short T relative to the number of break parameters.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 3, 6a, 6b

selective_reporting.why: Abstract and conclusions foreground significant country results; conclusions claim 'significant positive influence' on both indices 'in both the short and long run' although panel Internet to FIA is negative and insignificant, panel mobile to FMA is insignificant, and no short-run causality involves FMA.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Internal inconsistencies for the reviewer: (1) text p.732 says no-cointegration is rejected 'for both models for no break and regime shift', but Table 6a Model 1 Zf(N) no-break p=0.091 and the level-break tests are not significant; (2) Conclusions say Internet positively affects FIA in several countries 'but weak in the panel' while Table 7a panel coefficient is negative (-0.0012) and insignificant; (3) Table 5 first-difference CIPS statistics for D(FIA) and D(INTERNET) with trend (0.079, 0.094) are positive and flagged significant, which looks like a reporting error. Standard errors are not given for coefficients. No instruction-like text found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel cointegration (AMG) and Granger estimation, 11 economies, mobile and internet exposure: those criteria hold. The outcomes, though, are the IMF financial institutions access index (bank branches and ATMs per 100,000 adults) and financial markets access index (market capitalisation outside the top 10 firms, number of debt issuers). These are financial-sector supply and depth measures, not output, labour, poverty or distribution, or living standards beyond income; poverty is only mentioned as a motivation and never estimated. Judgement call: exclude unless financial inclusion is accepted under 'living standards beyond income'.

corrections.correction: Stated FIA numbers are right (Mobile to FIA: Hungary 0.000899, Latvia 0.0070361, Lithuania, Poland, Slovenia positive; Czech Republic -0.0014063; Internet to FIA: Latvia -0.015668). But the entry claims 11 countries x 2 outcomes x 2 exposures and omits the FMA country results: Mobile to FMA positive in Bulgaria, Croatia (10%), Hungary and negative in Czech Republic and Poland (10%); Internet to FMA positive in Latvia (5%) and Slovenia (0.0168589, 1%).
corrections.quote: mobile cellular subscriptions positively affect financial markets access in Bulgaria, Croatia, and Hungary and negatively in the Czech Republic and Poland

corrections.correction: Statistics and p-values are right (DMOBILE to DFIA W 4.77462, Zbar 2.93274, p 0.0034; DINTERNET to DFIA Zbar 2.07345, p 0.0381; DFIA to DINTERNET Zbar 1.97332, p 0.0485; FMA links p 0.2617 to 0.9447). However, a Dumitrescu-Hurlin test has no sign, so direction 'positive' is unsupported; it should be 'not signed (Granger predictive causality in first differences)'. Horizon is short-run (differences), not contemporaneous.

title: Impact of Economic Integration and Information and Communication Technology on Economic Growth for European Union: Dynamic Panel GMM Approach

technology: internet use (users per hundred, labelled ICT usage)
exposure_measure: Natural log of internet users per hundred population (IU) and log of mobile phone subscriptions (MS), from World Bank/ITU; interacted with log trade/GDP (economic integration).

sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (EU countries only; no income classification given)

design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged log GDP per capita, log trade/GDP, log human capital (PWT), log employment (persons engaged), log inflation; time effects not mentioned; 18-21 instruments

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita (labelled economic growth) vs log internet users (Model 1)
results.estimate: 0.16262 (log-log coefficient)
results.evidence: Table 4, col (1), p.10; 'impact of ICT on economic growth positive and significant' p.11

results.evidence: Table 4, col (3), p.10

results.evidence: Table 4, col (2), p.10

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita vs log mobile subscriptions, with interaction with economic integration (Model 4)
results.evidence: Table 4, col (4), p.10

income_group_results.low: not applicable (no such economies in sample)

AR(1) not rejected at 5% in Models 1 and 4 (p = 0.056, 0.146). Causal 'impact' language used.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3 p.5-6; Table 4 diagnostics p.10

selection_of_countries_years.why: EU-27 only (homogeneous, high/upper-middle income); 3-year averages leave 6 periods and 162 obs, but only 138 enter the regressions without explanation; Figure 1 includes the UK while text says 27 EU countries.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 4 p.10; Table 3 correlations p.9

title: The effect of information and communication technology on economic growth high-income countries
decision_rationale: Own panel regression of GDP growth on fixed telephone, mobile, internet and broadband indicators for exactly 10 economies (the minimum), so it meets the 10-economy threshold; outcome is output growth.

sample.income_groups_covered: high

confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Equation 2, p.627; Table 6, p.628; Abstract p.621

title: Reducing Gender Inequality in Education in Developing Countries: Do Information and Communication Technologies Matter?
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (Driscoll-Kraay, quantile, system GMM) of mobile phone and internet diffusion on male-to-female primary and secondary gross enrolment ratios in 64 low and lower-middle income economies; meets exposure, sample (>=10 economies) and outcome (family 5, schooling) criteria.
technology: ICT in general (fixed broadband and ICT service exports as alternative measures)
exposure_measure: Mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people; share of individuals using the Internet (WDI). Robustness: fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 people and ICT service exports as % of service exports.

sample.economies_or_groups: 64 developing countries described as low-income and lower-middle income (list in Appendix A, e.g. Angola, Bangladesh, India, Egypt, Tunisia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam)
sample.income_groups_covered: low and lower-middle (as stated by authors); group membership not reported per country, and some listed countries (e.g. Tunisia, Jordan, Sri Lanka) may be upper-middle in parts of the period

design.estimator: Country fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors (baseline); OLS (Appendix B); trimming outliers; quantile regression (Q10-Q90); two-step system GMM with lagged dependent variable; quadratic ICT term; ICT x GDP growth interaction
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country FE; controls GDP growth, government education spending (% GDP), population growth, trade openness; no year fixed effects reported. GMM uses internal lagged instruments only.

results.uncertainty: SE 0.000 (reported to 3 decimals), p<0.01, N=845, 64 countries, within R2 0.355

results.estimate: -0.001 per percentage point of internet users (rounded)
results.evidence: Table 3 col 2, p.6: 'Internet -0.001*** (0.000)'

results.estimate: -0.003 per subscription per 100 people; outcome mean 1.170 (SD 0.363)
results.uncertainty: SE 0.000, p<0.01, N=638, 61 countries, within R2 0.412
results.evidence: Table 3 col 3, p.6: 'Mobile phone -0.003***'

results.estimate: -0.004 per percentage point
results.evidence: Table 3 col 4, p.6: 'Internet -0.004*** (0.001)'

heterogeneity.evidence: Table 9, p.10

income_group_results.lower_middle: not reported separately; pooled estimates only
income_group_results.low: not reported separately; pooled estimates only

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Authors use causal language ('direct causal effect') but the baseline is a country-FE panel with four controls and no year effects, so common trends (ICT diffusion and enrolment parity both rising 2001-2022) and omitted variables (income level, urbanisation, schooling policy) can drive the result. Authors acknowledge reverse causality (skills bias). System GMM uses internal instruments only, with up to 56 instruments for 62 groups in one model, and gives smaller coefficients.

Outlier-trimming robustness cuts the top and bottom 5% of the outcome distribution (selects on the dependent variable). Income classification is not applied per country; some listed countries are upper-middle income.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3 p.4; Table 3 obs rows p.6; Section 5.3.1 p.7

outcome_measurement.why: Male/female gross enrolment ratio (not net enrolment, completion or learning). Ratio below 1 (min 0.72-0.84) means girls ahead, so a lower ratio is not always 'less inequality'; interpretation of negative coefficients as reduced inequality is not qualified. GER can exceed 100% because of repeaters and over-age pupils.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3 p.4: 'ratio of male to female primary school gross enrollment'; Table 1 p.5 (min 0.842 and 0.723)

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Many estimators and variants (DK, OLS, trimming, quantile, GMM, quadratic, interaction) but headline spec is the pre-stated baseline. Four controls, no time effects, no lags in baseline. Threshold from quadratic form is computed from rounded coefficients without a test of the turning point or CI. Descriptive text in Section 3 contains units inconsistencies (GDP min stated -0.46% vs -46.082 in Table 1).
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 4 p.5; Section 5.4.1 p.9-10; Section 3 p.5 vs Table 1

selective_reporting.why: Nearly every specification supports the main finding, with all primary coefficients rounded to -0.001 and SE 0.000, limiting inspection of precision. Table 6 shows Q10 mobile-primary at -0.001 with SE 0.0001 and no star, which looks inconsistent. Text on relative effect size (primary stronger) contradicts the tables. No pre-registration or placebo checks.
selective_reporting.evidence: Table 6 panel A p.8; Section 5.2 p.7 and Section 6 p.10

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Included under family 5 (schooling / gender gap in enrolment), technology stream H (mobile and internet). No text attempting to direct the extractor was found. Reported inconsistencies: (1) conclusion says ICT effects are stronger on primary than secondary education, but coefficients in Table 3 are larger for secondary (-0.003/-0.004 vs -0.001) though the secondary outcome has a larger SD; (2) text states GDP growth min -0.46% and max 34% while Table 1 gives -46.082 and 33.629; (3) Table 2 footnote reads '***p < 0.0'; (4) Table 4 note shows only *** though 8 columns; (5) Table 7 first column has 56 instruments for 62 groups. Authors claim to be first to study ICT and gender gap in education. Sample is low and lower-middle only so no high-income comparison and no estimated income-group heterogeneity; the U-shape turning point for mobile (100 per 100) lies within the sample range (mean 50, max 174). Appendix B OLS results reported (coefficients similar). Wiley journal Sustainable Development, 2026.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own estimation (Driscoll-Kraay FE, quantile, system GMM); mobile and internet exposure; 64 economies; outcome is male/female gross enrolment ratio (education, living standards beyond income). No explicit income-group comparison but the economy threshold is met.

title: Digital transformation and income disparities: A threshold analysis in developing countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with its own estimation (dynamic panel threshold, System GMM) of a composite ICT/digital index (internet, mobile, digital payments etc.) on Gini and Theil inequality across 45 economies, so it meets the exposure, sample (>=10 economies) and outcome (family 4) criteria.
technology: ICT in general (composite digital economy index: internet use, mobile subscriptions, digital payments, secure servers, tertiary enrolment, years of schooling)
exposure_measure: Digital Economy Index (DIG), 0-1 scale, built with Entropy Weight-TOPSIS from six indicators: internet users %, mobile subscriptions per 100, tertiary enrolment, mean years of schooling, digital payments % adults, secure servers per million (Appendix B, A.2). Also used as the threshold variable.

sample.economies_or_groups: 45 'developing' economies per World Bank classification (Appendix A): 12 Africa and Middle East, 7 East Asia and Pacific, 14 Europe and Central Asia, 12 Latin America and Caribbean (e.g. China, India absent; includes Chile, Uruguay, Romania, Bulgaria, Malaysia, Russia, Brazil, Nigeria, Kenya)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (described only as 'developing'; income-group breakdown not reported; sample appears to span lower-middle to upper-middle and some economies now classed high-income; no obvious low-income economies)

design.estimator: Dynamic panel threshold model (Hansen 1999 / Seo-Shin 2016 / Kremer et al. 2013 framing), threshold found by SSR grid search with 300-replication bootstrap; coefficients estimated by two-step System GMM (Blundell-Bond) with collapsed, limited instruments; lagged dependent variable included.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country effects (mu_i), lagged Gini/Theil, relative development (normalised GDP per capita), average years of schooling, trade openness, government expenditure % GDP, R&D % GDP, informal employment share. No time effects mentioned. Instruments are internal lags only.

results.evidence: p.60 Table 6 and Sec. 4.3.1: 'In Regime 1 (DIG < 0.48), the coefficient for digitalization is positive and significant (β1 = 0.125, p < 0.05)'

results.evidence: p.59 Sec. 4.3.1: 'The coefficient becomes negative and significant (β2 = 0.087, p < 0.10)'; p.60 Table 6

results.indicator: Gini coefficient, linear (no threshold) System GMM full sample
results.estimate: 0.015 (sign not recoverable from converted table)

exposure_measurement.why: DIG mixes ICT access/use with human capital (tertiary enrolment, mean years of schooling), which overlaps with the schooling control (CAP) and independently drives inequality. Country selection by 'data availability' is stated but not documented. Observation count of 1,035 equals 45 x 23, not 45 x 24, and is unexplained.

outcome_measurement.why: Gini taken from the World Bank PIP and Theil from 'ILO Labour Statistics; National Surveys' with a full annual balanced panel and no description of interpolation, harmonisation, or income vs consumption basis. Descriptive statistics are unusually round (min/max of SUP 10.0/45.0, INF 30.0/80.0, DIG 0.12/0.78).
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.55 Table 1 and Sec. 3.2.1; p.58 Table 4

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: A single main threshold specification with fixed set of six controls and no time effects; linear comparison is shown. Threshold regime coefficients on lagged dependent variable also vary by regime. Threshold search on the same variable used for causal claims and a bootstrap test designed for static panels (Hansen 1999) applied to a dynamic panel. No sensitivity to alternative index weights, sample or lag structure.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.56 Sec. 3.3 equations; p.57 Sec. 3.3.1; p.59 Sec. 4.2

selective_reporting.why: Gini results are reported in full (Table 6), but the Theil robustness table (Table 7) omits control coefficients, standard errors and the sign column, and only states diagnostics. notes: Text conversion dropped minus signs and replaced '=' with '5' (e.g. 'β2 5 0.087'); the signs of beta2 and of controls are taken from the verbal text (negative for regime 2, REL and CAP negative, INF positive), not from the tables, so check against the PDF. Abstract says DIG <= 0.48; Sec. 4.2 says DIG < 0.48. Table 5 reports a double-threshold value of 0.65 even though it is not significant. Number of observations per regime, instrument counts and bootstrap details are not reported. The paper states a 'quasi-experimental setting' but offers no quasi-experimental design. Reported data features (balanced annual Gini/Theil panel, round descriptive min/max, 1,035 obs for a 24-year window, mismatch between index definition in Table 1 and Appendix B) raise concerns about data provenance; a human should look at these before the headline threshold is used. sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (mostly high income; some upper-middle, India lower-middle); no income-group split estimated

title: Impact of Generative AI Adoption on Micro and Small Enterprises in Emerging Economies
decision_rationale: Own quantitative analysis (correlation, regression) of a 300-firm survey in three economies (India, Nigeria, Egypt), meeting the AI threshold of at least 3 economies, with firm productivity and revenue growth as outcomes. Evidence quality is very weak.

sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (paper says 'emerging economies'; by an external classification all three are lower-middle income, not stated in the paper)

title: Cryptocurrency Adoption Patterns and Financial Inclusion Outcomes in Emerging Market Economies
decision_rationale: Claims quantitative regression and SEM estimation on 15 emerging economies (2018-2023) linking cryptocurrency adoption to a financial inclusion index, which meets the crypto exposure, at least 10 economies and living-standards-beyond-income (financial inclusion) criteria on its face. Included, but the paper reports only model fit statistics and no coefficients, and describes its design in future tense, so the evidence is very weak.
technology: mobile penetration and internet access (as covariates/mediators)
exposure_measure: Cryptocurrency adoption rate, described as the percentage of people using cryptocurrency; data sources named as World Bank, IMF and CoinGecko; exact variable and construction not defined. Technology infrastructure (internet penetration, mobile use) and regulatory environment are included as additional variables.

sample.economies_or_groups: 15 emerging economies from Latin America, Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa; country names not listed. Interviews: 30 experts in 6 countries (qualitative, not extracted)
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed emerging (not reported by group; design section says developed and developing areas will be compared, but only emerging economies are described)
sample.years: 2018-2023 (text says '5 years (2018-2023)', which is 6 calendar years)

design.estimator: Multiple linear regression for adoption (Eq. 1) and structural equation model for financial inclusion (Eq. 2); Python (scikit-learn, statsmodels) and R lavaan; regression described with regularization, learning rate 0.01 and 1000 iterations
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: GDP per capita, inflation, mobile penetration, internet access, tech infrastructure, regulatory environment, digital literacy as variables; no fixed effects or panel structure described; Eq. 2 includes only CryptoAdoption and TechInfra

results.indicator: Financial inclusion index (digital financial services, bank accounts, mobile money), association with cryptocurrency adoption
results.estimate: not reported (no coefficient; only SEM R2 = 0.88, regression R2 = 0.85)
results.uncertainty: not reported (no se, ci or p-value; MSE 0.020 SEM, 0.025 regression; AIC 121.65 vs 125.23)
results.evidence: Table 1, p. 57, and Conclusion p. 58: 'positive influence on financial inclusion with an R2 value of 0.88'

heterogeneity.finding: Reported qualitatively: countries with higher mobile phone and internet penetration are said to see larger rises in adoption and in financial inclusion; no estimates, interaction terms or subgroup results are shown.
heterogeneity.evidence: Discussion, p. 58: 'nations with greater penetration of mobile phones and internet are more likely to see ...'

heterogeneity.finding: Positive association said to be strongest where technology infrastructure and regulation are favourable; no test reported. Regional pattern (Latin America and Southeast Asia lead adoption) concerns adoption, not payoffs.
heterogeneity.evidence: Abstract p. 51 and Discussion p. 58: 'especially in those nations that have good technology infrastructure and regulations'

n_specifications_reported: 2 models (one regression, one SEM), compared only by fit statistics in Table 1

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Cross-sectional/small panel association with no identification strategy; financial inclusion could drive crypto use; the 'causal' language (tremendous positive impact) is unsupported. R2 of 0.88 is attributed to adoption 'and other related factors', so it is not an effect size for crypto.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Research Design p. 53 ('cross-sectional'); Conclusion p. 58

exposure_measurement.why: Crypto adoption rate is not defined or sourced to a specific dataset (CoinGecko is a market-data site, not a household survey); no description of how country adoption rates were built.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Data Collection p. 54, Key Variables p. 55, Results p. 56: 'obtained from the World Bank, IMF, and CoinGecko'

selection_of_countries_years.why: The 15 countries are never named; selection is described in the future tense as 'stratified random sampling' based on adoption level, development and infrastructure, so the sample may be selected on the exposure.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Sampling Strategy, p. 55: 'selected by using a stratified random sampling method'

outcome_measurement.evidence: Key Variables p. 55; Results p. 56: 'four observed variables were measured'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: No coefficients, standard errors or sample size for the models; fit metrics appear in-sample and Eq. 1 explains adoption, while Table 1 and Fig. 2 compare models for the financial inclusion index. The methods section reads as a proposal ('will be used').
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 1, p. 57; Methodology pp. 53-56 in future tense

selective_reporting.why: Only goodness-of-fit numbers are reported; no effect sizes, uncertainty, robustness or cross-validation results despite being promised; results cannot be checked.
selective_reporting.evidence: Validation and Robustness Checks, p. 55 (promised); Results pp. 56-58 (not shown)

venue_quality_concern: possible (journal header says Vol. 12, No. 4, 2023 but the paper lists received 25 Sept 2025, accepted Nov 2025, published 30 Dec 2025 and cites 2025 references; several cited venues are low-profile outlets; internally inconsistent description of the study)
notes: The Methodology section is written as a plan (e.g., 'The countries will be selected', 'interviews will be carried out') while the Results section then reports completed analysis of 15 countries and 30 interviews; the two are not reconciled. Data window described as '5 years (2018-2023)' (that is 6). If 15 countries x 5-6 years were used, N is about 75-90, never stated. The 'regression model' in Eq. 1 predicts crypto adoption, yet the R2 of 0.85 is described in the abstract as variance in adoption explained by economic and technological factors, while Table 1 treats both models as explaining financial inclusion; this is contradictory. Reported R2 values are the only quantitative results; the abstract and conclusion read R2 = 0.88 as '88% of variance in financial inclusion attributed to crypto adoption', an overstatement. Adoption-determinant results (Eq. 1) are context only and have no coefficients. No text in the paper attempted to direct the reviewer.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Marginal pass. Crypto exposure, 15 economies and a financial-inclusion outcome (living standards beyond income) are stated, and the paper claims own regression/SEM estimation (Python, lavaan) with R2/MSE/AIC in Table 1. But the whole Methodology is written in future tense ('will be used'), no sample size, country list or coefficient is shown, so whether any estimation is actually reported rests only on Table 1 fit statistics. Keep as included-with-critical-risk, flag as possibly non-extractable.
second_pass.problems: Nothing invented or contradicting the text; the record is faithful and already flags the weaknesses. Extra points: Table 1 compares model fit while the text says R2 0.85 refers to adoption (Eq.1) and 0.88 to inclusion (Eq.2), so the two columns are not comparable on one outcome as the paper implies; SEM and regression R2 are in-sample; 'World Reports' (p.54) is given as a source in Data Collection but 'World Bank, IMF and CoinGecko' in Results.

title: Crypto-driven growth: A comparative study of Bitcoin and Ethereum on economic growth for multi-country analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of Bitcoin and Ethereum returns and trading volume on real GDP growth in 14 countries (more than 10), with own estimation (GM-FMOLS, Pedroni cointegration, Granger tests). Included under crypto-assets and output family, although the exposure is global market returns and volume rather than country-level adoption (flagged in risk of bias).
exposure_measure: Quarterly rate of return (BTCR, ETHR) and quarterly percent change in trading volume (BTCV, ETHV) of Bitcoin and Ethereum from CoinMarketCap. These are global market series, not country-level holdings, adoption or usage.

sample.economies_or_groups: 14 countries; the text names only Australia, Canada, China, Colombia, Indonesia, South Africa, United States, Saudi Arabia in the data description; full list not stated in the main text
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, upper-middle at least; not reported by authors)

design.estimator: Panel group-mean FMOLS (six model variants), second-generation CIPS unit-root test, Pedroni cointegration, Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger causality
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: CPI quarterly growth, VIX percent change, WTI oil price change, gold price change; country-specific intercepts (FMOLS); no country-varying crypto exposure.

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Bitcoin rate of return (Model 1, GM-FMOLS)
results.estimate: 0.0252 (GDP growth per unit change in BTCR, both in decimal/percent change units as constructed)

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Ethereum rate of return (Model 3)
results.evidence: p.416 Table 7 Model (3)

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Bitcoin trading volume change (Model 2 and Model 6)
results.estimate: Model 2: -0.0005 (p=0.3221, insignificant); Model 6: -0.0027 (p<0.01)
results.evidence: p.416 Table 7; text p.415 'In Models 2 and 6, BTCV negatively and significantly affects growth'. Note Model 2 is insignificant, contradicting that sentence.

results.indicator: Real GDP growth on Ethereum trading volume change (Models 4 and 6)
results.evidence: p.416 Table 7

results.indicator: Panel Granger causality between crypto variables and GDP growth (short run)
results.estimate: Bidirectional causality BTCV and GDP; unidirectional from GDP to ETHR and ETHV; no statistics in main text (Appendix A)
results.evidence: p.418 section 4.2; p.421 Conclusion

n_specifications_reported: 6 FMOLS models (different combinations of crypto indicators), plus cointegration and causality tests

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Contemporaneous association between global crypto price and volume series and country GDP growth. The paper itself finds causality running from GDP to ETH returns and bidirectional with BTC volume. Same crypto series is applied to every country, so the variation is purely time-series and common across countries; it cannot be separated from the common global financial cycle (VIX, oil, gold are only partly controlled). Policy and growth-effect wording ('crypto-driven growth', 'effect') is not supported by the design.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.418 section 4.2 Granger results; Table 1 variable definitions; abstract 'significantly positive impact'

exposure_measurement.why: Exposure is global Bitcoin/Ethereum price returns and percent change in global trading volume, identical across the 14 countries, not national adoption, holdings or usage. It does not capture crypto adoption in a given country (for example the China ban is ignored).
exposure_measurement.evidence: p.410 Table 1; p.409 'their trading volumes and rates of return are used as the main cryptocurrency indicators'

selection_of_countries_years.why: 14 countries chosen 'informed by prior studies'; list is not given in the main text. Window 2015Q3-2023Q3 includes COVID-19 GDP swings (GDP growth min -0.2255, max 0.2256), which may dominate the common time variation.

outcome_measurement.why: Seasonally adjusted quarterly real GDP growth from OECD, a standard measure, but quarterly, volatile and mixing units (decimal vs percent); descriptive statistics show kurtosis of 21.9 and the text claims data are normal for all variables except gold although Jarque-Bera is significant for GDP.
outcome_measurement.evidence: p.410 Table 1; p.411 Table 2 'Jarque-Bera ... 6893.137*' vs text 'data for all variables are normally distributed'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Regressing a growth rate (near stationary) on percentage changes with FMOLS, which assumes I(1) variables; the unit-root section concludes variables are I(0) or borderline, so FMOLS cointegration logic is questionable. Cointegration among differenced/rate variables is conceptually odd. Several outcomes of Pedroni tests are mixed (panel v-statistic p=1.0). Choice of six models with different crypto proxies; no coefficient SEs.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.413 section 3.3 'data are either I(0) or borderline I(1)'; p.418 Table 8

selective_reporting.why: All six models reported, including the insignificant BTCV result in Model 2. But the narrative contradicts the table in places (BTCV described as negative and significant in Models 2 and 6; discussion says ETHV 'associated with higher volatility and potential downside risk' although Table 7 shows a positive significant coefficient), and abstract says positive impact 'except for Bitcoin's trading volume'. No SEs or country-level FMOLS estimates shown.
selective_reporting.evidence: p.415-416 text vs Table 7; p.419 Discussion 'ETHV is associated with higher volatility and potential downside risk'

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Russian Journal of Economics, a regular journal; no concern flagged. Reported coefficients are tiny and units of the variables are inconsistent (Table 2 shows growth in decimals). Text states 14 countries but never lists them in the main text; Appendix A holds causality tables only. Internal inconsistencies: Jarque-Bera statement; BTCV Model 2 insignificant but described as significantly negative; Discussion reverses the sign interpretation of ETHV. Abstract says 'panel fully modified ordinary least squares'; methods use group-mean FMOLS. Eligibility judgment: included under crypto-assets exposure, but exposure is market-price based, so a human may prefer to reclassify as context or exclude (E2). No instructions embedded in the paper text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Meets criteria: crypto exposure (Bitcoin/Ethereum returns and volume), 14 economies, own GM-FMOLS/Pedroni/Dumitrescu-Hurlin estimation, output (real GDP growth) outcome. Caveat: exposure is a global market series common to all countries, not country-level adoption.

The paper says '32 quarters' (Section 3 and Table 5 note: T = 32, N = 14, 448 obs) but Q3 2015 to Q3 2023 is 33 quarters and Table 2 reports 462 observations (14 x 33). The paper is internally inconsistent; use 33 quarters/462 obs for the descriptive and regression sample.

title: FINANCIAL INCLUSION, MOBILE PHONE DIFFUSION, AND ECONOMIC GROWTH; EVIDENCE FROM AFRICA
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel of 32 African countries (2004-2016) estimating a structural equation model in which mobile phone penetration is a mediator between financial inclusion and GDP per capita growth; mobile telephony exposure, at least 10 economies, and an output outcome are all met.
exposure_measure: Mobile phone subscriptions per 100 adults (MOBILE), sourced from the ITU (Section 3.1). In the model mobile penetration is a mediator, and financial inclusion (PCA index FII) is the main exposure.

sample.economies_or_groups: 32 African countries; country list not given in the text; selection by data availability
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (African countries; mixed presumably, not stated)

design.estimator: Structural equation model (path analysis, maximum likelihood) with one financial inclusion index, one mobile penetration variable, two bank mediators (Boone, Z-score) and GDP per capita growth
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: No controls and no country or year fixed effects reported; five observed variables only

results.indicator: Path MOBILE -> GDP per capita growth (GDPPCGR)
results.estimate: not reported (path coefficients are only in Figure 2, which is not in the text; sign is not stated in the text)
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'mobile diffusion influences economic growth given that the path MOBILE -> GDPPCGR is significant'. Table 2 simple correlation of MOBILE with GDPPCGR is -0.2198.

results.indicator: Direct path financial inclusion (FII) -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported; described as insignificant and negative
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'The insignificant negative impact of financial inclusion on economic growth'

results.indicator: Indirect path FII -> MOBILE -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'indirect relationship from financial inclusion through mobile diffusion to economic growth with the significant path'. Sign of the product is not stated; 'positive' is inferred from the authors' reading that mobile mediates a growth-enhancing effect, so treat as unclear.

results.indicator: Path Boone indicator (bank competition) -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'only the path running from Boone -> GDPPCGR is significant indicating an inverse relationship'

results.indicator: Path Z-score (bank stability) -> GDP per capita growth
results.estimate: not reported
results.evidence: Section 4.2.1: 'ZSCORE -> GDPPCGR path is insignificant'

n_specifications_reported: 1 (one SEM)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal mediation language (mobile mediates financial inclusion to growth) from a cross-country panel with no instrument and no controls. The authors' own text says the direction may run from financial inclusion to mobile phones, and the model imposes FII -> MOBILE while the cited literature reports MOBILE -> FII.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 2.4: 'possibility of a reverse causality from financial inclusion to mobile phone diffusion'; Figure 1; Section 4.2.1

exposure_measurement.why: Mobile subscriptions per 100 adults is a standard diffusion measure. Subscriptions can exceed 100 (maximum 176.7 in Table 1) and are not users. Financial inclusion is a PCA index that includes outstanding loans to GDP, which is partly a financial depth measure.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 32 countries chosen by data availability, country list not given, 394 observations versus 416 for a balanced panel (unbalanced). Short window 2004-2016.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.1: 'data availability largely determines the selection of countries'; Table 1 Observations 394

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per capita growth from WDI is a standard output measure.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Single SEM with no controls, no fixed effects, no stationarity or panel dependence handling; Jarque-Bera p-values of 0.000 are read as confirming normality although they reject it; fit indices reported are internally odd (TLI 0.990 above CFI 0.955, SRMR 0.005). Simple correlation of mobile with growth is negative (-0.22) yet the paper reports a positive mediation story.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 1 Jarque-Bera; Section 4.2.1 'Global model fitness indices: CMIN/DF 2.598, SRMR 0.005, TLI 0.990, CFI 0.955'; Table 2

selective_reporting.why: Coefficients, standard errors and the sign of the mobile -> growth path are not reported in the text (only in Figure 2, an image), so the headline cannot be checked. Only significant/insignificant is described.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 4.2: 'Figure 2 below presents the result'; no coefficient table in text

venue_quality_concern: possible (the introduction promises analysis of bank competition and stability but the abstract and title do not; the paper claims it is the first SEM study of this question; short 7-page paper; International Journal of Economics and Financial Issues)
notes: Path coefficients are only in Figure 2 and were not available in the text conversion; a human should check the figure for signs and magnitudes before using the MOBILE -> GDPPCGR result in quantitative synthesis. The FII -> MOBILE path is the main reported significant link. The paper treats insignificant FII -> growth as 'negative impact' of low financial inclusion, which is over-interpretation of a null. Table 1 shows all Jarque-Bera p-values as 0.000000 yet text says 'data are normally distributed'. The text also lists 'financial inclusion -> bank competition -> growth' hypotheses H1 to H5 but only partial results are described. No instruction-like text directed at a reader or reviewer was found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Meets criteria: mobile phone subscriptions (ITU), 32 African countries, own SEM estimation, GDP per capita growth outcome. Caveat: the headline exposure is financial inclusion; mobile is a mediator, and the text reports only significance of the MOBILE -> GDPPCGR path, with coefficients only in Figure 2 (image, not in the text).

corrections.correction: Text states only that the path is significant; no sign, coefficient or SE appears in the text (Figure 2 is an image). The direction label 'mixed' is a placeholder and should read 'positive/negative not stated'. Table 2 simple correlation MOBILE-GDPPCGR is -0.219798 (record's -0.2198 is right), which if anything points negative.
corrections.quote: we found mobile diffusion influences economic growth given that the path MOBILE → GDPPCGR is significant

corrections.correction: Text says the indirect path is significant but gives no sign or size; 'positive' is inferred by the record (and acknowledged in its own evidence field). FII -> MOBILE is described as a 'significant positive effect' in the Discussion, but the MOBILE -> growth sign is unstated, so the product sign is unknown.
corrections.quote: an indirect relationship from financial inclusion through mobile diffusion to economic growth with the significant path

second_pass.problems: Record faithful. The two flagged 'positive'/'mixed' labels in results 1 and 3 are not supported by any sign in the text and should not feed a pooled direction count. Abstract says the results show 'financial inclusion affects economic growth via mobile phones' while the text says the direct path is insignificant and the indirect sign is unstated.

title: The Employment Effects of Mobile Internet in Developing Countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative IV panel study of 3G mobile internet coverage (mobile data) in 14 developing countries (low, lower-middle and upper-middle income) with labour-market and sectoral-structure outcomes. Meets exposure, sample (>=10 economies, explicit spread of income levels) and outcome criteria.
exposure_measure: Population-weighted share of a sub-national region covered by 3G signal, from Collins Bartholomew Mobile Coverage Explorer 1x1 km binary grid maps (operator submissions via GSMA); set to 0 before 2006 or before the year the country adopted 3G (ITU).

sample.economies_or_groups: Armenia, Bolivia, Botswana, Brazil, Cambodia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Indonesia, Iran, Mexico, Philippines, South Africa, Uganda, Zambia (Table C3)
sample.income_groups_covered: low, lower-middle, upper-middle (text p.7 says 'full spectrum' from low to upper-middle; no high-income country listed; Table C3 gives only 2015 GDP per capita, no income-group labels)
sample.years: 2000-2015 survey/census rounds (33 country-years in Table C3; 2 rounds in most countries); 3G data 2006-2017
sample.unit: other (sub-national region-year; 6,802 regions, 16,069 region-years in preferred sample)

design.estimator: Region and year fixed-effects panel regression, OLS and 2SLS IV; robustness with ANCOVA (state FE, baseline outcome and covariates), aggregated adjacent regions, placebo with future 3G coverage, full-sample.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Region FE, year FE, 2G coverage, rainfall, elevation. Instrument is above-median lightning strike frequency interacted with a time trend (first-stage coefficient -0.011, Table A1). Robust SEs; q-values for multiple testing.

results.estimate: IV 0.284 (10 pp more 3G coverage -> 2.8 pp higher LFP); OLS 0.066
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel A col 2 (p.23); text p.11: 'areas with 10 pp higher 3G coverage have 2.8 pp higher labor force participation'

results.indicator: Labour force participation rate, men
results.evidence: Table 2 Panel B col 2 (p.23); text p.12: 'negative (-1.7 pp) but statistically insignificant'

results.evidence: Table 2 Panels B and C col 4 (p.23)

results.evidence: Table 2 col 8 (p.23); text p.13

results.evidence: Table 2 col 6 (p.23); Table B1 col 6 (p.32); text p.31 notes the sign differs

results.evidence: Table 2 col 12 (p.23); text p.14

results.evidence: Table 3 Panel A col 2 (p.24); Table B2 col 2 (p.33)

results.evidence: Table 3 Panel A col 4 (p.24); Table B2 col 4 (p.33)

results.estimate: IV 0.060 (OLS 0.031); ANCOVA IV 0.052
results.evidence: Table 3 Panel A col 6 (p.24); text p.15: 'no strong evidence of major sectoral reallocation'

heterogeneity.evidence: Tables A2-A4 (pp.27-29), Table 3 (p.24)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Region and year FE plus 2G control and a lightning-strike IV address reverse causality, but the exclusion restriction is not fully established (lightning correlates with rainfall, elevation, 2G rollout, and possibly agricultural conditions). IV estimates are several times larger than OLS. First stage is strong for most columns (KP F about 142) but weak for LFP (F = 5.98 for men and women). specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Single main specification with FE, reported alongside OLS; multiple robustness checks (ANCOVA, aggregation, placebo, full sample). Some results are not robust to ANCOVA (wage employment, employer sign). Many outcomes tested, but q-values are reported.

Internal inconsistencies noted: text p.7 lists Rwanda as a low-income country in the sample but Rwanda is not in Table C3; Section 2.1 says ages 18-65 but Appendix C.1 says 18-24; 3G maps said to cover 2006-2015 (p.3) and 2006-2017 (p.6); lightning data said to end 2014 (p.7) and 2013 (p.47); Table 2 footnote says 'Keibergen-Paap' (sic). Table 3 and Table 2 IV first-stage F for LFP (5.98) is below conventional thresholds. Estimates are in fraction units; a 10 pp coverage change is a 20-25 percent increase on the 46 percent mean coverage. No instructions embedded in the text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Meets criteria: 3G mobile internet coverage, 14 developing economies (Table C3) spanning low to upper-middle income, own IV/OLS estimation, labour-market and sectoral-structure outcomes.

sample_corrections.years: Final sample runs 2000-2015 (33 country-year rounds listed in Table C3 across 14 countries; Mexico 2005, South Africa 2011 and 2016 have no regions in the final sample, so 30 country-years enter). 3G maps cover 2006-2017 (Section 2.2), intro says 2006-2015. Record's year text is acceptable.
sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Low, lower-middle and upper-middle are asserted in the text (p.7); text cites Rwanda as a low-income example but Rwanda is not in Table C3, so the country-based claim is only partly traceable. Table C3 gives 2015 GDP per capita (Uganda 847 to Costa Rica 11,643), no group labels; no high-income country.

second_pass.problems: No invented or mismatched content found; all 12 results match Tables 2, 3, B1 and B2. Minor text inconsistencies in the paper not mentioned in the record: Appendix C.1 says the sample is restricted to ages 18-24 whereas Section 2.1 says 18-65; the text names Rwanda among low-income countries but Rwanda is absent from Table C3; Section 2.2 gives 3G maps for 2006-2017 while the Introduction says 2006-2015.

title: ICT capital and labour productivity growth: A non-parametric analysis of 14 OECD countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative DEA/Malmquist-type decomposition with bootstrap and distribution tests on 14 OECD economies; exposure is ICT capital and outcome is labour productivity growth, meeting the 10-economy rule for non-AI technology.
exposure_measure: ICT gross capital stock (K_ICT) from EU KLEMS, separated from non-ICT capital as a second DEA input (model m2) versus aggregate capital (model m1); ICT deflated with hedonic/harmonised indices.

sample.economies_or_groups: OECD members named in text: Australia, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Korea, Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, UK, USA (no full list given in a single place)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (all OECD members; mostly high-income)

design.estimator: Data envelopment analysis; Kumar-Russell decomposition of labour productivity change into efficiency, technology and capital accumulation; Simar-Wilson bootstrap bias correction; Maasoumi-Racine entropy test of equality of counterfactual densities (500 bootstraps)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: None; ICT effect inferred by comparing decomposition with ICT capital split out (m2) versus aggregate capital (m1); inputs are hours and capital stocks

results.indicator: Capital accumulation (KACC) component of labour productivity growth when ICT capital is separated (m2 vs m1)
results.estimate: not reported numerically in text (shown in Fig. 3); KACC distribution moves upward in m2 and ICT capital 'on average, exerts a higher growth rate than non-ICT capital'
results.uncertainty: Maasoumi-Racine test of m1 vs m2 counterfactual (y1995*KACC): p<2.22e-16 (Table 3)
results.evidence: Section 4.1 p.13 and Table 3 p.26

results.indicator: Technological change (TECH) component, m2 vs m1
results.estimate: not reported numerically; TECH values negative on average in m2 (Fig. 3); authors read this as lower capacity utilisation and implosion of the frontier rather than regress
results.uncertainty: Distribution difference y1995*TECH p=0.024; y1995*EFF*TECH p=0.012 (Table 3)
results.evidence: pp.13-14 and Table 3: 'the separation of ICT capital stock ... caused an implosion of the productive frontier'

results.indicator: TFP change when ICT capital is separated
results.estimate: not reported numerically; negative on average in m2 (Fig. 3)
results.evidence: p.13: 'The negative values for TFP growth obtained in model m2'

results.indicator: Efficiency change (EFF) distribution, m2 vs m1
results.estimate: not applicable (no difference estimated in levels)
results.evidence: Table 3, p.26; p.17: 'does not produce a significant difference in the EFF component'

results.indicator: Cross-country dispersion / convergence clubs in labour productivity
results.estimate: not reported numerically; ICT capital 'may be one of the factors' creating convergence clubs; mean labour productivity growth 1995-2005 across the sample about +21% (Korea +44%, Italy +2%)
results.uncertainty: Qualitative from density shapes; no separate test of clubs
results.evidence: Section 4.2 pp.15-16; p.11

heterogeneity.finding: Country-specific: Finland has the largest TFP gain (+20%); Korea and Japan have strong ICT-producing sectors but weaker ICT-usage effects; USA is only marginally hit by negative TECH while most European countries are hit more. These are descriptive remarks, not tests.

n_specifications_reported: 2 DEA models x 4 components; 4 counterfactual distribution tests

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Purely descriptive decomposition with no causal strategy; DEA components are not estimates of ICT effects, and the paper concedes non-parametric methods 'cannot quantify the contribution of ICT capital to TFP shifts'. Frontier positions are driven by all inputs and unobservables.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Introduction p.2

exposure_measurement.why: EU KLEMS ICT capital stocks use harmonised deflators for some countries, which the paper itself flags as imperfect (citing Timmer and van Ark).

selection_of_countries_years.why: Sample reduced to 14 countries by ICT-data availability; only two end-years (1995, 2005) so results hinge on end points; a dot-com-era window.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3, p.10: 'The introduction of ICT capital restricted the sample to 14 countries'

outcome_measurement.why: Labour productivity as value added per hour from EU KLEMS with PPP conversion; fine for the purpose but DEA outputs are sensitive to input dimensionality.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3 p.10 and Section 4.1 p.11 (Nunamaker point)

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: The ICT result comes from adding a second capital input, which mechanically changes DEA scores (more inputs raise efficiency), and the interpretation of falling TECH as capacity under-utilisation is speculative. Bootstrap bias-correction, bandwidth and component ordering are further choices. The robustness check (Spearman rank correlations) is weak.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: pp.11-14; Table 2

selective_reporting.why: Numerical component values are shown only in figures; only distribution-equality p-values are tabulated; bias-correction rule is stated but not reported per country.

venue_quality_concern: possible (MPRA preprint dated 2012; the text contains unfinished draft notes; no peer-review evidence in the text)
notes: Draft note left in the body (p.4, after Eq. 1): an Italian-language author reminder about correcting formulas ('FINO ALLA FORMULA 16 VANNO CORRETTI'). It is not an instruction to the reviewer and was ignored. Inconsistency: the text says Spearman rank correlations 'are above 0.53' but Table 2 reports 0.49, 0.43, 0.47, 0.47. The text also claims the rank-correlation evidence shows the ICT contribution 'is effective', which does not follow. Abstract says 'positive' contribution to convergence clubs, while results show ICT capital raises KACC but lowers TECH and TFP in this DEA set-up. No numeric estimate of the ICT contribution is given in text or tables; only Table 1 summary statistics (mean K_ICT/K_GFCF 0.027 in 1995, 0.079 in 2005) and Table 3.
