title: ICT capital–skill complementarity and wage inequality: Evidence from OECD countries
decision_rationale: Own GMM/IV estimation of a sector-level production function on 14 OECD economies (>=10 economies, non-AI); exposure is ICT equipment capital and outcome is the skill premium (distribution/labour market).
exposure_measure: Quantity of ICT equipment capital (k_i) and its rental price (r_i) from EU KLEMS, by country-sector-year; ICT equipment share rose from 0.2-2.4% in the 1970s to 5-21% in the 2000s.

sample.economies_or_groups: Australia, Austria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Sweden, UK, US
sample.income_groups_covered: high only (advanced OECD economies; paper does not report income classification)
sample.unit: industry-country (country-sector-year, goods and service sectors; 682 observations)

design.estimator: Joint GMM on first-differenced (five-year) first-order conditions of a four-factor nested CES production function (ICT capital, non-ICT capital, skilled labour, unskilled labour); Shapley decomposition of the skill premium
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country-sector-specific polynomial trends in share parameters (orders chosen to fit each country-sector); differencing removes time-invariant country-sector wedges; robustness with collective bargaining coverage; shift-share IV built from the other sector's industries in other countries.

results.indicator: Elasticity-of-substitution parameters: sigma (ICT-skilled composite vs unskilled) and rho (ICT vs skilled); capital-skill complementarity requires sigma>rho
results.estimate: sigma=0.888, rho=-0.162 (difference about 1.05) under factor-biased technological change; sigma=0.642, rho=-0.053 under factor-neutral change
results.uncertainty: SE clustered at country-sector: sigma 0.029, rho 0.051 (Newey-West SE 0.026 and 0.057); factor-neutral sigma SE 0.248
results.evidence: p.15 Table 1; 'ICT equipment is much more complementary to skilled labor than unskilled labor even in the presence of factor-biased technological change'

results.indicator: Contribution of ICT capital-skill complementarity effect to change in the skill premium (w_h/w_u), decomposed with relative labour quantity and unobserved factor-augmenting technology effects
results.estimate: Not reported as a single coefficient; shown graphically (log changes, Figs 8-9). Complementarity effect widens the premium in all countries; the relative labour quantity effect narrows it; the rise in the US premium from the 1980s to 2000s is attributed mostly to the complementarity effect.
results.uncertainty: not reported (no confidence intervals for decomposition)
results.evidence: p.21 Sec 6.2.2: 'capital–skill complementarity effect associated with a rise in ICT equipment is large enough to account for a rise in the skill premium in almost all countries'

results.indicator: Observed factors (complementarity + quantity effects) track actual skill premium trend
results.estimate: Observed factors line up with actual trends in the goods sector of 8 of 14 countries and the service sector of 9 of 14; they do not line up in the goods sector of 6 countries and the service sector of 2 (Finland, Italy)
results.evidence: p.26 Sec 6.2.2: 'Unobserved factors cannot be disregarded as determinants of changes in the skill premium in these countries.'

results.indicator: Cross-country differences in change in the skill premium relative to the US explained by ICT equipment and labour quantities
results.estimate: Table 4 decomposition, e.g. goods sector log-point gaps vs US: data 0.225 vs model 0.182 for Australia; ICT component ranges from -0.501 (Austria) to 0.624 (Japan)
results.evidence: p.27 Table 4; 'differences ... attributable at least in part to ICT equipment in almost all countries'

results.indicator: Relative demand for skilled labour (ln(l_h/l_u)) and the contribution of the falling ICT rental price
results.estimate: e.g. US goods sector: change in ln(l_h/l_u) data 1.066, model 1.207; part due to r_i 2.538 (offset by w_h -4.600, w_u +2.795, technology terms 8.371 and -7.897)
results.evidence: p.29 Table 5; 'a fall in the rental price of ICT capital is large enough to account for a rise in relative labor quantity'

results.indicator: Effect of higher education expansion on the skill premium with versus without capital-skill complementarity
results.estimate: Impact of rising skilled labour on the log skill premium is 1.78x (goods) and 1.58x (service) larger on average when complementarity is accounted for; e.g. US goods -0.274 total (-0.154 complementarity, -0.121 quantity)
results.evidence: p.30-31 Table 6 and text

heterogeneity.finding: Complementarity effect is larger in the goods than the service sector in most countries; sigma and rho estimates are similar across sectors (goods sigma 0.847, rho -0.114; service sigma 0.889, rho -0.123).
heterogeneity.evidence: p.16 Table 2; p.26 'capital–skill complementarity effect was greater for the goods sector than the service sector in the majority of countries'

heterogeneity.finding: Country heterogeneity: the complementarity effect is particularly large in Denmark, Finland and the US; the quantity effect is particularly large in the UK; Finland's gap to the US is mostly unobserved technology.
Adding collective bargaining coverage to the wedge leaves sigma and rho almost unchanged (0.873, -0.119) and the coefficient is insignificant.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.15-16 Table 2 last row

income_group_results.high: All 14 economies are advanced OECD members; complementarity effect widens skill premium in all, sigma>rho pooled (Table 1)

n_specifications_reported: about 6 (baseline factor-biased, factor-neutral, goods only, service only, collective bargaining control; plus Czech/Slovenia exclusion mentioned in a footnote without table)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Shift-share IV uses other-sector, other-country industry growth to instrument factor quantities, which addresses simultaneity in principle, but validity (exogenous shares or shocks, no common global shocks) is asserted not tested; no first-stage strength or overidentification statistics reported in the main text; unobserved technology is a residual absorbed by flexible trends.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: p.13 Sec 5.1.4 and fn 8

exposure_measurement.why: ICT equipment capital and user cost from EU KLEMS national-accounts data capture ICT investment directly; user cost computed without a competitive-market assumption.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 14 advanced OECD economies, data ending 2005, unbalanced panel ('as many countries and years as possible'); results do not speak to middle- or low-income economies or the post-2005 period.

outcome_measurement.why: Skill premium is high-skilled (college) versus all other workers, from labour compensation divided by hours including part-time, self-employed and family workers, with composition adjustment; not a standard wage-survey measure, and the paper notes it differs from other studies.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Polynomial order of the time-varying share parameters is chosen separately for each country-sector to fit the relative factor prices, so the model fit (Figs 4-7) is largely by construction and the split between observed-factor and unobserved-technology effects depends on this choice; decomposition depends on parametric nested-CES form and Shapley ordering.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: p.12 Sec 5.1.1 'We choose the orders of polynomials ... to fit the trends'; p.21 fn 9

selective_reporting.why: Few robustness specifications shown; no sensitivity of decompositions to alternative trend orders or instruments; footnote claims Czech/Slovenia exclusion leaves results unchanged without a table. Mixed fit across countries is reported honestly (Sec 6.2.2).

venue_quality_concern: possible (arXiv preprint v5 as supplied; peer-review status of this version cannot be confirmed from the text, although the acknowledgements thank anonymous referees)
notes: Structural estimation, so the headline is the pair of substitution parameters and a decomposition, not a reduced-form effect of ICT on wages. Outcome is relative wages (skill premium), so the sign 'positive' means ICT raises inequality. Sample is exclusively high income. No instruction-like text found in the paper. Possible duplicate/published version elsewhere; check against other records.

title: The role of governance in the effect of the internet on financial inclusion in sub-Saharan Africa
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study (system GMM) of internet use and a financial inclusion index in 42 sub-Saharan African economies, so it meets the 10-economy rule for non-AI technology. Outcome falls in family 5 (financial inclusion).
exposure_measure: Individuals using the internet (% of population), World Development Indicators.

sample.economies_or_groups: 42 sub-Saharan African countries (list not given in the text)
sample.income_groups_covered: not reported (SSA only; no income-group split)
sample.years: 2004-2019 in Section 3.3; abstract and conclusion say 2004-2020

design.estimator: System GMM (Blundell-Bond) dynamic panel with lagged dependent variable and internet x governance interactions; one-step or two-step not stated
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Lagged financial inclusion index, log GDP per capita, education index, trade openness, gross capital formation, governance indicator; no explicit country/time fixed effects reported; internal (lagged) instruments, 19-20 instruments, 42 groups

results.indicator: Direct (unconditional) effect of internet users (% pop) on supply-side financial inclusion index (IFI: bank branches and ATMs per km2 and per 100,000 adults)
results.estimate: -0.0003 to -0.0005 per percentage point of internet users in Table 1 (five of six columns; RQ column 4.17e-06, not significant); -0.001 in Table 2 for economic, institutional and general governance columns
results.uncertainty: p<0.01 for -0.0003 (political stability, voice) and -0.0005 (corruption control); p=0.021 (govt effectiveness); p=0.007 (rule of law); p=0.979 (regulatory quality); p=0.860 (political governance composite)
results.evidence: Table 1 'Internet (INTERNET)' row; Table 2 same row; Section 4.1: 'the internet negatively and significantly affect on financial inclusion at the 1% level'

results.indicator: Interaction of internet with governance on financial inclusion index (conditional effect)
results.estimate: Table 1: INTERNET x VA 0.001, x RQ 0.001, x GE 0.001, x RL 0.0008 (significant); x PS -0.0001 and x CC -0.0004 (not significant). Table 2: x EG 0.0004, x IG 0.001, x GG 0.001 (significant); x PG -0.0001 (not significant)
results.evidence: Table 1 and Table 2 interaction rows

results.indicator: Net effect of internet on financial inclusion at mean governance
results.estimate: -0.0009 (voice and accountability), -0.001 (government effectiveness), -0.0008 (rule of law); composite indicators reported only as 'nsa'
results.uncertainty: not reported (computed from point estimates, no standard error)
results.evidence: Table 1 'Internet net effects' row; Section 4.1: '–0.0009 ([-0.0003]+ [0.001× –0.648])'

heterogeneity.finding: Internet effect on the supply-side financial inclusion index rises with governance quality: the internet x governance interaction is positive and significant for voice and accountability, regulatory quality, government effectiveness, rule of law, and for economic, institutional and general governance, but not for political stability, corruption control or the political governance composite.
heterogeneity.threshold_value: 0.300 (voice and accountability), 0.300 (government effectiveness), 0.250 (rule of law); 2.500 (economic governance), 1.000 (institutional governance), 1.000 (general governance)
heterogeneity.evidence: Abstract and Table 1/Table 2 'Gov. thresholds' rows; Eq. (6) threshold = |alpha2/alpha4|

income_group_results.high: not applicable (sample is sub-Saharan Africa only)

n_specifications_reported: 10 (six governance indicators in Table 1, four composites in Table 2)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('the internet can be effectively complemented...') rests only on system GMM with internal lagged instruments; no external instrument and the paper does not say which regressors are treated as endogenous. The lagged dependent variable coefficient is 0.93-0.997, close to a unit root, which weakens lagged-level instruments. Sargan p-values of 0.96-1.000 are a sign of an overfitted instrument set. Governance and internet use are both likely to respond to financial development.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.2; Table 1 'Financial inclusion (IFI) (-1)' row and Sargan/Hansen rows

exposure_measurement.why: Share of individuals using the internet is a standard WDI measure, but the argument is about internet quality and cost, which it does not capture. Mobile internet and fixed broadband are not separated.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Section 3.3: 'individual using the internet (% of population)'; Introduction on cost and quality

selection_of_countries_years.why: 42 SSA countries, 2004-2019, unbalanced (426-435 observations against about 672 possible). Country list is not given, and the text states both 2004-2019 and 2004-2020. No income-group breakdown.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3.3; Table 1 'Observations' row; Abstract vs Section 3.3

outcome_measurement.why: The index uses only four supply-side access indicators (branches and ATMs per km2 and per 100,000 adults), min-max normalised within the sample. It omits account ownership, digital payments and mobile money, which are the channels through which the internet would act. A negative internet coefficient may reflect substitution away from branches and ATMs. The text also refers to 'eight dimensions' but lists four.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Section 3.1, Eqs. (1)-(3); text 'we measure financial inclusion using eight dimensions such as: (i)...(iv)'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Six governance indicators and four composites are interacted separately, with thresholds computed from ratios of rounded coefficients (0.0003/0.001). A threshold of 2.5 sits at the edge of the WGI range. No sensitivity checks beyond the composite re-grouping.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 1, Table 2; Eq. (6); Section 4.2

selective_reporting.why: The abstract reports thresholds only for the significant interactions and states the internet 'can be effectively complemented'. It does not say that the direct internet effect is negative in nearly every column and that net effects at mean governance are negative (-0.0008 to -0.001). Thresholds above the sample mean governance (-0.65 to -0.75) imply most observations are below them.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract; Table 1 'Internet net effects' and 'Gov. thresholds' rows; Table 1 note on means

venue_quality_concern: possible (AGDI working paper WP/23/004, not peer reviewed in this form; assignment lists year 2022 while the working paper is dated January 2023)
notes: Several internal inconsistencies: years 2004-2019 vs 2004-2020; 'eight dimensions' vs four; the narrative says 'an increase in internet users by one person decreases financial inclusion' while the variable is % of population; the second-step or one-step choice, collapse of instruments and the instrument list are not stated; the text states Fisher statistics but no country list. Table 1 'Internet net effects' and thresholds are shown only for voice and accountability, government effectiveness and rule of law. No instruction-like text found.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own system-GMM estimation on 42 sub-Saharan African countries; exposure is internet users (% of population); outcome is a supply-side financial inclusion index (bank branches and ATMs per km2 and per 100,000 adults). Meets the 10-economy rule. Borderline on outcome: branch/ATM density is a financial-access measure and fits 'living standards beyond income' only loosely; accepted as family 5 on the record's classification.

sample_corrections.economies_or_groups: Country list IS given: Table A1 in the Appendix lists the 42 countries (Angola ... Zimbabwe). Record said the list is not given.
sample_corrections.years: Text conflicts: Sec 3.3 says 2004-2019; abstract and conclusion say 2004-2020. Table A3 reports 714 observations for governance and control variables, which equals 42 x 17 (2004-2020), not 42 x 16 = 672.
sample_corrections.observations: Estimation sample 426-435 observations (Tables 1-2); Table A3 non-missing counts: IFI 558, internet 686, education 671, capital 676 of 714.

corrections.correction: Table 1 internet coefficients are -0.0003 (political stability), -0.0003 (voice), 4.17e-06 (regulatory quality, p=0.979), -0.0003 (government effectiveness, p=0.021), -0.0002 (rule of law, p=0.007), -0.0005 (corruption control). Range of significant coefficients is -0.0002 to -0.0005, not -0.0003 to -0.0005. Table 2: -0.0002 (political governance, p=0.860), -0.001 (economic, institutional, general). All p-values in the record are otherwise correct.

second_pass.problems: Record errors: (1) says country list not in text, but Table A1 lists all 42; (2) Table 1 internet coefficient range misstated (rule of law is -0.0002); (3) '672 possible' observations should be 714 (Table A3), consistent with 2004-2020; (4) '2.5 at the edge of the WGI range' is wrong because economic governance is a PCA composite; (5) Sargan p near 1 described as overfitting while Hansen p-values (0.37-0.75) are in the acceptable range. Direct effect coefficients are conditional on governance equal to zero, and mean governance is negative (about -0.65 to -0.76), which the paper's 1 person/'increase in internet users' wording obscures. No invented numbers found in the results.

title: The association between mobile phones and the risk of brain cancer mortality: a 25-year cross-country analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study with own estimation of mobile subscriptions (per 100 people) on brain cancer mortality in 88 countries, 1990-2015. Outcome is health (family 5, living standards beyond income); sample exceeds 10 economies. Included for the health payoff, not for output.
exposure_measure: Mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people (World Bank), lagged 5 to 25 years, or averaged in 5-year lag bins (0-4, 5-9, ..., 20-24 years).

sample.economies_or_groups: 88 countries with WHO cause-specific mortality data; the full country list is in an appendix table not in the text. OECD and non-OECD split reported only in Appendix Table 3.
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (income groups not reported in the main text; OECD and non-OECD only)
sample.years: 1990-2015 (mortality); mobile subscriptions lagged back to the 1960s-1990s

design.estimator: Two-way fixed effects (difference-in-differences style) regression of log cause-specific mortality rate on lagged mobile subscriptions; population-weighted; SEs clustered by country. Differential-effects models stack brain cancer with other causes and add cause-by-country and cause-by-year FE.
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country and year FE, country-specific linear time trends; controls for smoking, alcohol, CO2, health spending, real GDP per capita, internet use, education spending, population shares (female, 15-65, over 65). Falsification outcomes (other cancers, ischemic heart disease) and differential-effects model used as checks.

results.indicator: Brain cancer mortality rate (log, per 100,000), mobile subscriptions lagged 15 years
results.estimate: 0.003 (semi-elasticity; 0.3% per extra subscription per 100 people); marginal effect [0.012] deaths per 100,000

results.estimate: Mostly small and insignificant at 15 and 20 years (e.g. rectal 15y -0.002*, lung 15y 0.001, heart disease 20y 0.002); positive significant at 10-year lag for pancreatic 0.001**, stomach 0.001**, lung 0.002**

results.estimate: Brain cancer x cell use lagged 15-19 years: 0.006* (main); 0.150* (no country weights); 0.002 (not logging); 0.007** (excluding country trends); 0.148* (no log, unweighted, no trends)

results.indicator: Differential effect, brain cancer relative to other causes, lag 20-24 years
results.evidence: Table 4, row 'Brain cancer x Cell use lagged 20-24 years', p. 266

results.evidence: Table 4, column 'Brain Cancer Only', p. 266

results.estimate: not reported in main text (Appendix Table A4 not in the text)

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Health outcome only (brain cancer mortality); no GDP, growth or productivity outcome is estimated (real GDP per capita is a control). Authors explicitly disclaim causality, but the abstract and discussion use suggestive language ('risk of brain cancer', practical advice on speaker phone use). Table 2 header says elasticities in 'braces' but values are in square brackets; they are marginal effects (coefficient times mean mortality). Introduction describes coefficients 0.003 and 0.02 as 'additional brain cancer deaths per 100,000', which conflicts with the Results text that identifies them as semi-elasticities (marginal effects 0.012 and 0.073 deaths per 100,000). In Table 4 column 'Main', the non-interaction coefficient on 15-19 years lag is negative (-0.004***) while the interaction is +0.006*, so the net differential effect for brain cancer is about +0.002; the text does not discuss this. sample_corrections.years: Mortality 1990-2015 (N = 1,766 country-years). Mobile subscription lags of 5-25 years in Eq. 1, plus a 0-4 year bin in Eq. 2, so subscriptions run from about 1965 to 2015, not '1960s-1990s'.

second_pass.problems: No invented numbers. Minor: sample years description of lags is imprecise (see corrections). The record rationale for the specification rating (lag length chosen post hoc) is not in the text. The paper's own Introduction (p. 258) states 0.003 and 0.02 'additional brain cancer deaths per 100,000', which conflicts with Table 2 (semi-elasticities 0.003 and 0.020; marginal effects 0.012 and 0.073); the record correctly uses the table. Table 2 and 3 notes say 'elasticities in braces' but values are printed in brackets.

title: ICT Infrastructure, Economic Growth and ASEAN Income Heterogeneity: A Panel Analysis
decision_rationale: Own panel estimation (FGLS and PCSE) of ICT infrastructure indicators (fixed and mobile broadband, mobile subscriptions, internet users, internet retail) on GDP per capita for 10 ASEAN economies, split into lower-middle, upper-middle and high income groups; family 1 outcome and an explicit income-group comparison, so E1 to E4 do not apply.
exposure_measure: World Bank indicators entered in logs (lnFBPH fixed broadband penetration per household, lnMBP mobile broadband penetration per population, lnMCSMI mobile cellular subscriptions per 100 people, lnFTSFLI fixed telephone subscriptions per 100 people) and apparently in levels (IRPTR internet retail % of retail, IUI individuals using the internet %), plus two price variables (lnRFLC residential fixed-line connection fee, lnMCPOC mobile prepaid connection fee, both adjusted for GDP per capita). Descriptive statistics show FBPH (mean 2,387,831) and MBP (mean 67,293,895) as very large numbers, not rates.

sample.economies_or_groups: ASEAN-10. High income: Brunei, Singapore. Upper-middle: Malaysia, Thailand. Lower-middle: Indonesia, Philippines, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Myanmar (World Bank 2024 classification as stated by the authors).
sample.income_groups_covered: high, upper-middle, lower-middle (no low-income economy)
sample.years: 1995-2020 (stated); text also says '1000 observations over 10 years'

design.estimator: Static panel FGLS and PCSE (Beck-Katz) with AR(1) correction, four nested models per sample, estimated separately for lower-middle, upper-middle, high-income and all 10 ASEAN countries
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Controls: TRADE, FDI, INFL, EXPT. Equation (1) lists country and time fixed effects but the regression tables report none and the PCSE/FGLS estimators do not obviously include them. No education, institutions or capital controls (authors concede this in Limitations).

results.estimate: 0.060 (log-log, ln GDP per capita on lnFBPH)
results.evidence: Table 11 (p.17), PCSE Model 4, row lnFBPH: '0.063 0.016 0.060 0.009' (Models 3 and 4)

results.estimate: -0.138 (log-log)

results.estimate: 0.090 (PCSE Model 4); FGLS 0.317

results.estimate: lnFBPH 0.0332; lnMBP -0.0645

results.estimate: lnMCSMI 0.1102; IUI 0.0060
results.evidence: Table 8 (p.14), PCSE Model 4 rows lnMCSMI '0.1102 0.0000' and IUI '0.0060 0.0000'

results.estimate: 0.923 (all ASEAN, PCSE Model 4); 0.5181 (lower-middle); 1.0492 (upper-middle); 0.3042 (high, p = 0.690)
results.evidence: Tables 8-11, row lnRFLC, Model 4 PCSE. Table 2 and Section 2.6.2 define RFLC as 'residential fixed line connection fee adjusted for GDP per capita', but Section 4.1 and Conclusion call it 'remittances'

heterogeneity.finding: Mobile broadband (lnMBP) coefficient is negative in lower-middle (-0.0645) and upper-middle (-0.1174) groups but positive in the high-income group (0.1895, 2 economies). Fixed broadband (lnFBPH) is positive in lower- and upper-middle groups and insignificant in the high-income group. Signs differ across groups, with no formal interaction test.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 8-10 (pp.14-16), PCSE Model 4 rows lnMBP; Section 4.1 high-income paragraph: 'MBP shows strong positive effects in Models 3-4'

heterogeneity.finding: Internet users (IUI) positive in lower-middle (0.0060), negative in upper-middle (-0.0017) and negative/borderline in high income (-0.0009, p = 0.054). Authors interpret as diminishing returns or saturation, but this is not tested with a threshold or nonlinear term.
heterogeneity.evidence: Tables 8-10, PCSE Model 4 row IUI; Section 6.1.1 claims 'non-linear effect' but no squared or threshold term appears in any table

income_group_results.high: Brunei and Singapore only (2 economies). PCSE Model 4: lnMBP +0.1895 (p=0.000), lnFBPH -0.0266 (p=0.333), lnFTSFLI -0.1212 (p=0.004), lnMCSMI -0.18344 (p=0.000), IUI -0.0009 (p=0.054). Table 10, p.16.
income_group_results.upper_middle: Malaysia and Thailand only (2 economies). PCSE Model 4: lnFBPH +0.0036 (p=0.012), lnMBP -0.1174 (p=0.000), lnMCSMI +0.1061 (p=0.000), IUI -0.0017 (p=0.000). Table 9, p.15.
income_group_results.lower_middle: Six economies. PCSE Model 4: lnFBPH +0.0332 (p=0.0050), lnMBP -0.0645 (p=0.0000), lnMCSMI +0.1102 (p=0.0000), IUI +0.0060 (p=0.0000). Table 8, p.14.
income_group_results.low: not covered (no low-income economy in the ASEAN-10 sample)

n_specifications_reported: 32 (4 nested models x 2 estimators x 4 samples), all printed

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Static PCSE/FGLS regressions of GDP per capita on ICT indicators, with causal wording ('impact', 'affects'), no instrument, no lags and no strategy for reverse causation. The authors concede they cannot capture endogeneity and read results as 'short-run associations'. No controls for education, institutions or capital. A price variable deflated by GDP per capita (RFLC, MCPOC) sits on the right-hand side of a GDP per capita equation, which builds in a mechanical link (coefficient near 1 on lnRFLC in Tables 9 and 11).
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 6.2 Limitations (p.18-19); Section 2.6.2; Tables 9 and 11 row lnRFLC

exposure_measurement.why: Several labels do not match the data or text. Descriptive statistics show FBPH and MBP as counts in the millions despite being called 'per household' and 'per population'. RFLC (a connection fee) is called 'remittances' in the results and conclusion, and FTSFLI (fixed telephone subscriptions) is called 'fintech'. IRPTR and IUI are logged in diagnostic tables (Inirptr, Iniui) but appear unlogged in regression tables. The tables therefore do not give a clean read of broadband or mobile adoption.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 7 (p.13) means for FBPH and MBP; Table 2; Section 4.1 and Section 6 Conclusion; Tables 3a vs 8

selection_of_countries_years.why: Only 10 ASEAN economies. The high- and upper-middle-income subsamples have 2 economies each, so subgroup coefficients rest on 2 countries. No low-income economy. Observation counts are inconsistent: text says '1000 observations over 10 years' while the panel is 10 countries over 1995-2020 and Table 7 sums imply about 144 country-years (my inference from the Sum and Mean rows). No N is printed in the regression tables.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Section 3 and 4.1 (pp.4, 7); Table 7 (p.13); Section 4.1 country list

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per capita from World Bank, used in logs. The text repeatedly describes the outcome as GDP 'growth' although it is a log level, and Equation (1) uses GDP. The mislabelling is a clarity problem more than a measurement failure.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Tables 3a and 8-11 (lnGDP / lnGDPcapita); Section 6.1.1 'accelerate economic growth'

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Variables are I(1) (level tests fail, first differences stationary) and the Westerlund test finds no cointegration, yet levels are regressed on levels, which risks spurious regression (R-squared 0.98 to 1.000). Four nested models, two estimators and four samples are run without a preferred specification. Coefficient signs change when variables are added (e.g. lnMCSMI, lnMBP). Equation (1) shows fixed effects that the reported tables do not include, and Equation (1) indices are mis-specified.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.2.2 (p.6) 'static estimators such as FGLS and PCSE are generally appropriate'; Tables 3a-6a cointegration columns; Tables 8-11 R square rows

selective_reporting.why: All models and both estimators are printed, which limits selection. The narrative, however, selects and reinterprets: one ASEAN-level sentence reports 'FBPH ... b = 0.046, p = 0.001', which matches no entry in Table 11 (0.060, p=0.009). Text says FTSFLI is significant in the full sample while Table 11 shows it is not. Significance stars are described in the notes but not printed.

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: No text addressed to a reader or model was found. Internal inconsistencies a reviewer should know: (1) RFLC defined as a connection fee but described as remittances; FTSFLI called fintech; (2) FBPH and MBP in Table 7 are large counts, not rates; (3) number of observations stated as 1000 over 10 years but Table 7 implies about 144 and no N appears in regression tables; (4) high-income correlation and diagnostic tables are cited as 'Table 10' and 'Table 11' in Section 3.2.1 although those are regression tables; (5) text claims of non-linear effects and 'optimal level of digital integration' are not backed by any quadratic or threshold specification; (6) Table 8 note says 'low- and middle-income countries' while the group is lower-middle income; (7) the Ethics and Consent statements refer to human participants and informed consent although only World Bank secondary data are used; (8) Indonesia is placed in the lower-middle group by the authors, while the World Bank 2024 list can differ, so the group assignment is unclear. Regression tables print p-values only, no standard errors; stars are not shown. Dependent variable is log GDP per capita (level), so coefficients on logged ICT variables read as elasticities, but several ICT variables may be in levels.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel estimation (PCSE/FGLS); exposure is ICT/broadband/mobile/internet; 10 ASEAN economies plus explicit income-group comparison; outcome is GDP per capita (output family 1). Eligible.

sample_corrections.years: 1995-2020 confirmed ('annual observations from 1995 to 2020'); the '1000 observations over 10 years' statement is internally inconsistent with 10 economies x 26 years (max 260) and should not be used as N
sample_corrections.n_economies: 10 confirmed; subgroups 6 / 2 / 2 confirmed (Section 4.1 country list)

corrections.correction: Numbers correct, but direction 'mixed' is wrong: both PCSE (0.090, p=0.052) and FGLS (0.317, p=0.000) are positive; PCSE is only borderline significant. Direction should be positive.

second_pass.problems: Only one error: result 4 direction labelled mixed though both estimators are positive. Record's 'Table 7 sums imply about 144 country-years' is the extractor's own inference and not checked. Source mislabels (RFLC as remittances, FTSFLI as fintech) are real, as the record says.

title: Internet and Economic Growth Across Income Levels: a Panel Data Analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel study of 78 economies (LMI, UMI, high income) estimating the effect of internet use and fixed broadband on GDP per capita growth (family 1), with explicit income-group comparison. Meets all inclusion criteria.
exposure_measure: Main: log of individuals using the Internet (% of population, WDI). Robustness: log of fixed-broadband subscribers (FbrdP, WDI; unit not stated in Table 2).

sample.economies_or_groups: 22 lower-middle-income, 30 upper-middle-income, 26 high-income; low-income countries excluded for data gaps
sample.income_groups_covered: high, upper-middle, lower-middle (low excluded)

design.estimator: Pooled OLS, fixed effects (preferred after Hausman test) and random effects, run by income group and full sample; country-clustered SEs
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Country FE; lagged dlnGDP per capita; ln gross capital formation, d ln wage/salaried workers, d ln broad money, d ln trade, ln youth employment ratio, d ln secondary enrolment; dummies for 2009 and pandemic year (equation also lists time effects but only dum09 and dum19 are reported)

results.evidence: Table 3, p. 8625, lnIntUsage row, Models 10-12: '-0.006*** -0.012** -0.006***'; N=780, 78 countries

results.uncertainty: FE se (0.009), not significant; pooled/RE se (0.005), p<0.1

results.uncertainty: FE se: full (0.002), LMI (0.004), UMI (0.003), HIC (0.003); only full sample (p<0.05) and HIC (p<0.1) significant

heterogeneity.finding: Sign pattern shifts from positive and insignificant (LMI FE) to negative and insignificant (UMI FE) to negative and significant (HIC FE, p<0.1; pooled/RE p<0.01). Authors interpret as absorptive-capacity gaps in LMI and saturation in HIC. No formal test of coefficient equality across groups and no interaction term.

income_group_results.upper_middle: Negative but insignificant: FE -0.012 (se 0.009) (Table 3, Model 5). Broadband FE -0.003 (se 0.003).
income_group_results.lower_middle: Positive but insignificant in FE: 0.006 (se 0.009) (Table 3, Model 2); pooled/RE 0.008* (p<0.1). Broadband FE -0.003 (se 0.004).
income_group_results.low: Not covered (excluded for fewer than ten countries with substantial data gaps, p. 8619).

n_specifications_reported: 24 (3 estimators x 4 samples x 2 ICT measures)

confounding_reverse_causality.why: Mostly associational wording, but policy conclusions are causal-sounding. Only FE, a lagged dependent variable and controls; no instrument or timing design. FE with a lagged dependent variable and short T (about 4.5 obs per country in LMI) risks Nickell-type bias. Authors concede reverse causality remains.
confounding_reverse_causality.evidence: Methodology p. 8623 ('mitigate the risk by incorporating a lagged dependent variable'); Limitations p. 8632 ('reverse causality ... remains a limitation')

exposure_measurement.why: Share of population using the internet is a standard but coarse diffusion proxy; broadband used as a second proxy. Levels of usage near saturation in high-income countries leave little variation, which authors themselves cite as the explanation.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Low-income countries dropped; sample cut from 985 to 959 to 780 observations after differencing, unit-root and lag requirements, so panel is unbalanced and thin (LMI: 99 obs for 22 countries). Selection rests on data availability; reduction to 780 is only loosely explained.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Sample section pp. 8618-8619; Table 3 observation counts p. 8626

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per capita in constant 2015 US$ from WDI, a standard growth measure.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Variable mix of logs, first differences and levels in the same regression; winsorising at 1/99 percent; only two year dummies reported although the equation includes time effects; choice of FE over RE via Hausman test (statistic not shown). Pooled, FE and RE are all reported, so no hiding of alternatives.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Equation p. 8623; Sample p. 8618; Table 3 notes p. 8626

selective_reporting.why: Abstract and text describe a negative association for UMI countries although UMI coefficients are insignificant in all models; text also says LMI is 'potentially favourable' while some LMI pooled/RE estimates are significant at 10 percent. Hausman statistics, unit-root results and appendix tests are not shown in the main text. All pre-stated models are reported though.
selective_reporting.evidence: Abstract p. 8613 ('negative association emerges in upper-middle-income'); Results pp. 8623-8628

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: No instructions directed at the reader were found in the text. Internal inconsistencies: Table 3 and 4 label the dependent variable 'lnPCGDP' although the model is the first difference of ln GDP per capita; abstract/conclusion claim negative UMI effect while UMI estimates are insignificant, and the results text says LMI effects 'favour EG' then 'not significant'; observation counts of 985, 959 and 780 appear in the sample section. Coefficients are small semi-elasticity-type values: change in log-difference of GDP per capita per one-unit change in log internet use. Appendix tables A1-A6 (country lists, descriptive statistics, VIF) are not in the supplied text. AI is mentioned only in the introduction and future work; the study is non-AI.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel estimation (pooled OLS, FE, RE) of internet users and fixed-broadband subscribers on GDP per capita growth (output outcome) for 78 economies with explicit LMI/UMI/HIC comparison; non-AI so the 10-economy threshold is met.
second_pass.problems: No invented or mixed-up content found; all extracted coefficients, standard errors, N and country counts match the text. Minor omissions: Table 4 pooled/RE broadband estimates (HIC and full sample significant at 5 percent) are not listed in result 5. The record's description of the lagged variable as 'lagged dlnGDP per capita' matches the tables (L.dlnPCGDP), but the printed equation uses ln(GDP t-1).

title: ICT Diffusion, Industrialisation and Economic Growth Nexus: an International Cross-country Analysis
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel VAR-GMM study of ICT diffusion (mobile, fixed telephone, internet) for 171 countries split into four World Bank income groups, with real GDP (family 1) and manufacturing value-added share (family 2) as outcomes. Meets exposure, sample and outcome criteria.
exposure_measure: ICT diffusion index: first principal component of mobile-cellular subscriptions per 100, fixed-telephone subscriptions per 100 and % of individuals using the internet (ITU data); missing values filled by linear trend extrapolation and moving-average interpolation (Table 1, p. 2043).

sample.economies_or_groups: 25 low, 41 lower-middle, 48 upper-middle, 57 high-income countries (Table 2, pp. 2044-2045)
sample.income_groups_covered: high, upper-middle, lower-middle, low

design.estimator: Panel VAR in GMM (Abrigo and Love 2016), forward orthogonal deviations; plus Johansen-Fisher and Westerlund cointegration, panel VAR Granger causality, FEVD and IRFs
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Three-variable system (ICT, MAV, RGDP), country-specific effects removed by Helmert transformation; no other controls; lag order not reported ('available upon request').

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Lagged PVAR in GMM is the only response to endogeneity, no external instrument, no control variables (investment, human capital, trade). Authors use causal language ('impact') and report bidirectional Granger causality.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Table 11 p. 2057; Table 5-9 legends; p. 2047 'optimum lag length results are not reported'

selective_reporting.why: Only one model per sample; no robustness checks with alternative ICT measures or lag choices; Table 11 and text and IRF descriptions disagree on signs; abstract reports global effects while subgroup signs are mixed.

venue_quality_concern: possible (Received 14 March 2021, accepted 2 April 2021; Declarations name 'Economic Change and Restructuring' as the target journal although published in Journal of the Knowledge Economy; many internal inconsistencies in tables)
notes: No instructions aimed at the extractor were found in the text. Table 11 layout is ambiguous: columns are labelled lagged variables, rows dependent variables, but the authors' text reads the rows as the causing variable and the columns as the outcome (e.g. row ICT(t), column MAV(t-1) = -34.3608 is read as the effect of ICT on MAV; row RGDP(t), column ICT(t-1) = 0.0389 is read as growth raising ICT). I followed the authors' reading. Under the literal reading the ICT-to-RGDP coefficients would be 0.0389, 0.2751, 0.0215, 0.0149 and 0.0175 (all positive, significant). Table 10 shows RGDP does not Granger-cause ICT in the full sample (p=0.798) while Table 11 gives a significant coefficient. Stars in Tables 5-9 legends are inverted (*** said to be 10%). Table 8 header says 'telecommunication infrastructures'. Text claims in Fig. 3 discussion on signs conflict with Table 11. Descriptive RGDP values in Table 4 (max 100) do not look like GDP in billions. Also reports panel unit root, cointegration (Johansen-Fisher, Westerlund) and causality results, not coded as payoff estimates. Industrialisation (MAV) coded as family 2 (structural change).

title: Information and Communication Technology (ICT), Growth and Development in Developing Regions: Evidence from a Comparative Analysis and a New Approach
decision_rationale: Quantitative panel VAR-GMM study with its own estimation, ICT diffusion (mobile, fixed telephone, internet index) as exposure, 73 economies across three regions (SSA, MENA, LAAC), and outcomes real GDP (family 1) and the Human Development Index (family 5).
technology: ICT in general (PCA index of mobile-cellular, fixed-telephone and internet use)
exposure_measure: ICT diffusion index: first principal component of mobile-cellular subscriptions per 100, fixed-telephone subscriptions per 100 and % of individuals using the Internet (ITU data); component 1 eigenvalue 2.319, 77.3% of variance (Table 3).

sample.economies_or_groups: Sub-Saharan Africa (40), MENA (14), Latin America and the Caribbean (19); described by authors as developing regions
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (regional groups, not income groups; sample includes some high-income economies such as Israel, Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Chile, Uruguay, Seychelles, Trinidad and Tobago, although no income classification is reported)

design.estimator: Panel VAR in GMM (Abrigo and Love 2016 Stata routine), forward orthogonal deviations; also Granger causality Wald tests, FEVD, IRFs; panel unit root and cointegration tests (Johansen-Fisher, Westerlund)
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Three-variable system only (ICT index, log real GDP, log HDI); country-specific effects removed by Helmert transformation; no other controls; lag order not reported (said to be available on request).

results.indicator: Real GDP (constant 2010 US$; proxy for growth) response to lagged ICT index, entire sample
results.estimate: -0.437 (Table 11, RGDP(t) row, ICT(t-1) column)
results.evidence: Table 11, p.14728, Entire sample row RGDP(t): '-0.437 (0.000)***'. Text p.14727 reads the 0.01% effect as positive; policy section p.14738 notes 'negative impact of ICT on economic growth at the panel level'.

results.indicator: Real GDP response to lagged ICT index, SSA
results.evidence: Table 11, p.14728, SSA RGDP(t) row: '-0.548 (0.044)**'. Table 10 gives p = 0.000 for the same ICT-to-RGDP Granger test.

results.indicator: Real GDP response to lagged ICT index, MENA
results.evidence: Table 11, p.14728, MENA RGDP(t) row: '0.435 (0.000)**'. Text says impact of ICT on growth is 'more pronounced' in MENA (p.14728).

results.indicator: Real GDP response to lagged ICT index, LAAC
Authors' headline reading of ICT effect on growth, entire sample (text)
results.estimate: 0.01% increase in growth per 1% increase in ICT (text only)
results.uncertainty: 'at a 1% significance level' (text); no coefficient in Table 11 matches
results.evidence: p.14727: 'if ICT diffusion increases by 1%, economic growth will increase by 0.01%'. Contradicts Table 11 sign for ICT(t-1) in RGDP equation.

results.indicator: Human Development Index response to lagged ICT index, entire sample
results.evidence: Table 11, p.14728, Entire sample HDI(t) row: '0.697 (0.010)**'. Text p.14728 reports 0.01% rise per 1% ICT, which does not match.

results.indicator: HDI response to lagged ICT index, SSA
results.evidence: Table 11, p.14728, SSA HDI(t) row: '0.972 (0.036)**'. Table 10 gives p = 0.001 for ICT to HDI.

results.indicator: HDI response to lagged ICT index, MENA
results.evidence: Table 11, p.14728, MENA HDI(t) row: '-3.259 (0.000)**'. Abstract says ICT is a positive predictor of development in all regions, so table and abstract conflict.

results.indicator: HDI response to lagged ICT index, LAAC

heterogeneity.finding: Region differences only (no income-group split): ICT-to-growth coefficient is positive in MENA and negative in the entire sample, SSA and LAAC per Table 11; the authors state the effect on growth is larger in MENA and the effect on development larger in SSA.
heterogeneity.evidence: p.14728: 'impact of ICT diffusion is more pronounced on growth in the MENA region'; 'For SSA, the impact of ICT diffusion is more pronounced on development'.

n_specifications_reported: 4 PVAR systems (entire sample, SSA, MENA, LAAC), each with 3 equations; one lag structure; no robustness variants of the PVAR

confounding_reverse_causation.why: All three variables treated as endogenous with internal GMM lag instruments, which addresses simultaneity only partly; no controls (investment, human capital, trade, institutions); series are I(1) and results are interpreted causally ('causal-effect relationship'); lag order and instrument validity tests not reported.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Methodology p.14712-14713; p.14703 'causal-effect relationship'; p.14721 lag length 'not reported to save space'

exposure_measurement.why: PCA index mixes fixed-telephone, mobile and internet penetration, so the index units are arbitrary (mean about 0, SD 1.5) and the coefficient has no natural unit; interpolation and extrapolation used for missing data.
exposure_measurement.evidence: Table 3 p.14717; Table 1 footnote p.14715-14716; Table 4 p.14718

selection_of_countries_years.why: 73 countries in three regions chosen by region, 2000-2018, with interpolated data; labelled developing but includes some high-income economies; no income-group comparison.

outcome_measurement.why: Real GDP (apparently in logs, Table 4 means about 23.9, while Table 1 says billion dollars) is called a proxy for 'economic growth' although it is a level; HDI (log, negative values) is a slowly moving composite and used as 'development'; the variable transformation is not stated.

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Lag order not reported; unit root results are inconsistent across tests (e.g. LLC results with implausible statistics); PVAR on I(1) series with cointegration found but no error-correction treatment; coefficient interpretation in text is inconsistent with the table.

selective_reporting.why: Abstract and conclusion state ICT is a significant positive predictor of growth and development in all regions, but Table 11 gives negative ICT coefficients for growth (entire, SSA, LAAC) and for HDI in MENA; the text reads -0.437 as a growth-to-ICT effect and p-values and stars in Tables 10 and 11 do not match (e.g. SSA 0.044 vs 0.000; MENA '0.590***').

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: Table 11 is laid out with equation variable in rows and lagged regressors in columns; I read coefficients under the ICT(t-1) column as the effect of lagged ICT on that row's variable, which matches the p-values in Table 10 (e.g. ICT to HDI entire sample p = 0.010; RGDP to ICT p = 0.088 appears at 0.018 in the ICT(t) row). The authors' text instead describes -0.437 as the effect of growth on ICT and states a positive 0.01% ICT-to-growth effect that is not in the table; the policy section (p.14738) separately says the ICT effect on growth is negative at the panel level. Reported effects are coefficients of a VAR with an ICT index and log levels, no marginal-effect units. No regression observation counts are printed (Table 4 lists 1387, 760, 266, 361 descriptive observations). Heavy self-citation of the authors' own work. No instructions directed at the reader were found in the text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own PVAR-GMM estimation; ICT (mobile, fixed, internet PCA index); 73 economies (>=10); outcomes real GDP (output) and HDI (living standards beyond income). Eligible.
second_pass.problems: Extractor's table reading is right: Table 11 signs are negative for ICT(t-1) in the RGDP equation (entire -0.437, SSA -0.548, LAAC -0.406) and positive only for MENA (0.435). Abstract, p.14727 text ('growth will increase by 0.01%') and conclusion ('positive and significant impact on growth') contradict the table; the authors also misread -0.437/-0.548/-0.406 as growth-to-ICT effects (p.14728), while their own policy section says 'negative impact of ICT on economic growth at the panel level' (p.14737) and 'significant negative impact of technology (ICT)' (p.14738). Notes field correctly says no regression n printed; Table 4 Obs are 1387/760/266/361. No invented content found.

title: The impact of ICT on economic growth-Comparing rich and poor countries
decision_rationale: Quantitative IV-GMM panel of 123 economies (45 high, 58 middle, 20 low income) with an explicit income-group comparison; exposure is mobile, internet and fixed broadband (plus a PCA ICT index); outcomes are GDP per capita and labour productivity (family 1).
technology: ICT (PCA index of mobile, internet, fixed broadband)
exposure_measure: Logs of mobile subscriptions per 100 people, internet users (% of population), fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 people (WDI 2019), and a first-principal-component ICT index built from the three logged series, estimated separately for each income group (Table 2, Section 3.3).

sample.economies_or_groups: 45 high-income, 58 middle-income, 20 low-income economies (Table A1)
sample.income_groups_covered: high, middle (upper and lower middle pooled), low

design.estimator: IV-GMM (robust), estimated separately for HIC, MIC and LIC; Hansen over-identification test; Pedroni cointegration and LLC/IPS unit-root tests reported
design.key_controls_fixed_effects: Controls are log investment (gross fixed capital formation) and log labour force; instruments are the first and second lags of investment (lags of ICT were first tried but Hansen test rejected in some cases); no country or year fixed effects mentioned (p. 5, Eq. 6).

results.indicator: Log GDP per capita (constant 2010 US$), elasticity w.r.t. log ICT index, HIC
Log GDP per capita, elasticity w.r.t. log ICT index, MIC
Log GDP per capita, elasticity w.r.t. log ICT index, LIC
Log GDP per capita, individual indicators (mobile, internet, fixed broadband) by group
Log labour productivity (output per worker, Conference Board), elasticity w.r.t. log ICT index (HIC / MIC / LIC)

heterogeneity.finding: ICT-index elasticity for GDP per capita is largest in MIC (0.422), then LIC (0.158), then HIC (0.094); authors conclude poor countries gain more. For internet and fixed broadband the HIC coefficients are the largest, and for mobile MIC is largest. No formal test of coefficient differences is reported.
heterogeneity.evidence: Section 4, p. 8: 'MIC gains more than LIC and HIC from the ICT revolution'; Table 8, p. 9

income_group_results.high: ICT index elasticity 0.094*** (SE 0.032) for GDP per capita; 0.065*** for labour productivity
income_group_results.upper_middle: not reported separately (pooled in MIC: 0.422*** GDP per capita; 0.374*** labour productivity)
income_group_results.low: ICT index elasticity 0.158*** (SE 0.028) for GDP per capita; 0.218*** for labour productivity

n_specifications_reported: 24 (12 per outcome: 4 ICT measures x 3 income groups) in Tables 8 and 9; further specifications with ICT-lag instruments are in supplementary material, not seen

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Causal language ('ICT increases economic growth'). Instruments are lags of investment, which is also an included control, and have no stated link to ICT beyond persistence; ICT-lag instruments were abandoned after Hansen rejections. Only two controls (investment, labour); no human capital or institutions; no stated fixed effects. Hansen p-values of 0.062 and 0.077 in some models are marginal.
confounding_reverse_causation.evidence: Section 3.2, p. 5; Table 8 Hansen rows, p. 9

exposure_measurement.why: PCA index of three logged indicators with group-specific weights, so index scales are not comparable across income groups; cross-group comparison of elasticities is therefore fragile. Index elasticity in HIC (0.094) is far below each component's (0.26-0.75), which is unexplained.

selection_of_countries_years.why: 123 economies over 2002-2017 from WDI, broad coverage, but panel is unbalanced (observations in Table 8 are below 45 x 16 = 720 for HIC and as low as 224 for LIC); MIC pooled upper and lower middle; the stated income thresholds are applied to a fixed list with no explanation of year of classification.
selection_of_countries_years.evidence: Table 3, p. 6; Table 8 observations row, p. 9; Table A1 footnote, p. 14

outcome_measurement.why: GDP per capita level (constant 2010 US$, in logs) is labelled 'economic growth'; this is a level, not a growth rate. Labour productivity is from the Conference Board and has fewer observations.
outcome_measurement.evidence: Table 2, p. 6; Section 4.1 and footnote 4, p. 11

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Instrument set was changed after over-identification tests rejected in some models; unit-root results say variables are stationary though several IPS(0) statistics are not significant; one specification per measure and group; no sensitivity to controls, lags or estimators.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Section 3.2, p. 5; Table 6, p. 12; Section 3.4, p. 6

selective_reporting.why: Only ICT coefficients shown ('For brevity'); first-stage and ICT-lag results relegated to supplementary material; conclusion that poor countries gain more rests on the index and mobile while internet and fixed broadband coefficients are largest in HIC; no test of group differences.
selective_reporting.evidence: Section 4, p. 6 and p. 8; Table 8, p. 9

venue_quality_concern: none
notes: No instruction-like text aimed at the reader was found. Oddities for a reviewer: (1) the authors read elasticities as percent changes ('increases HIC economic growth by 0.26%'); (2) Table 3 reports lnk with a max of 25.177 for HIC, implausible for a log of investment % of GDP; (3) the Section 4.1 text says 'MIC economic growth' where labour productivity is meant; (4) Table 8 observation counts (e.g. 630 for 45 HIC) imply about 14 years per country, not 16; (5) Section 3.4 states variables are stationary although IPS(0) is not significant for several series; (6) Table A1 leaves Guinea-Bissau's code blank and the list is classified under a single set of income thresholds; (7) 'poor countries gain more' is not supported for internet and fixed broadband. Supplementary material with ICT-lag instruments was not available in the text.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own IV-GMM estimation on 123 economies (45 HIC, 58 MIC, 20 LIC) with explicit income-group comparison; exposure is mobile, internet, fixed broadband and a PCA ICT index; outcomes are GDP per capita and labour productivity (family 1).

title: Mobile Phones and Local Economic Development: A Global Evidence
decision_rationale: Own quantitative estimation of mobile network (2G/3G/4G) coverage on district-level economic activity in about 120 countries; the outcome (nightlights) is treated as an output proxy under family 1, per the assignment instruction.
exposure_measure: Share of district population living in areas covered by 2G, 3G/4G or any mobile network (0-1), from GSMA/Collins Bartholomew coverage maps combined with 1km population grids

sample.n_economies: 120 (abstract/intro); 106 in main IV regressions with controls (119 in Table 1 col 1; 86 for 3G/4G)
sample.economies_or_groups: Global, over 34,000 second-level administrative districts; developing vs developed split at baseline World Bank income class
sample.income_groups_covered: mixed (high, upper-middle, lower-middle, low; grouped as developed = HIC+UMIC, developing = LIC+LMIC)

design.key_controls_fixed_effects: District and year FE; temperature, precipitation, trends x distance to coast/lat/long; Polity IV, baseline income class, resource dependence, no-universal-electricity dummy x trends; regional spatially weighted GDP growth and trade; SE clustered by district

n_specifications_reported: about 40 (6 columns each in Tables 1-6, plus A2, A4)

confounding_reverse_causation.why: Author concedes TWFE/C&D are not causal (pre-trends, endogenous rollout). IV uses regional leave-one-out coverage; exclusion restriction plausible but contestable (common regional shocks, regional policy and trade/GDP controls only). Second instrument gives smaller estimates (0.0464 vs 0.0777).

exposure_measurement.why: Coverage share from operator-submitted maps, not usage or subscriptions; 2005 and 2010 coverage interpolated; coverage shows population-weighted area access, not adoption.

selection_of_countries_years.why: Near-global district panel (106-120 countries); sample varies by specification (86 countries for 3G/4G). Leave-one-country-out check reported in appendix figure.

outcome_measurement.why: Nightlights are a proxy for economic activity; GDP-growth interpretation relies on an external 0.3 elasticity from Henderson et al. 2012; DMSP/VIIRS harmonised series; lights may reflect electrification, not output (partly controlled by electricity-access trend).

specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.why: Several instruments, controls, and technology splits; preferred spec stated (cols 2,4,6). Estimates sensitive: 3G/4G col 5 insignificant, 2G TWFE and IV differ; Table A4 2G/3G estimates much larger than main.
specification_and_researcher_degrees_of_.evidence: Tables 3, A4

selective_reporting.why: Reports null/insignificant and pre-trend placebo failures openly; mixed results shown.

venue_quality_concern: possible (World Bank Policy Research Working Paper, not peer reviewed; some table notes contain draft artefacts such as stray '....')
notes: Nightlights treated as an output proxy under family 1 (per assignment). No GDP outcome estimated directly; GDP elasticity 0.018-0.023 is a back-of-envelope conversion using an external elasticity. Table 1 has mislabelled panels (Panel A then 'Panel C'; text says panel B) and Table 1 3G/4G TWFE col 5 is -0.0008 (ns). Table 5 title duplicates Table 6 title and its note mentions 'Low Fixed Telephone Penetration' (copy-paste). DIDpl,2 for 3G/4G shows 0.0525*** and -0.0536*** in cols 5-6 (sign inconsistency, possibly typo). Text says 'mobile broadband (3G/4G) ... 2.1 pp increase' loosely. The developing-country 'about 0.9 pp' is from text, not a printed coefficient. No instruction-like text found in the paper.

second_pass.eligibility_note: Own panel estimation (TWFE, C&D DiD, 2SLS) of mobile 2G/3G/4G coverage; 106-120 countries (>=10) with explicit developing vs developed income-group comparison. Outcome is district nightlight growth, which the paper uses as a proxy for local economic activity (Henderson et al. 2011, 2012). Reading it as a family-1 output proxy is acceptable: nightlights are a standard, validated proxy for subnational activity, and the paper itself says it measures activity, not GDP. Two caveats: lights can also capture electrification or lighting rather than value added, and the GDP elasticity of 0.018-0.023 is an external back-of-envelope conversion (0.3 from Henderson et al.), not an estimate. Eligibility holds; the nightlight outcome should be flagged as a proxy.

sample_corrections.n_economies: Record is correct: abstract/intro say 120 countries (p.1, p.3); Table 1 col 1 has 119, main IV tables 106 (105 for 2G, 86 for 3G/4G); Table 6 has 104/103/85. 'over 34,000 districts' confirmed (34,387 in Table 1 col 1).
sample_corrections.years: Record correct: 2G 1998-2018, 3G/4G 2006-2018 (Sec 2.1). Add: 2005 and 2010 coverage is linearly interpolated (fn 7); Table A4 robustness restricts to 1998-2013.
sample_corrections.income_groups_covered: Record correct: HIC+UMIC pooled as 'developed', LIC+LMIC pooled as 'developing' at baseline World Bank class (fn 31); no separate four-way estimates.

second_pass.problems: Estimate field of result 1 is garbled but numbers are right. Result 2 is a derived conversion, not an estimate. Result 6 'positive' overlooks the null 3G/4G TWFE in col 5. Paper has typos (Table 1 panel labels, Table 5 note copied from Table 6, 'DIDpl,2' printed twice, DIDpl,2 3G/4G shows 0.0525*** and -0.0536*** in cols 5-6, as printed). Nothing invented or mixed with another paper. Venue is a World Bank working paper (PRWP 10526, July 2023). No instruction-like text in the paper.
